articles.title: Why Is the US Stock Market Mixed Today (October 12)? Dow Jones Gains 0.4%, S&P 500 Slips 0.1% & Nasdaq Falls 0.3% as Oil Prices Surge and Fed Rate Hike Bets Weigh; Check What Investors Should Know - The Sunday Guardian
articles.summary: Why Is the US Stock Market Mixed Today (October 12)? Dow Jones Gains 0.4%, S&P 500 Slips 0.1% & Nasdaq Falls 0.3% as Oil Prices Surge and Fed Rate Hike Bets Weigh; Check What Investors Should Know  The Sunday Guardian
articles.full_text:
US Stock Market Mixed Today (October 12): The US stock market ended mixed on Monday, October 12, 2026, as rising crude oil prices, geopolitical uncertainty and concerns about inflation kept investors cautious. The Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced 0.4%, gaining around 215 points, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.1% and the Nasdaq Composite declined 0.3%, according to the Associated Press (AP).
US Stock Market Mixed Today
The mixed performance reflected a divide between sectors benefiting from higher energy prices and technology stocks facing pressure. Investors were also preparing for a busy week of corporate earnings and fresh US economic data that could influence expectations for the Federal Reserve’s next interest-rate decision.
Dow Jones Today
The Dow Jones Industrial Average outperformed the other major US stock indexes on Monday, rising 0.4%, or approximately 215 points. Gains in selected blue-chip companies helped the index advance despite uncertainty surrounding oil prices and the economic outlook.
According to Reuters, Salesforce shares were among the contributors to the Dow’s strength after an analyst upgrade, while energy stocks also benefited from higher crude prices. However, the gains were not broad enough to lift the entire market, as investors continued to assess the impact of higher energy costs on inflation and corporate earnings.
S&P 500 Today
The S&P 500 declined 0.1% as gains in energy and selected communication services stocks were offset by weakness elsewhere. The benchmark index remained close to its recent record levels, but the modest decline indicated that investors were reluctant to make aggressive bets ahead of key economic releases and quarterly earnings reports.
The broader market faced competing forces: higher oil prices supported energy companies but also raised concerns about business expenses, household spending and the possibility that inflation could remain elevated for longer.
Nasdaq Today
The Nasdaq Composite fell 0.3%, underperforming the Dow as technology stocks faced pressure. Higher energy costs and elevated bond yields can weigh on growth-oriented companies because they may increase operating expenses and reduce the present value investors assign to future earnings.
Investors are also watching technology companies’ earnings and spending plans, particularly as markets continue to assess the sustainability of the artificial intelligence investment boom. The Nasdaq’s decline, however, does not by itself indicate a broader collapse in technology shares.
Why Is the US Stock Market Mixed Today?
1. Oil Prices Surge Above $106 a Barrel
Rising crude oil prices were a major factor shaping Monday’s trading. Reuters reported that Brent crude futures climbed above $106 a barrel, reaching their highest levels in about two weeks amid geopolitical concerns following strikes on Riyadh’s international airport over the weekend.
The increase in oil prices supported energy shares but created uncertainty for the wider market. More expensive crude can raise transportation, manufacturing and fuel costs, potentially putting additional pressure on consumers and businesses. If these costs feed into inflation, the Federal Reserve could have less room to lower interest rates.
Oil prices remain sensitive to developments in the Middle East, particularly the conflict involving the US and Iran and the risks it poses to energy supplies and shipping routes.
2. Inflation Concerns Keep Investors Cautious
Investors are closely monitoring whether rising energy costs could reverse progress on inflation. Higher petrol, diesel and transportation prices can affect a wide range of goods and services, making the trajectory of consumer prices an important consideration for markets.
The Associated Press reported that investors are looking ahead to fresh US inflation figures and retail sales data this week. These releases could provide further clues about consumer demand and the extent to which higher energy costs are affecting the economy.
A stronger-than-expected inflation reading could reinforce concerns that interest rates may remain elevated for longer. Conversely, signs of easing price pressures could help support expectations for a less restrictive monetary policy.
3. Federal Reserve Rate Expectations Remain in Focus
The Federal Reserve’s interest-rate outlook is another important factor for Wall Street. When inflation remains persistent, policymakers may be more cautious about cutting borrowing costs. Higher interest rates can increase financing expenses for companies and households while making bonds more competitive with equities.
Reuters reported that markets were watching the upcoming inflation data and corporate earnings for clues about the economic outlook and the Fed’s next steps. Although interest-rate expectations can shift quickly as new information emerges, Monday’s mixed trading does not establish that the Fed will raise rates at its next meeting.
Investors should distinguish between market pricing, analyst expectations and an actual policy decision by the central bank.
4. Bond Market Closure Limits One Source of Trading Signals
US bond trading was closed on Monday in observance of Columbus Day. This meant investors had fewer fresh signals from Treasury yields, which have recently been an important influence on stock valuations.
Bond yields matter because they affect borrowing costs and the returns available from fixed-income investments. When yields rise, some investors may become less willing to pay high valuations for stocks, particularly companies whose expected profits lie further in the future.
With the bond market closed, investors had to assess other indicators, including oil prices, company-specific developments and expectations for the week’s economic releases.
What Economic Data and Earnings Should Investors Watch This Week?
The market’s attention is turning to two major developments: inflation data and the start of another round of corporate earnings reports.
Investors are expected to monitor consumer and producer price figures, retail sales and other economic indicators for signs of whether inflation is easing and whether consumer spending remains resilient. The data could influence expectations for interest rates and the outlook for corporate profitability.
Major US banks, including JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup and Wells Fargo, are scheduled to report quarterly results. Their earnings and commentary could provide insight into lending activity, consumer finances, investment banking and the broader health of the US economy.
Technology and other large-cap companies will also remain in focus as investors assess revenue growth, profit margins and spending on artificial intelligence. Strong results could support stocks, while weaker guidance or higher costs could add to volatility.
US Stock Market Today: What Should Investors Know?
Monday’s trading shows that the major US indexes can move in different directions when investors are balancing energy-sector gains against concerns about inflation, interest rates and technology valuations. The Dow’s advance does not mean the entire market rallied, just as the S&P 500 and Nasdaq declines do not necessarily signal a broad market sell-off. The relatively modest percentage changes suggest a mixed session rather than a decisive market move.
Investors should watch the incoming inflation data, earnings announcements, oil prices and changes in Treasury yields for clearer signals about the market’s next direction. Individual stocks may also react differently depending on their exposure to energy costs, interest rates and consumer demand.

articles.title: Fed minutes: Another rate hike likely coming this year to combat persistent inflation - ABC11 News
articles.summary: Fed minutes: Another rate hike likely coming this year to combat persistent inflation  ABC11 News
articles.full_text:
Federal Reserve officials are expecting another interest rate increase in 2026.
WASHINGTON, D.C. -- Most Federal Reserve officials expect that another interest rate increase will likely be needed this year to combat inflation, according to minutes released Wednesday from the central bank’s most recent meeting.
The officials unanimously agreed that inflation was still elevated and had not made much progress toward their 2% target in recent months, the minutes said. The Fed increased its key interest rate at the Sept. 15-16 meeting by a quarter-point to about 3.9%, its first increase in three years.
The increase defied President Donald Trump’s repeated calls for the Fed to cut rates and prompted the president to criticize the Fed’s rate-setting committee, though he still expressed support for Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom he appointed earlier this year. The rate increase comes as Americans are already struggling with high costs for groceries, gas, and housing, and as affordability has taken on a leading role in the upcoming midterm elections, just seven weeks away.
Longer-term interest rates for mortgages and other borrowing have also jumped in the past few months for a range of reasons, including rising government debt, heavy borrowing by tech firms to finance data center construction, climbing oil and gas prices, and signs that growth and inflation remain elevated. The Fed’s rate hike has likely played only a limited role in the increase.
Still, key policymakers have said since the meeting that the Fed can take some time to monitor the economy and the impact of last month’s rate hike before making another move. Wall Street investors now forecast the Fed will keep its rate unchanged at its next meeting Oct. 28-29, according to futures pricing, and raise it when they meet in December.
Philip Jefferson, vice chair of the Fed’s board of governors, said last week that policymakers “will need to come to our own judgment, which may take more time.”
Inflation, according to the Fed’s preferred measure, came in lower than many economists expected in August but remained elevated. Overall prices rose 3.4% compared with a year earlier, while core prices — which exclude volatile food and energy categories — increased 3%. On a monthly basis, prices rose 0.3% from July to August, and core prices just 0.2%.
According to the minutes, even with the rise in longer-term rates, many officials said that financial conditions—which includes rising stock prices — “appeared to be supportive of economic growth,” a sign that more rate hikes may be needed to cool the economy.
Several policymakers said that they saw the Fed’s rate as too low to restrain the economy, or only acting as a mild restraint. That suggests they would support multiple rate hikes to rein in inflation.
Higher oil and gas prices stemming from the Iran war and the lingering effects of tariffs have lifted costs in recent months. But even excluding those trends, many Fed officials believe inflation is stuck between 2.5% and 3%, above its target. Spiking prices for semiconductors, computer equipment, and electrical components due to the rapid surge in data center construction have also played a big role in accelerating inflation.
The Fed lifted its key interest rate to about 3.9% at its Sept. 15-16 meeting, its first increase in three years. Higher rates are intended to slow borrowing and spending, cool the economy, and bring down inflation.
Warsh emphasized after the announcement that the economy has shown signs of gathering speed since the central bank decided to keep rates unchanged in late July.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh said at a news conference after last month’s meeting. “We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective clearly and at sufficient speed. Today the FOMC decided that this standard has not been satisfied,” he added, referring to the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee, an arm of the Fed.
Trump criticized the committee for voting to raise rates, calling them “very political,” but he did not single out Warsh.
“They’re raising rates to make Trump do as bad as they can possibly do,” the president said.

articles.title: Gold prices struggle to hold early gains as U.S. dollar nears 18-month high, bond yields remain elevated - Kitco AM Report - Kitco
articles.summary: Gold prices struggle to hold early gains as U.S. dollar nears 18-month high, bond yields remain elevated - Kitco AM Report  KitcoGold, silver soften as markets price in December Fed hike risk - Kitco PM Report  KitcoGold eases on strong dollar, oil prices; US inflation data eyed  ReutersGold steady as markets strap in for inflation data  ET RetailGold Falls as Markets Focus on U.S. Data  WSJ
articles.full_text:
(Kitco NewsWire) – The gold market is struggling to maintain its recent recovery as persistent inflation pressures, elevated bond yields and a U.S. dollar trading near an 18-month high continue to create significant headwinds for the precious metal ahead of another critical week of economic data.
Gold prices started the week with modest gains, briefly trading above $4,200 an ounce during the Asian session; however, bullish momentum has faded as investors remain reluctant to take significant positions ahead of Wednesday's U.S. Consumer Price Index report.
Spot gold was last quoted around $4,156.20 an ounce ahead of the North American trading session, down nearly 1% on the day. The precious metal has been unable to build on last week's recovery after prices briefly fell below $4,100 an ounce. Despite the recent buying momentum, gold remains well below its August highs as investors continue to assess the implications of tighter monetary policy and stubborn inflation.
Silver is also struggling to maintain its recovery, with prices trading around $60.35 an ounce after briefly pushing above $61 earlier in the session.
The latest U.S. economic data continues to paint a complicated picture for financial markets as weakening consumer confidence contrasts with persistently elevated inflation expectations.
On Friday, the University of Michigan reported that its preliminary consumer sentiment index fell to 46.3 in October, down from 48.1 in September and below expectations of 47.6. The current economic conditions index dropped sharply to 44.7, its lowest reading on record.
At the same time, consumers' one-year inflation expectations increased to 4.7%, up from 4.6%, while longer-term expectations rose to 3.5% from 3.4%.
The disappointing sentiment data follows September's weaker-than-expected employment report, which showed that the U.S. economy created only 29,000 jobs, while the unemployment rate increased to 4.2%. Although signs of slowing economic growth would normally support expectations for looser monetary policy, persistent inflation pressures continue to complicate the Federal Reserve's outlook.
Market positioning remains tilted toward further monetary tightening, with interest rate futures reflecting roughly an 85% probability of at least one additional rate hike by December. Investors see only about a 17% chance of a rate increase at the October meeting. The divergence between slowing employment growth and elevated inflation expectations is keeping Treasury yields and the U.S. dollar supported, limiting gold's ability to sustain its recent recovery.
The U.S. dollar remains a significant obstacle for the precious metal, with the U.S. Dollar Index holding near 102.20, close to its highest level in approximately 18 months. (Kitco Global Index shows how much of today's gold move is the dollar versus the gold market itself.)
Simon-Peter Massabni, Head of Business Development at XS.com, said that the dollar continues to benefit from the combination of persistent energy inflation, geopolitical uncertainty and elevated U.S. Treasury yields.
Massabni added that persistent inflation pressures are preventing central banks from easing monetary policy and forcing fixed-income markets to adjust to expectations for higher interest rates.
Although the dollar's strength is weighing on gold, analysts note that the precious metal continues to attract safe-haven interest as investors navigate deteriorating economic conditions and growing geopolitical uncertainty.
The ongoing conflict between the United States and Iran remains a significant source of uncertainty, particularly as negotiations to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have failed to produce a lasting resolution. Iranian officials have rejected U.S. proposals as inadequate, while renewed attacks on Saudi Arabian infrastructure and continued military deployments have raised concerns about further regional escalation. Although oil prices have eased following President Donald Trump's announcement of a proposed energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, the risk of renewed disruptions to Middle Eastern energy supplies remains elevated. Brent crude has retreated toward $105 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate is trading above $92 a barrel. For gold, the conflict remains a double-edged sword: geopolitical uncertainty supports safe-haven demand, but higher energy prices threaten to keep inflation elevated, reinforcing expectations for tighter monetary policy.
Meanwhile, the U.S. bond market continues to present another significant challenge for gold as the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield remains well above 5%, near levels not seen in almost two decades. Although rising yields increase the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets such as gold, analysts note that the reasons behind the bond market's weakness are becoming increasingly important. With U.S. sovereign debt exceeding $40 trillion and annual interest costs surpassing $1 trillion, investors are demanding greater compensation for the risks associated with holding long-term government debt. Persistent inflation, growing borrowing requirements and concerns about the sustainability of U.S. fiscal policy are contributing to higher term premiums. While these developments create immediate headwinds for gold, they could also reinforce its longer-term appeal as an alternative monetary asset and portfolio diversification tool.
Massabni said that despite the current headwinds, gold is approaching an important technical and fundamental turning point.
"The key question is not simply whether gold can rebound from this area, but whether the underlying economic and fundamental conditions are strong enough to turn a potential recovery into a more sustainable bullish trend," he said.
He identified the area between $4,155 and $4,177 an ounce as an important support zone, adding that a sustained recovery will depend on whether inflation data allows Treasury yields and the U.S. dollar to lose momentum.
However, he warned that stronger-than-expected inflation could reinforce expectations for additional monetary tightening, potentially exposing gold to renewed selling pressure.
The market's next major test will come Wednesday with the release of September's Consumer Price Index. Investors will be watching whether rising energy prices are becoming embedded in broader inflation pressures, particularly core consumer prices.
A softer-than-expected inflation report could ease expectations for further Federal Reserve rate hikes, providing some relief for gold and silver. Conversely, another upside inflation surprise could push bond yields and the dollar higher, increasing the risk of renewed selling pressure across the precious metals complex.
Gold's near-term outlook remains bearish as prices continue to trade below a descending trendline and longer-term moving averages. Initial support is seen at $4,175.03 an ounce, followed by $4,141.86 and $4,103.24. A break below these levels could expose further downside toward $4,067.42. On the upside, initial resistance is seen at $4,226.82, with a sustained break above that level potentially opening the door to $4,271.57 and $4,311.17. Analysts note that gold will need to overcome its declining trendline to establish a more sustainable bullish recovery.
Meanwhile, silver's technical outlook also remains cautious as the precious metal struggles to overcome resistance from its declining trendline. Analysts are watching initial support at $59.96 an ounce, followed by $58.74 and $57.64. On the upside, initial resistance is seen at $61.72, followed by $63.06 and $65.09. A sustained move above $61.72 would be an important indication of improving bullish momentum, while a break below $59.96 could signal renewed selling pressure.
Although precious metals remain vulnerable to further near-term volatility, underlying investment demand continues to provide some support. Global gold-backed exchange-traded funds attracted approximately $10 billion in September, with holdings rising to a record 4,256 tonnes. Central bank demand also remains elevated, with official-sector purchases projected at approximately 720 tonnes this year.
With U.S. Treasury markets closed Monday for the Columbus Day holiday, trading conditions could remain relatively subdued as investors wait for fresh inflation data and further clarity on the Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook.

articles.title: What to Expect in Markets This Week: Big Bank Reports Fire Up Earnings Season; Inflation, Retail Sales Figures Land - Investopedia
articles.summary: What to Expect in Markets This Week: Big Bank Reports Fire Up Earnings Season; Inflation, Retail Sales Figures Land  InvestopediaWelcome back to earnings season: What to watch this week  Yahoo FinanceWall Street’s record-breaking trading streak set to cool  Financial TimesWall Street’s Busy Week: Bank Results, CPI and Retail Sales in Focus  Investing.com IndiaUS bank stocks near correction as earnings loom, consumer outlook in focus  The Economic...
articles.full_text:
Bank executives called consumers and companies resilient this summer. We’ll see if they still feel that way later this week.
Several major banks are slated to hand in third-quarter results in the coming days, including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup, Wells Fargo, Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs.123456 Last quarter, several financial services firms handily beat expectations. But many market watchers may tune in for the commentary—from executives like Jamie Dimon, David Solomon and others—as much as the numbers.
Bank executives this summer generally described the U.S. economy as healthy and investors and businesses as resilient. These remarks came amid enthusiasm for bank stocks. Trading volume was up, merger and acquisition activity was brisk, and the prospect of higher interest rates seemed to bode well for net interest income (NII).
Elevated interest rates tend to increase NII, the spread between what banks earn on assets and pay on deposits. A high-interest-rate environment tends to bolster bank profits, though it can also curtail borrowing. That risk may be one reason bank stocks have slumped in recent weeks.
The S&P 500 Financial Sector has fallen more than any other sector in the past month, dropping about 4%. In contrast, the sector was climbing and among the index’s top performers heading into the second quarter.
Besides hearing from banks, investors will get updates from UnitedHealth, supermarket operator Albertsons, chipmaker TSMC and shipping giant J.B. Hunt.78910 The government, meanwhile, is slated to release inflation and retail spending data.
Market Recap
Major indexes finished Friday’s session on a high note as tech shares rebounded from a sharp selloff, leaving the S&P 500 and Nasdaq near records set Tuesday. The S&P 500 logged a 1.2% gain for the week, while the Nasdaq and Dow Jones added 0.9% and 0.6%, respectively. The major indexes had pulled back Wednesday, when the yield on the 10-year Treasury note climbed to levels not seen since 2002. For more, read Friday’s market recap here.
This Week’s Top Events
Here’s a rundown of major events happening this week. TradingView publishes a more detailed calendar, but clicking the link will take you off the Investopedia site.
- Monday, Oct. 12: The bond market will be closed for Columbus Day. The stock market will remain open.
- Tuesday, Oct. 13: Domino’s Pizza (DPZ) is set to release its third-quarter results at 6:05 a.m. ET, followed by a conference call at 8:30 a.m. ET.11 The pizza delivery company beat expectations last year when it introduced stuffed crust pizza. Inflation has curbed how often low-income consumers eat at quick-service restaurants.
- Tuesday: JPMorgan Chase (JPM) is slated to release its third-quarter results at 7 a.m. ET, followed by a conference call at 8:30 a.m. ET. Every line of business posted record quarterly revenue in July, the bank said. Other financial service firms scheduled to report this week include: Wells Fargo (WFC), Citigroup (C), Bank of America (BAC), Morgan Stanley (MS) and Goldman Sachs (GS).
- Tuesday: UnitedHealth Group (UNH) is scheduled to share its third-quarter results before the market opens, and host a teleconference at 8 a.m. ET. The health care and insurance company handily beat expectations in July for the second quarter in a row. Still, UnitedHealth shares haven’t fully recovered from an early 2025 selloff. Medical device and drugmaker Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) also reports this week.12
- Tuesday: Albertsons Cos. (ACI) is set to publish its fiscal second-quarter results before the opening bell and host a conference call at 8:30 a.m. ET. Large grocers have reduced prices to appeal to inflation-weary shoppers, which could put pressure on smaller players as well as on the big companies’ own profits.
- Wednesday, Oct. 14: The Bureau of Labor Statistics is slated to publish the September Consumer Price Index reading at 8:30 a.m. ET.13 The CPI rose 3.4% year-over-year in August, as it did in July. The September reading will start to capture pricing trends in the wake of the Fed’s interest rate hike in mid-September. BLS will also update the wholesale Producer Price Index this week.
- Wednesday: The Federal Reserve is scheduled to publish its Beige Book at 2 p.m. ET.14 The central bank published the latest anecdotal-based analysis in July.
- Thursday, Oct. 15: The Census Bureau is set to release September retail data at 8:30 a.m. ET.15 Retail spending rose 1.2% from July to August.
- Thursday: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSM) is scheduled to host a call on its third-quarter results at 2 p.m. ET. The contract chipmaker reported more profit than expected last quarter, but shares fell after the print, potentially because investors envisioned greater earnings amid the AI boom. ASML Holding (ASML), which makes equipment used by chipmakers, will also report this week.16
- Thursday: J.B. Hunt Transport Services (JBHT) is slated to publish its third-quarter results after the closing bell and host a conference call at 5 p.m. ET. The shipping giant recently said elevated fuel costs could reduce earnings by 5% to 10%.
More Investopedia Reads
The lifetime cost of the American Dream has risen 4.1% over the past year to $5.3 million, Peter Gratton writes. The man who coined the term “bond vigilantes” doesn’t see investors dumping U.S. bonds en masse, Polo Rocha reports. The stock market, Crystal Kim wrote, could continue to rise even if earnings growth loses steam. And here’s how to find out whether your child has $250 in their Trump account, also from Peter.

articles.title: British Pound trades subduedly against Japanese Yen, BoE’s Greene supports quick rate hikes - FXStreet
articles.summary: British Pound trades subduedly against Japanese Yen, BoE’s Greene supports quick rate hikes  FXStreet
articles.full_text:
The British Pound (GBP) trades marginally lower against the Japanese Yen (JPY) at around 209.25 during the late Asian trade on Tuesday. The cross faces mild selling pressure even as Bank of England (BoE) policymaker Megan Greene has argued in favor that the central bank should act now to contain inflationary pressures before it gets too late and it starts spreading to wages and broad consumer prices.
So far this year, the BoE has kept interest rates steady at 3.75%. Meanwhile, market experts see the BoE raising interest rates in the November meeting on the back improved economic outlook.
Analysts at Commerzbank highlight that the UK economy has “remained relatively resilient so far this year,” noting that “following growth of 0.6% q/q in the first quarter, second-quarter GDP was revised up to 0.5% in the final release.” They add that “monthly GDP data for July, showing a 0.4% m/m increase, also point to a solid start to the third quarter,” reinforcing the picture of firmer underlying momentum.
Against this backdrop, Commerzbank argues that “the improved growth outlook should make it easier for the BoE to raise rates further in order to lean against inflation.” The bank acknowledges that “until now, we had not expected the BoE to hike rates again,” but says “recent developments… have led us to conclude that a November rate hike is now more likely than not.” Moreover, Commerzbank “do[es] not expect it to be a one-off move,” and now “anticipate[s] another hike in February, taking Bank Rate to 4.25%.”
For fresh cues regarding the UK economic strength, investors await monthly Gross Domestic Product (GDP) data for August, which is scheduled for Thursday. According to estimates, the UK economy contracted 0.1% in August after a 0.4% expansion in July.
Meanwhile, the Japanese Yen outperforms its major peers despite market experts arguing against back-to-back interest rate hikes from the Bank of Japan (BoJ).

BoJ seen shifting to inflation stabilisation but not yet ready for rapid hikes
Analysts at Rabobank argue that the Bank of Japan has reached an important inflection point, noting that “it now appears to have reached the point when it can instead shift its focus to stabilising price pressures around the target level.” However, they caution that this does not herald an aggressive tightening cycle, stressing that “even so, the Bank is still not widely viewed as being in a position in which back-to-back rate rises are appropriate.”
Central banks FAQs
Central Banks have a key mandate which is making sure that there is price stability in a country or region. Economies are constantly facing inflation or deflation when prices for certain goods and services are fluctuating. Constant rising prices for the same goods means inflation, constant lowered prices for the same goods means deflation. It is the task of the central bank to keep the demand in line by tweaking its policy rate. For the biggest central banks like the US Federal Reserve (Fed), the European Central Bank (ECB) or the Bank of England (BoE), the mandate is to keep inflation close to 2%.
A central bank has one important tool at its disposal to get inflation higher or lower, and that is by tweaking its benchmark policy rate, commonly known as interest rate. On pre-communicated moments, the central bank will issue a statement with its policy rate and provide additional reasoning on why it is either remaining or changing (cutting or hiking) it. Local banks will adjust their savings and lending rates accordingly, which in turn will make it either harder or easier for people to earn on their savings or for companies to take out loans and make investments in their businesses. When the central bank hikes interest rates substantially, this is called monetary tightening. When it is cutting its benchmark rate, it is called monetary easing.
A central bank is often politically independent. Members of the central bank policy board are passing through a series of panels and hearings before being appointed to a policy board seat. Each member in that board often has a certain conviction on how the central bank should control inflation and the subsequent monetary policy. Members that want a very loose monetary policy, with low rates and cheap lending, to boost the economy substantially while being content to see inflation slightly above 2%, are called ‘doves’. Members that rather want to see higher rates to reward savings and want to keep a lit on inflation at all time are called ‘hawks’ and will not rest until inflation is at or just below 2%.
Normally, there is a chairman or president who leads each meeting, needs to create a consensus between the hawks or doves and has his or her final say when it would come down to a vote split to avoid a 50-50 tie on whether the current policy should be adjusted. The chairman will deliver speeches which often can be followed live, where the current monetary stance and outlook is being communicated. A central bank will try to push forward its monetary policy without triggering violent swings in rates, equities, or its currency. All members of the central bank will channel their stance toward the markets in advance of a policy meeting event. A few days before a policy meeting takes place until the new policy has been communicated, members are forbidden to talk publicly. This is called the blackout period.
Author
Sagar Dua is associated with the financial markets from his college days. Along with pursuing post-graduation in Commerce in 2014, he started his markets training with chart analysis.

The two-year JGB yield, which is particularly sensitive to expectations for BOJ interest rates, rose 1 basis point to 1.915%, while the five-year yield climbed 1.5 basis points to 2.350%, Reuters reported.
Read more: US stocks: Nasdaq ends lower as oil prices surge ahead of earnings, economic data
At the longer end of the curve, the 30-year JGB yield fell 1 basis point to 4.045%, extending its decline for a fourth consecutive session. The 20-year and 40-year yields were unchanged. The benchmark 10-year yield held steady at 3.01%.
Global bond markets offered limited direction, with US Treasury markets closed on Monday for the Columbus Day holiday. Eurozone bond yields edged lower amid mixed energy prices and contained geopolitical risks.

articles.title: CPI Forecasts Show Moderated Inflation in September, Keeping the Fed on Hold - Morningstar
articles.summary: CPI Forecasts Show Moderated Inflation in September, Keeping the Fed on Hold  Morningstar
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways
- Wednesday’s CPI report is expected to show that core inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, continued to slow last month despite accelerating overall inflation, driven by surging energy prices.
- Economists are watching for signs of surging diesel prices rippling through supply chains, which would mean upward pressure on goods and services prices.
- Markets expect the Fed to leave interest rates unchanged later this month, but Bank of America economists warn a hot inflation print could revive rate hike speculation.
Economists predict Wednesday’s Consumer Price Index report will show key inflation metrics continued to moderate in September, giving Federal Reserve officials breathing room to advocate for a patient approach to future rate hikes.
Wednesday’s report comes as investors attempt to predict the Fed’s next move. Last month, the Federal Open Market Committee, citing stubbornly high inflation and a stable labor market, raised interest rates by a quarter point and penciled in at least one more hike. Officials are focused on reigning in rising prices, and this week’s CPI and Producer Price Index data will be the last inflation readings they get before their next meeting in late October.
For September, economists expect CPI to increase 0.5% after rising 0.4% in August, according to FactSet. Elevated energy prices are expected to drive the year-over-year inflation rate to 3.6% from 3.4% in August. Core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, is seen rising 0.2% in September, a slowdown from August’s 0.3%. The annual core inflation rate is expected to hold steady at 2.4%.
“You’ve seen supply shocks create a sticky situation,” says Jeffrey Schulze, head investment strategist at the Franklin Templeton Institute, referring to oil supply disruptions in the Middle East, AI-related electronics shortages, and tariff shocks. “But as we move toward 2027, some of these risks are going to start to moderate,” he says. That moderation may already be underway. “I think you see softening across the board [in September].”
September CPI Inflation Report Highlights
- CPI report date and time: Wednesday, Oct. 15, 2026, at 8:30 a.m. EDT.
- CPI is forecast to increase 0.5% in September after rising 0.4% in August.
- Core CPI is expected to rise 0.2% over the month after increasing 0.3% in August.
- CPI is predicted to rise 3.6% year over year after posting a 3.4% increase in August.
- Core CPI is forecast to increase 2.4% over the year, unchanged from August’s rate.
Core Inflation Seen Continuing to Moderate
Though high energy prices are expected to keep overall inflation elevated, economists expect prices to cool under the surface.
Policymakers have been watching core prices closely for evidence businesses are passing higher oil and diesel prices along to consumers rather than absorbing them at the expense of margins. Economists say the oil price shock’s second-order effects are most visible in airfares, which rose more than 2% in both July and August. But they haven’t seen much pass-through in other categories this year, and they don’t believe last month was any different. “I think that’s going to be something that potentially shows up closer toward the end of the year, rather than in the September release,” says Franklin Templeton’s Schulze.
Officials have been eyeing the AI data center buildout for the same reason. Surging demand for semiconductors, networking equipment, and other data center hardware has driven up prices on consumer and industrial electronics. In their September meeting, policymakers judged that AI-related price pressures were increasing and blunting some of the benefits of waning tariff-related pressures.
“Second-round inflation effects from higher energy prices and AI-related demand should remain relatively contained,” wrote Bank of America economists in a recent note. But they warned that “risks appear modestly skewed to the upside,” and could result in a second consecutive 0.3% month-over-month increase in core prices.
While oil and AI spending threaten to aggravate core inflation, many economists and officials are confident that wages are not currently a source of inflation pressure. Some officials last month described wage growth as “moderate and consistent with inflation moving toward 2%.” That assessment was supported by September’s jobs report, which showed job gains and wage growth were weaker than expected. According to Schulze, the report “suggests demand-driven inflation through the labor market is not problematic from the Fed’s vantage point.”
What the September CPI Report Could Mean for the Fed
Wednesday’s inflation data will loom large over the Fed’s deliberations when officials meet again on Oct. 27 and 28. Last month, policymakers voted unanimously to raise rates for the first time since 2023. Chair Kevin Warsh indicated that stubborn inflation was the main factor in that decision.
Policymakers signaled to markets that September’s hike likely would not be a one-off. In their quarterly Summary of Economic Projections, most officials predicted raising rates by another quarter point before the end of the year. A few signaled they were open to hiking by half a point, and two indicated they were comfortable leaving rates unchanged for the rest of 2026.
Investors immediately priced in additional increases after the Fed’s September hike, but the market’s confidence in that call was shaken by dovish remarks from several officials and September’s soft jobs report, which economists say gives the central bank room to be patient. As of Monday, investors saw a 22% chance of an October hike, down from 55% immediately following the Fed’s September rate call.
“I think that the Fed stays on hold [in October], barring an upside surprise that’s meaningfully more than consensus is expecting,” says Franklin Templeton’s Schulze.
BofA economists say a hot core inflation reading “would likely revive speculation that the Fed may need to continue its tightening cycle” this month. That speculation could nudge Treasury yields (already hovering near multidecade highs) even higher and weigh on equities.

articles.title: The Federal Reserve is preparing for a rate hike cycle, along with the rest of the world - Cryptopolitan
articles.summary: The Federal Reserve is preparing for a rate hike cycle, along with the rest of the world  Cryptopolitan
articles.full_text:
- The Federal Reserve is preparing for another rate hike as global central banks tighten monetary policy.
- 54 central banks have raised interest rates in 2026, with 45% of major banks hiking over the past six months.
- Beth Hammack supports smaller, faster rate increases to bring inflation back to the Fed’s 2% target.
The Federal Reserve is preparing for another round of interest rate hikes, and central banks worldwide are moving in the same direction. Inflation is still causing problems, borrowing costs remain painful, and policymakers are increasingly convinced that keeping money expensive might be necessary. Anyone hoping interest rates would quickly return to pre-pandemic levels might want to reconsider.
Among the 33 major central banks, 15 have raised their interest rates within the last six months. This amounts to 45%, which is the largest percentage share since 2023 and is almost reaching 55% that was seen in 2011 and 2018.
In 2022, almost 95% had been tightening their monetary policies after using stimulus packages amid the pandemic, which pushed inflation globally. In 2026, 54 central banks have so far raised their interest rates. Among these three months, there have been more rate hikes than cuts since September 2023.
Federal Reserve officials aren’t finished fighting inflation
Cleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack believes the central bank should act before inflation becomes an even bigger headache.
Beth, speaking Monday at the annual National Association of Business Economists meeting, said policymakers would be better off taking small steps rather than waiting until they have to take drastic steps. She said:
“When feasible, I generally think it’s preferable to make smaller adjustments, and to do so relatively quickly, rather than to wait and risk needing a larger course correction.”
Beth is a voting member of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), which makes her position particularly relevant as officials prepare for their remaining meetings this year.
“Considering all the inputs that factor into my reaction function, a restrictive monetary policy stance is appropriate to ensure a timely return to 2 percent inflation.”
This issue lies in the fact that pressures on prices go beyond just a few items. These pressures are throughout the economy and make it more difficult for the Fed to hit its 2% inflation rate target.
Another concern from Beth is regarding the scenario where Americans start viewing high inflation as a permanent fixture of their life. This could lead to expectations by both businesses and individuals affecting wages, spending, and prices.
“Long-run inflation expectations have stayed remarkably well anchored despite actual inflation being above target for more than five years. But I’m not taking that for granted. With each passing month, persistently elevated inflation raises the risks of an inflationary mindset becoming entrenched in the economy.”
The Fed already raised rates in September, its first increase in three years. Chair Kevin Warsh said the decision would “support a timelier return” to the central bank’s inflation objective.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long.”
September’s meeting minutes revealed that most policymakers anticipated another hike before December ends. However, they left the timing open, with future decisions depending on economic conditions rather than a predetermined schedule.
The U.S. economy is making the Federal Reserve’s job complicated
Recent economic figures show exactly why the Fed has a difficult decision ahead.
August personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index was recorded at 3.4% annually, while core inflation, excluding both food and energy, stood at 3%.
Alternatively, another view on the August data stated that both the headline PCE rate and the core rate were at 3% levels each matching July’s data and underestimating forecasts.
However, U.S. second-quarter GDP growth was upgraded from 1.5% to 2.2%, meaning that the economy was performing better than initially thought.
On the other hand, the labor market looks much weaker. The monthly change in payrolls in September was at only 29,000, being the weakest month of 2026.
As a result, policymakers face a dilemma. Raising rates will help curb inflation, however, the further hike will hurt the labor market.
Markets now do not see a rate hike in October. According to CME FedWatch estimates there is greater than 78% chance of no changes, while another estimate comes at 81%, which exceeds approximately 54% a month earlier.
In December markets see a chance of a rate hike at more than 88%. Borrowers and businesses now face the prospect of financing costs remaining elevated as the Fed considers further tightening and other central banks increasingly abandon rate cuts.

articles.title: Bitcoin price prediction: Why BTC USD can drop before a Fed rate hike and rally after - The Economic Times
articles.summary: Bitcoin price prediction: Why BTC USD can drop before a Fed rate hike and rally after  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
Listen to this article in summarized format
The seemingly conflicting move is a reflection of how markets react to expectations. Often investors are moving before an official announcement. Meaning some of the expected impact may already be reflected in prices by the time the decision arrives.
Why Rising Interest Rates Could Weigh on Bitcoin (BTC USD)
Bitcoin does not give any interest or dividends. It relies on its price rising to make a return on it which can make it less attractive when traditional investments give a higher yield
Treasury bonds, savings accounts and certificates of deposit can provide interest income. When interest rates rise, these alternatives can become more appealing to investors weighing where to put their money.
Bitcoin has also tended to behave like a risk-sensitive asset rather than a dependable hedge against market turmoil. Former Federal Reserve Vice Chair Lael Brainard discussed the correlation between crypto assets, riskier stocks and broader investor risk appetite in a speech on cryptocurrency and financial stability, as per MoneyLion report.
Why Bitcoin Rebounded After the Fed’s September Rate Hike
BTC USD came under pressure in September as traders anticipated a rate increase. On September 16, the Federal Reserve raised its target interest rate range by a quarter of a percentage point, marking its first increase in more than three years.
The explanation was that much of the expected negative news had already been reflected in prices, while the rate increase was not more aggressive than anticipated. Attention then shifted to the Fed’s next moves.
The central bank’s September projections pointed to only limited additional rate increases, easing concerns about a prolonged series of aggressive hikes. Bitcoin subsequently staged a relief rally.
How Cooler Inflation Helped Bitcoin Rise in July
A similar pattern emerged in July, when some market participants were preparing for a possible rate hike but inflation came in cooler than expected.
Bitcoin increased about 3.6% on July 15, as per CoinDesk. The softer inflation reading reduced concerns about further rate increases, giving risk sensitive assets more room to recover.
The July and September episodes had different immediate triggers but both illustrated how expectations about monetary policy can influence Bitcoin before the outlook becomes clearer.
Fed Policy Is Not the Only Factor Affecting Bitcoin
Interest rates are an important influence on BTC but they are not the only factor moving its price, supply and demand, geopolitical developments, exchange-traded fund flows, regulation and cryptocurrency specific news can also affect market movements.
So this makes it difficult to predict BTC's direction based on a single Federal Reserve announcement. Even when rates rise the cryptocurrency can recover if investors have already accounted for the decision and become less concerned about what comes next.
Bitcoin’s reaction to the Fed highlights the importance of expectations. A rate hike can put pressure on the cryptocurrency before the announcement, while the decision itself can trigger a rebound if it proves less worrying than investors had anticipated.

articles.title: Cleveland Fed's Beth Hammack backs smaller, more frequent rate hikes - Quartz
articles.summary: Cleveland Fed's Beth Hammack backs smaller, more frequent rate hikes  Quartz
articles.full_text:
Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack said Monday that she favors making smaller, more frequent adjustments to interest rates rather than delaying action and potentially requiring a larger move later.
“When feasible, I generally think it’s preferable to make smaller adjustments, and to do so relatively quickly, rather than to wait and risk needing a larger course correction,” Hammack said in a speech at the National Association for Business Economics annual meeting in Cleveland.
Hammack, who votes on policy decisions this year, said she views inflation pressures as relatively broad-based rather than concentrated in any single component of the economy. A restrictive monetary policy stance is appropriate to ensure inflation returns to the Fed's 2% target in a timely fashion, she said.
Much of the speech centered on the value of transparency, with Hammack arguing that officials should articulate the logic behind their decisions — a so-called "reaction function" — while stopping short of offering "firm predictions" about where rates are headed. "I want to draw a sharp line here. A reaction function is not forward guidance," Hammack said, according to Bloomberg. "Treating the two as interchangeable can turn a well-meaning explanation of logic into the expectations of a promise."
Hammack also said that with each passing month, persistently elevated inflation raises the risk of an inflationary mindset becoming entrenched in the economy. She stopped short of backing a rate increase at the Fed’s Oct. 27-28 meeting, according to Bloomberg.
Hammack's preference for steady, incremental tightening reflects a position she has held for months. She argued in August that more than one rate increase would likely be needed to bring inflation back under control and that interest rates at the time were not placing meaningful restraint on the economy. She dissented at the Fed's July meeting, when the committee voted 9-3 to hold rates steady, preferring a quarter-point increase alongside Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan.
The Fed ultimately raised its benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point in September, a unanimous 12-0 decision that brought the federal funds rate to a target range of 3.75%–4%. The decision reflected a shared view among Fed officials that rising prices — fueled by the Iran war and surging demand connected to artificial intelligence buildout — required a policy response, according to Bloomberg. Sixteen of 18 meeting participants at that time projected at least one additional rate increase.

articles.title: Are Fed officials changing their tone ahead of October’s FOMC meeting? Here’s what they’re saying - Chase Bank
articles.summary: Are Fed officials changing their tone ahead of October’s FOMC meeting? Here’s what they’re saying  Chase Bank
articles.full_text: Compared to the June dot plot, September reinforced a higher-for-longer message, with the median projected policy path moving toward higher rates across the next several years. The more telling change, however, was how many officials moved into higher-rate territory with their individual projections: The number of officials projecting rates at 4% or higher by year-end 2027 rose to 14 in September, from three in June.

articles.title: Colombian Peso Slides 2.9% as Hawkish Fed Lifts the Dollar and Central Bank Surprises With a Hike - Finance Colombia
articles.summary: Colombian Peso Slides 2.9% as Hawkish Fed Lifts the Dollar and Central Bank Surprises With a Hike  Finance Colombia
articles.full_text:
Carry Trade and IMF Talks May Cap a Dollar-Driven Peso Sell-off
The Colombian peso weakened 2.9% against the US dollar in September 2026, closing the month at 3,307.50 COP per dollar, 92.50 COP above its August close, according to the Monthly Foreign Exchange Market Report published October 6 by Bancolombia‘s Economic, Industry & Market Research Area. Bancolombia is the Colombian banking subsidiary of Grupo Cibest (NYSE: CIB; BVC: CIBEST, PFCIBEST), the holding company formed in 2025. The report, signed by Manuela Bernal, regional analyst; José Luis Mojica, macroeconomic manager; and Laura Clavijo, chief economist, attributed most of the depreciation to a more hawkish stance from the US Federal Reserve, which strengthened the dollar against most of the world’s currencies. The peso’s losses were concentrated in the second half of the month.
September extended a reversal that began in late August. The peso surged 7.5% in July, then weakened 1.8% in August to close at 3,215 COP after the government of President Abelardo de la Espriella disclosed a sharply wider fiscal deficit in its 2027 National Budget. In September, the exchange rate’s lowest daily close was 3,085 COP, in the first half of the month, and its highest was 3,362 COP, in the final week, according to closing-rate data in the report.
A Rate Increase in Washington and a Stronger Dollar
At its September 16 meeting, the Federal Reserve raised the target range for the federal funds rate by a quarter percentage point to 3.75% to 4.00%, in a 12-0 vote, its first increase since July 2023, as Finance Colombia reported after the decision. The Federal Open Market Committee said in its statement: “Inflation remains elevated. Today’s policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2 percent goal.” The statement also cited geopolitical developments as a source of elevated uncertainty, and Bancolombia’s analysts tied the persistence of US inflation to the conflict in the Middle East. The report also cited revised US data. First-quarter growth was revised up from 2.1% to 2.5% at a seasonally adjusted annual rate and second-quarter growth from 1.5% to 2.2%, while the September Composite PMI came in at 58.4, its strongest reading since July 2021. As a result, the probability of another 25-basis-point Fed increase in October rose above 70%, the report said.
The US Dollar Index (DXY), which tracks the dollar against a basket of major currencies, gained 2.0% in September. In Bancolombia’s comparison of selected currencies, the Mexican peso depreciated 6.4% against the dollar, the Swedish krona 4.5% and the Chilean peso 4.1%. The Colombian peso’s decline measured 2.2% in that comparison, which draws on a different data source from the 2.9% figure, according to the report’s source notes, and was roughly in line with the euro and the British pound. The Brazilian real and the Japanese yen were the only currencies in the comparison to gain ground.
Lower local dollar liquidity added to the pressure, according to the report. The net spot foreign currency position of Colombia’s foreign exchange market intermediaries turned negative on September 9 for the first time this year and stood at -$634 million USD as of September 13, according to data from the Superintendencia Financiera de Colombia (Financial Superintendency of Colombia) compiled by Grupo Cibest. Bancolombia estimates the position stayed negative through the second half of the month and approached -$810 million USD, which the analysts said suggests liquidity pressures persisted.
A Split Vote at the Central Bank
On September 30, the board of the Banco de la República (Bank of the Republic), Colombia’s central bank, raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 12.25%, according to the bank’s statement. Four directors voted for the increase, two voted to hold the rate unchanged and one voted for a 50-basis-point increase. The decision ran counter to both Bancolombia’s forecast and the market consensus, which had anticipated a hold, according to the report; earlier in September, Bancolombia’s economists had expected the rate to stay at 12%. The meeting was the first rate decision in which the De la Espriella government participated, through Miguel Gómez, head of the Ministerio de Hacienda y Crédito Público (Ministry of Finance and Public Credit), Vanguardia reported. At the bank’s post-meeting press conference, Gómez explicitly backed the majority position and a continued commitment to the inflation target, according to Bancolombia.
The board’s minutes set out the three positions. The directors in the majority cited several factors, among them: “headline inflation has continued to rise, reaching levels more than twice the inflation target,” and “expectations continue unanchored from the 3% target, even over longer horizons.” The two directors who favored a hold argued that monetary policy was already highly contractionary, with an ex post real interest rate close to 6%, and they warned: “a considerable interest rate differential relative to advanced economies still encourages carry trade operations that contribute to pressure for peso appreciation.” The director who sought a larger increase argued: “waiting does not eliminate the cost but rather shifts it, and may ultimately increase it.”
Annual consumer inflation reached 6.24% in August, according to the Departamento Administrativo Nacional de Estadística (National Administrative Department of Statistics, DANE), and inflation excluding food, one of the central bank’s traditional core measures, reached 6.30%, according to Bancolombia. Analysts’ forecasts for year-end 2026 inflation cited in Bancolombia’s report have climbed to 6.77%, and expectations for 2027 stand at 5.10%, both well above the central bank’s 2% to 4% target range. After the report was published, DANE reported on October 7 that annual inflation rose to 6.29% in September, according to Portafolio.
Colombia Opens Talks With the IMF
In a presidential address on September 27, President De la Espriella said the country’s fiscal situation was the most critical in its history, Publimetro reported. He said he had instructed Gómez and the economic team to lead talks with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in search of a negotiated way out of the crisis his government inherited.
“Public finances, my fellow citizens, can’t take any more. The balance is in the red.”
— President Abelardo de la Espriella, September 27, 2026
The announcement came during a September 25-28 visit to Colombia by IMF Deputy Managing Director Nigel Clarke, who met with Vice President José Manuel Restrepo, Gómez, Banco de la República Governor Leonardo Villar and members of the central bank’s board, according to the IMF’s statement at the end of the visit. The government asked the fund to begin an assessment of the economy and of the new administration’s macroeconomic plans, Bloomberg Línea reported. Clarke wrote in a post on X: “The IMF stands ready to support Colombia and looks forward to continuing our close and constructive dialogue in the weeks ahead.” The IMF said in the statement that prompt and credible steps to narrow fiscal imbalances can bolster confidence, cut borrowing costs and improve conditions for private investment and hiring. The IMF also said a Ministry of Finance delegation would visit Washington the following week to continue the dialogue.
Bancolombia’s report noted that several former finance ministers have suggested an Extended Fund Facility or a Precautionary and Liquidity Line could be appropriate, and that Colombia could potentially access between $15 billion USD and $20 billion USD. Colombia signed a $2.7 billion USD Extended Fund Facility in 1999 and later had Stand-By Arrangements approved in 2003 and 2005, according to Bloomberg Línea. More recently, the IMF suspended Colombia’s access to its Flexible Credit Line in April 2025, and Colombia canceled the credit line in September 2025, under former President Gustavo Petro.
Ministry of Finance figures compiled by Grupo Cibest show the central government deficit at 6.4% of gross domestic product in 2025, with projections of 7.2% in 2026 and a peak of 7.9% in 2027 before narrowing to 3.7% by 2030. Colombia’s five-year credit default swap spread stood at 168 basis points at the end of September, compared with an average of 87 basis points for its regional peers, according to the report.
Oil Rises and Gold Falls
Brent crude rose 14.4% in September to close at $103.53 USD per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate ended the month at $90.42 USD per barrel, up 5.4%, according to the report. Bancolombia attributed much of the move to escalating tensions in the Middle East, including Saudi Arabia’s closure and subsequent partial reopening of the East-West pipeline following drone attacks originating from Iraq. The report also cited a late-month announcement of a potential ban on US diesel exports intended to contain domestic fuel prices, which it said placed further pressure on international fuel markets. Gold fell about 6.0% as rising US Treasury yields reduced the appeal of non-yielding assets, the report said.
The October Outlook
Bancolombia expects the exchange rate to trade between 3,190 COP and 3,390 COP in October, against a backdrop of dollar strength, fiscal adjustment announcements and negotiations with the IMF. The bank sees a risk of a weaker peso from further global dollar strengthening, citing a US economy that has proven more resilient than expected and Fed officials’ growing concern about inflation, and it expects both the DXY and Treasury yields to remain elevated during the month. On the technical side, the exchange rate broke above its 50-day moving average in mid-September and reached its 100-day moving average (3,348 COP at month-end) before retreating, leaving that level as key short-term resistance, according to the report. A death cross, with the 50-day average below both the 100-day and 200-day averages, remains in place

articles.title: Gradual Interest Rate Tweaks Preferred to Keep Inflation in Check, Fed’s Hammack Says - TradingView
articles.summary: Gradual Interest Rate Tweaks Preferred to Keep Inflation in Check, Fed’s Hammack Says  TradingView
articles.full_text:
- Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack favored smaller, more frequent rate adjustments over delaying action and risking sharp policy swings.
- Hammack highlighted price pressures beyond energy, citing elevated tariffs and higher electricity and component demand driven by artificial intelligence expansion.
- She distinguished between explaining the Fed's decision-making logic and providing "forward guidance," cautioning against giving the market rigid interest rate forecasts.
Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack said Monday that prompt, incremental policy shifts are preferable to waiting and forcing larger corrections later, as policymakers seek to keep inflation expectations grounded.
Speaking at the National Association for Business Economics annual gathering in Cleveland, Hammack noted that minor, agile policy shifts can maintain stability, though she did not explicitly support a benchmark rate increase at the upcoming Fed meeting.
Widening Inflationary Pressures
The Federal Open Market Committee unanimously agreed last month to raise borrowing costs to tame price hikes driven by conflict in Iran and booming demand linked to artificial intelligence development.
Hammack, a voting member of the monetary policy committee this year, cautioned that inflationary risks extend well beyond energy markets. She cited supply chain pressures tied to tariffs, as well as rising demand for energy and tech components needed for AI infrastructure build-outs.
Policymakers are set to meet Oct. 27–28. Hammack noted that officials still need to review crucial economic data ahead of the gathering, including the latest consumer price index figures scheduled for release Wednesday. Financial markets recently trimmed expectations for an October rate hike after key Fed officials signaled limited urgency to execute back-to-back increases.
Communication And Market Guidance
Focusing heavily on central bank communications, Hammack underscored the value of explaining the Fed’s "reaction function"—the data points and economic rationale behind interest rate choices—to help consumers, businesses, and investors plan effectively.
However, she warned against making firm predictions about where monetary policy is headed, drawing a clear line between explaining policy logic and offering explicit forward guidance.
"Treating the two as interchangeable can turn a well-meaning explanation of logic into the expectations of a promise," Hammack warned.
Her comments come as Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, appointed earlier this year by President Donald Trump, has deliberately scaled back public remarks on monetary policy to prevent financial markets from relying excessively on central bank guidance.
The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) edged 0.2% lower at the time of writing, the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (DIA) gained 0.3%, and the Nasdaq-100 tracking Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) slipped as much as 0.8%. Retail sentiment around QQQ on Stocktwits dropped to ‘bullish’ from ‘extremely bullish’ over the past day.

articles.summary: FX Daily: Dollar holds gains as geopolitics heats up  ing thinkDollar holds 18-month high as Gulf tension, US inflation keep investors on edge  ReutersUS dollar strength masks growing disconnect with Treasury yields  FOREX.comU.S. dollar rises, holding near 18-month high as oil prices climb, euro weakens  Investing.comDollar holds near 18-month high as geopolitical risks rise  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
News over the weekend of continued Houthi strikes in Riyadh and a supposed 'energy ceasefire' between Russia and Ukraine have had little meaningful impact on FX markets so far. The dollar remains well bid, and what could be a hot US September CPI this week will keep expectations of Fed tightening and a stronger dollar in play
USD: Geopolitics to keep the dollar supported
FX markets have been reasonably quiet at the start of the new week, barring a jump in the Indian rupee on some defensive measures instituted by the Reserve Bank of India. Energy prices do not quite know what to make of weekend developments, where Houthi strikes against Saudi Arabia have escalated local tensions, while at the same time US President Donald Trump has tried to present an 'energy ceasefire' between Russia and Ukraine. On the latter, Russia has yet to respond to the invite and continues to target energy infrastructure in Ukraine.
Instead, FX markets are preferring to concentrate on the cyclical story of decent US growth, above-target inflation and the prospect of the Federal Reserve hiking 75bp from current levels. Barring a big fall in energy prices this week, which seems unlikely, Wednesday's release of September US CPI inflation looks set to keep those Fed tightening expectations broadly intact. Our team see upside risks to the consensus of 0.2% month-on-month on the core reading. And as James Smith discusses in his weekly column, it may not be until next spring when tightening expectations can drop out of money markets. This points to the dollar staying supported by the cyclical story for a good while yet.
Other highlights this week include a new World Economic Outlook from the IMF and the US 3Q earnings season kicking off tomorrow when bulge bracket banks release.
With US bond markets closed for the Columbus Day public holiday, it should be a quiet day for FX markets. But DXY consolidation above 102 looks bullish, and our preference would be for a push up to 102.85 this week.
Chris Turner
EUR: Little reprieve for the euro
EUR/USD is consolidating near 1.12, and support remains fragile. French debt spreads remain near their widest, with Marine Le Pen's counter-budget proposal last week raising more questions than it answered. In theory, the French government's budget proposal of €43bn in new savings will be debated in parliament this week. Consensus seems to expect that this will make little progress, but that the government might ultimately be able to pass this budget by decree. Here, protagonists in parliament might avoid trying to bring down the government, which would make the French debt crisis worse than it already is. This is hardly a euro positive, however.
Speculators and the FX options market remain quite bearish on EUR/USD currently, although positioning is starting to get a little stretched. But barring a big US policy misstep, which again questions investors' long dollar exposure, the macro story remains EUR/USD bearish. For the near term, a further dip towards 1.1100/1120 looks more likely.
Chris Turner
CHF: Caught between higher rates and France
EUR/CHF is consolidating after its heavy fall just over a week ago. That move was driven by French debt problems being severe enough to curtail European Central Bank tightening expectations. However, it is not clear that short-dated euro rates need to fall a lot further from here, unless we see a sharp drop in energy prices. Currently, the market prices 22bp of hikes in December (we look for a 25bp hike) and then a further 30-40bp of tightening into next year. With eurozone inflation still pushing higher (September eurozone CPI should be confirmed at 3.8% year-on-year this week), it seems too early to expect 2027 hikes from the ECB to be cancelled.
This all adds up to a mixed picture for EUR/CHF. We cannot rule out a correction to the 0.9230/50 area should the OAT-Bund spread decisively push through the 150bp area, but any brief periods of calm can see EUR/CHF trade back up to 0.9350/9400.
Chris Turner
CEE: Inflation tests meet global FX headwinds
This week’s focus is on regional inflation releases and speakers. Romania’s September inflation is due tomorrow; we expect it to rise from 6.2% to 6.4% and, consistent with the central bank’s guidance last week, increase further through year-end. In the Czech Republic, final data should confirm September inflation at 2.5%, while Czech National Bank core inflation is likely to edge up from 3.0% to 3.1-3.2%, above the central bank’s forecast. Poland’s headline inflation should be confirmed at 4.0% on Wednesday, followed by a likely drop in core inflation from 3.3% to 3.1% on Thursday, giving the National Bank of Poland more room to manoeuvre. Hungary releases wage data on Friday; wage growth remains high relative to the region and continues to pose inflationary risks.
Beyond the data calendar, attention will turn to the IMF meetings in Bangkok, where CEE officials are expected to speak. Hungary may publish next year’s draft budget and medium-term fiscal outlook late in the week. Market expectations have moved from around 5.5% towards 5.0%; although this raises the bar for a positive surprise, the direction remains supportive for bonds. In Romania, talks on forming a new government continue. Signs of progress emerged late last week and should help stabilise EUR/RON.
CEE FX remains primarily driven by global factors, and our bearish regional bias is broadly unchanged. After the NBP meeting, EUR/PLN rose into our expected 4.380-4.400 range and is likely to stay near its upper end in the coming days. The forint is awaiting the government’s 2027 budget announcement but remains exposed to higher energy prices and a stronger US dollar. The koruna remains the outlier, supported by a wider interest-rate differential. We retain a bullish koruna view and expect EUR/CZK to move towards 24.250.
Frantisek Taborsky
