articles.title: Copper at a Record, but the Tariff Trade Is Fading for COMEX_MINI:MHG1! by mintdotfinance - TradingView
articles.summary: Copper at a Record, but the Tariff Trade Is Fading for COMEX_MINI:MHG1! by mintdotfinance  TradingView
articles.full_text:
On 9 September 2026, front-month LME copper set an all-time high of $14,940 per tonne. COMEX Copper Futures followed with its own record of $6.9285 per lb on 22 September. Both have since pulled back. 
The force behind the rally was not a shortage. Traders were pricing in an expected US tariff on imported refined copper. The logic was straightforward: copper already inside the US would be worth more than copper sitting elsewhere if a tariff came, so metal was shipped to COMEX warehouses ahead of it. The gap between the two, the tariff premium, opened to several hundred dollars per tonne before collapsing.
Two events drove that collapse. On 10 September, the White House signalled that refined copper tariffs remained unresolved. COMEX fell sharply intraday. On 28 September, the White House’s deadline for a decision passed without an announcement. The market read both as the tariff not coming, at least for now.
Copper still trades near record levels. But the clearest driver of the rally has weakened. That is the tension this paper examines. 
The Inventory Shift
US copper stocks more than doubled in a year. COMEX warehouses held around 711,600 metric tonnes, as of 7 October, still near record highs. LME stocks drained to multi-year lows by August and have only partially recovered. SHFE copper inventories stand at 58,744 tonnes as of this writing, down by nearly 86% from its March peak. The world did not produce more copper. Tariff anticipation moved it from London and Shanghai into US warehouses. 
The tightness in London looked alarming. The LME cash price rose sharply above the three-month futures price, a condition called backwardation that typically signals buyers are scrambling for metal right now. However, the International Copper Study Group (ICSG) was reporting a global refined surplus the entire time. The backwardation was the mirror image of the COMEX build, not a sign that the world was running short. 
The flow has now stopped. New shipments into the US stopped making economic sense once the tariff premium narrowed. The copper already in US warehouses is unlikely to move back quickly given the cost of re-exporting it.
What the Fundamentals Show 
China accounts for more than half of global copper consumption. Demand has grown this year on grid investment, electric vehicles, and renewables, but not at a pace that explains record prices. China’s Golden Week holiday runs through the first week of October, typically followed by a burst of factory restocking. When trading resumed, the premium buyers paid to import physical copper rose, but actual deals were thin.
On the supply side, Chile is adding risk. A strike began 7 October at Antofagasta’s Centinela mine, which produced 240,400 metric tonnes last year. Two unions representing 709 workers walked out after mediation failed over a pay dispute dating to 2020. Antofagasta expects no production impact; whereas the unions warn of supply effects by November. As copper prices have risen, so have tensions between miners and management across Chile, making disruptions harder to contain.
The International Copper Study Group projects a refined surplus of around 96,000 tonnes in 2026, widening to 377,000 tonnes in 2027. Its figures exclude unreported Chinese stocks, leaving some uncertainty. The headline balance does not support a shortage narrative. Sustained inventory draws paired with spot premiums backed by actual end-user orders would change that picture. That evidence does not yet exist.
The Macro Headwind 
The Federal Reserve raised rates by 25 basis points to 3.75-4.00% on 16 September, the first hike since 2023. The hike sent the dollar higher, a direct headwind for copper. US Treasury yields are at multi-decade highs, keeping that pressure in place. 
Through August, gold and silver rallied while copper moved sideways. Gold and silver then fell sharply from their August highs, and fell further after the Fed’s rate hike. Copper rose after the hike and has held up. 
Gold and silver fell as expectations of Fed hikes rose. The war pushed oil and inflation higher, which lifted real yields (the return on bonds after inflation) and the dollar, and neither metal pays a yield. We explain this in detail in a previous paper. Copper took the dollar hit too, but tight supply outside the US, covered above, limited the decline. 
If the dollar and real yields stay elevated, copper faces growing downside pressure even as physical supply outside the US continues to tighten. 
Historical Trade Setup
8 October 2025: Teck cuts copper guidance
Early October 2025 offers a useful historical analogue for today. Chinese demand was uncertain after the Golden Week holiday and the dollar was firm, but mine disruptions kept supply concerns alive. Teck cut its 2025 copper guidance on 8 October, and the trade enters at the 9 October open.
On 10 October, copper fell as much as 5% after President Trump threatened additional tariffs on Chinese imports, and the position moved below its entry price. It recovered from 13 October as trade fears eased and mine disruptions kept supply tight. By 29 October, hopes for a US-China trade framework and the Fed’s rate cut expectations supported a bullish view, though weak Chinese buying capped the upside. The Fed was easing then and is tightening now, so this illustrates a comparable setup, not a forecast.

articles.full_text:
NEW YORK - The US dollar held near its strongest level in 18 months in early Asian trading on Monday (12 October).
According to Reuters, escalating conflict in the Middle East has made investors cautious ahead of US inflation data due this week, which could influence the Federal Reserve's (Fed) interest rate policy.
Oil prices fluctuated after Iran-backed Houthi militants stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, while two oil tankers were also targeted over the weekend.
Oil price movements were also influenced by US President Donald Trump's announcement on Sunday of an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine.
Brent crude futures fell 1% to US$103.55 per barrel in Asian trading.
The US dollar index, which measures the greenback against six major currencies, edged down to 102.14.
Nevertheless, the index remained close to the 18-month high reached last week.
Trading was range-bound as Japanese markets were closed for a national holiday, reducing liquidity across Asia.
Analysts at Commonwealth Bank of Australia expect Houthi attacks on Saudi energy assets to continue, potentially supporting higher oil prices and a stronger US dollar.
They also believe a diplomatic breakthrough is unlikely in the near term, despite Iran confirming that it had received a US peace proposal through intermediaries.
Markets turn their attention to US inflation data
Beyond geopolitical developments, investors are focusing on the US consumer price index (CPI) report, scheduled for release on Wednesday.
The data represent one of the last major economic indicators ahead of the Fed's monetary policy meeting in late October.
Data released last week showed that US consumer sentiment deteriorated again in early October.
Rising living costs resulting from the Middle East conflict further worsened households' perceptions of economic conditions.
Last month, the Fed raised interest rates for the first time since 2023 in an effort to curb inflation.
Investors are now monitoring the latest economic data to assess whether the US central bank will raise interest rates again.
According to the CME FedWatch tool, markets put the probability of the Fed holding interest rates steady this month at 81%.
That figure was up from 51% a month earlier.
Nevertheless, Barclays analysts believe the US dollar rally could pause or even undergo a short-term correction.
They said rising bond yields had tightened global financial conditions.
This could prompt Fed officials to adopt a more reassuring tone ahead of the October meeting, particularly if inflation comes in below expectations.
Heavy selling in bond markets over recent weeks has heightened investor concerns.
Borrowing costs across countries have surged to their highest levels in decades amid concerns about inflation, energy prices and rising government debt.
Euro faces pressure from French fiscal concerns
In foreign exchange markets, the euro rose nearly 0.1% to US$1.121 after declining for five consecutive weeks.
The single European currency has been weighed down by investor concerns over France's fiscal position and political uncertainty ahead of the 2027 presidential election.
OCBC foreign exchange strategists said it was too early to determine whether higher borrowing costs would force the French government to adopt stricter fiscal discipline.
They expect the euro-dollar pair (EUR/USD) to consolidate as media coverage of France's fiscal and political challenges is likely to ease.
However, the euro's potential gains are also considered limited by structural challenges facing the European economy.
Meanwhile, sterling was stable at US$1.3245. The US dollar was also little changed against the offshore Chinese yuan at 6.6927 yuan.
Against the Japanese yen, the US dollar fell 0.14% to 158.160 yen.
The Australian and New Zealand dollars were relatively stable at US$0.6988 and US$0.5614, respectively.
In cryptocurrency markets, Bitcoin rose 0.2% to US$83,788.50, while Ether gained 0.15% to US$2,540.08. (DK/LM)

Germany’s 10-year government bond yield, the euro zone benchmark, fell 2.5 basis points to 3.46%, while the two-year German yield, more sensitive to monetary policy expectations, declined 2 basis points to 3.07%.

According to Reuters, Trump announced the agreement in a post on Truth Social on Sunday, saying Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an energy-related ceasefire. The development helped ease concerns about potential disruptions to energy supplies and their implications for inflation.
Investors have also increasingly bet that tensions in the Middle East will remain contained, reducing the risk of a sharp energy price spike ahead of the November US midterm elections. Lower energy prices could help temper inflationary pressures, although uncertainty surrounding geopolitical developments continues to influence the outlook for European monetary policy, the report stated.

ECB rate expectations remain elevated
Money markets were pricing in a European Central Bank deposit rate of 2.73% by December, compared with the current rate of 2.50%. Expectations pointed to the rate reaching 3.22% by late 2027, indicating that investors continued to anticipate tighter monetary policy over the longer term.
French, Italian bond spreads narrow
Risk premiums on French and Italian government debt also eased on Monday, reflecting a modest improvement in investor sentiment.
The yield spread between French government bonds, known as OATs, and German Bunds narrowed by 1 basis point to 136.50 basis points. The spread, which measures the additional yield investors demand to hold French debt over German government bonds, had climbed to 158.67 basis points in early October, its highest level since November 2011, the report stated.
Italy’s yield spread over German Bunds stood at 109 basis points, down from 129.74 basis points reached earlier this month.
The narrowing spreads suggest some easing in pressure on French and Italian debt, although both countries’ borrowing costs remain subject to fiscal concerns, political uncertainty and broader movements in euro zone bond markets.
Investors will continue to monitor geopolitical developments, energy prices and central bank rate expectations for clues about the direction of European government bond yields in the coming weeks, the report stated.

TradingKey - During the week of October 5 to October 11, 2026, the U.S. macroeconomic environment was defined by persistent inflation pressures, rising long-term Treasury yields, and a complex monetary policy outlook. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed to a 52-week high of 5.32% before ending near 5.24%, driven by heavy sovereign debt issuance, elevated term premiums, and rising crude oil prices amid Middle East conflict uncertainties. Labor market indicators delivered mixed signals; weekly initial jobless claims fell to 197,000 for the week ending October 3, reflecting underlying labor market strength, even as broader nonfarm payroll growth moderated. Meanwhile, consumer confidence deteriorated sharply, with the University of Michigan Index of Consumer Sentiment falling to 46.3 in October 2026, as year-ahead inflation expectations rose to 4.7%.
U.S. equity markets posted broad weekly gains for the period from October 5 to October 11, 2026, with benchmark indexes achieving new record highs before experiencing mid-week volatility. The S&P 500 rose 1.2% over the reporting period, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.9%. The Nasdaq Composite lagged with a 0.6% advance as semiconductor and mega-cap technology shares faced profit-taking. In style rotation, value and broad-market equities led the advance, with the equal-weighted S&P 500 outperforming the market-cap benchmark by rising 1.6%. Smaller capitalization equities underperformed, as the Russell 2000 index fell between 0.5% and 1.0% under the weight of higher borrowing costs. Sector performance showed nine of eleven S&P sectors advancing, led by defensive and energy segments including Utilities, Consumer Staples, and Energy, while Technology was among the few declining sectors.
Monetary policy dynamics and corporate announcements served as primary market drivers. The release of Federal Reserve meeting minutes showed a unanimous vote for the September rate hike to 3.75 percent to 4 percent, though softer nonfarm payroll data reduced market expectations for an October rate hike to below 20%. Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller noted during an October 8 address in Istanbul that upside risks to inflation remain a key concern, with core personal consumption expenditures inflation remaining sticky between 2.5% and 3.0%. In corporate news, third-quarter earnings season kicked off alongside strategic commercial deals, including Constellation Energy contracting power delivery to Google, which provided support to energy and industrial shares.
Market sentiment stabilized moderately despite pressure from the bond market, with the CBOE Volatility Index falling to approximately 14.84 by the end of the week. Equity fund flows and positioning indicators pointed to cautious repositioning, as the Fear & Greed Index rose from 31 to 45 into neutral territory, even though broader market breadth metrics remained cautious. Institutional flows favored high-dividend defensive sectors and equal-weighted indexes, reflecting a strategy to insulate portfolios against elevated risk-free yields. Investors trimmed momentum positions in high-multiple technology and semiconductor stocks, redirecting liquidity toward value segments that offer attractive intrinsic valuations and resilient balance sheets.
The overall market behavior reflects a late-cycle phase characterized by a widening divergence between corporate earnings resilience and restrictive macro-financial conditions. Resilient corporate profitability and secular artificial intelligence spending continue to support large-cap equity valuations, allowing benchmark indexes to trade near historic highs despite 10-year Treasury yields reaching levels not seen in over two decades. However, the persistent drag of elevated interest rates on small-cap stocks, stagnant housing activity, and weakening consumer sentiment suggests that the broad economy faces ongoing headwinds. The equity market is navigating an environment where strong micro fundamentals are balancing out macro policy tightening.
Looking ahead to the coming week, financial markets will focus on pivotal macroeconomic releases and the formal acceleration of the third-quarter earnings calendar. Key economic releases include the September Consumer Price Index and Producer Price Index reports, which will provide crucial evidence on whether inflationary pressures are continuing to broaden. Investors will also monitor monthly retail sales data and regional manufacturing surveys to gauge consumer spending health. On the corporate front, major Wall Street financial institutions will kick off third-quarter bank earnings, setting the tone for corporate profitability, net interest margin trends, and credit loss provision expectations.
Market price action in the upcoming week will likely be dictated by the interaction between inflation data and Treasury yield movements. If incoming inflation data prints higher than anticipated, bond yields could re-test multi-year highs, creating valuation pressure on high-duration growth equities and reigniting policy tightening concerns for the December FOMC meeting. Conversely, if inflation shows signs of moderation and initial bank earnings exceed expectations, equities could extend their broad-based rotation, allowing value and cyclical sectors to maintain momentum while helping major benchmarks digest high risk-free interest rates.
From a strategy perspective, institutional investors are advised to maintain a balanced and quality-oriented allocation framework. Equity portfolios should feature an overweight tilt toward high-quality value and defensive sectors, including Healthcare, Consumer Staples, and Utilities, which offer attractive dividend yields and earnings stability in a high-rate environment. Exposure to mega-cap technology leadership should be retained selectively to participate in artificial intelligence growth trends, but concentration risk should be managed by utilizing equal-weighted index strategies. Maintaining moderate cash reserves will also allow investors to capitalize on potential volatility spikes surrounding economic data releases.
Key market risk factors requiring close attention include potential upside spikes in inflation driven by volatile energy markets and ongoing Middle East geopolitical conflicts. A sustained break of the 10-year Treasury yield above recent highs would increase corporate borrowing costs and pressure equity market valuation multiples. Additional downside risks include potential credit quality deterioration reported in bank earnings, downward revisions to fourth-quarter corporate earnings guidance, and further declines in household consumer sentiment that could signal a sharper retrenchment in broad consumer spending.

articles.full_text:
Futures tied to the broad market S&P 500 were mixed early Tuesday, with traders bracing for a slew of corporate earnings reports from major companies such as JPMorgan Chase and UnitedHealth.
S&P 500 futures inched down about 0.2%, while Nasdaq-100 futures lost 0.7%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures rose 122 points, or 0.2%
In Asia, South Korea’s benchmark Kospi fell more than 6%, dropping below 6,000 to its lowest level since July 31, while the small-cap Kosdaq fell 3.25%. Japan’s Nikkei 225 declined 2.22% and the Topix was flat. Australia’s benchmark S&P/ASX 200 inched higher.
Big banks JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo are slated to release their results before the open on Tuesday. Dow member UnitedHealth is also on deck.
The early reports could set the tone for an earnings season with lofty expectations. Analysts on average expect S&P 500 profits grew by nearly 30% from the year-earlier period, according to FactSet.
“Three groups will likely shape how investors read the season: 1) Banks (consumer and business health), 2) Big Tech (AI monetization), and 3) Energy (the durability of oil-driven profits),” wrote Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise. “Underneath these areas, the health of consumers and businesses amid higher interest rates, elevated costs, and concerns about the macroeconomic environment will be closely monitored across sectors throughout the season.”
Investors on Tuesday will also parse through existing home sales figures along with commentary from Federal Reserve officials Christopher Waller, Tom Barkin and Susan Collins.
Later in the week, inflation data for September will be released – which could jolt Treasury yields after they reached multidecade highs recently. The U.S. bond market was closed Monday due to the Indigenous Peoples’ Day holiday.
Wall Street is coming off a mixed session. The Dow ended Monday more than 195 points higher, while declines in memory stocks pushed the Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 into negative territory for the day.

articles.title: Bond Expert Flags High Yields, Weak Dollar as Favorable for U.S. Treasury Investments - 조선일보
articles.summary: Bond Expert Flags High Yields, Weak Dollar as Favorable for U.S. Treasury Investments  조선일보
articles.full_text:
“It is highly unusual for U.S. bond prices and exchange rates to both decline simultaneously. This means it’s a good time to invest in bonds denominated in dollars.”
Shin Nyeon-ki, head of Hanwha Asset Management’s overseas bond investment team, said in a recent interview, “The past ‘rules’ regarding bond and foreign exchange markets have been broken this year,” adding, “This process has created a favorable environment for individuals to take an interest in overseas bonds.” Shin, who released the book *Bond Investment, Look at the Structure, Not Interest Rate Forecasts*—which simplifies understanding global bond market trends—last month, is one of South Korea’s leading experts with 23 years of experience in overseas bond management. We asked Shin how to interpret the recent surge in U.S. bond yields and what individuals should know before investing in overseas bonds.
◇“Unprecedented Market, Time to Focus on Bonds”
The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield, considered the most important global bond benchmark, rose sharply from 4.18% at the end of last year to 5.29% at the end of last month. Since bond prices move inversely to yields, bond prices have fallen significantly.
-How should we understand the current bond market?
“This year’s bond market has moved in the opposite direction of expectations at the start of the year. Until early this year, the Federal Reserve was expected to cut interest rates, but the outbreak of the Middle East war in late February, combined with rising oil prices and inflation concerns, led the Fed to raise rates instead. Even experts who believed it would be difficult for U.S. Treasury yields to exceed 5% were proven wrong. Recently, the 10-year Treasury yield has even surpassed 5.3%.”
-Why are U.S. Treasury yields rising so sharply?
“Historically, Treasury yields move in line with nominal economic growth rates, which reflect inflation. The U.S. real economic growth rate was 2.2% (annualized) in the second quarter, and the inflation rate was around 3.3%, totaling approximately 5.5%. Theoretically, this implies that the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield could rise to this level. The Middle East war, combined with the spread of new technologies like AI, has overheated growth and driven inflation. This has increased expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve will have no choice but to raise interest rates, further fueling bond yield increases. Multiple variables have converged, making this an unprecedented market.”
-What else makes this market unusual?
“Typically, when bond yields rise, stock markets decline as funds shift from equities to bonds. However, the U.S. stock market is currently rising instead. This is happening because AI is having a broad impact on the market. While AI-driven optimism boosts Big Tech stocks, these companies are issuing large amounts of corporate bonds to fund AI development, affecting the Treasury market. Increased bond issuance raises the likelihood of broader yield increases (price declines).”
◇“Check Your Financial Situation Before Bond Investments”
-How do you forecast future U.S. Treasury yields?
“Three major variables exist: the Middle East war, AI optimism, and the U.S. midterm elections. If the Middle East conflict subsides, AI optimism wanes, or the midterm election results aren’t overly skewed toward one party, the upward momentum in U.S. Treasury yields could slow. The challenge is that all three variables are highly unpredictable.”
-Is investing in U.S. Treasuries advisable amid such uncertainty?
“There are two ways to invest in bonds. One is to hold them until maturity and receive the predetermined interest rate. Bonds are called ‘fixed income’ in English, meaning they provide fixed returns as set at issuance. If investors can hold bonds until maturity due to their financial circumstances, they can receive the current high yields as if they were deposit interest, provided the issuer doesn’t default. The tax rate on U.S. bond interest is 15.4%, the same as deposit interest.”
-If there are two methods, what is the other approach?
“Unlike deposits, bonds can be sold on the market before maturity. If U.S. Treasury yields decline and bond prices rise, selling before maturity can generate capital gains. No taxes are levied on capital gains from directly purchased bonds, unlike ETFs. The problem arises if yields rise further, causing prices to fall. If funds are needed and bonds must be sold at a loss, investors risk losses. This is why investors must thoroughly assess their financial situation—when they might need to liquidate funds—before investing in bonds. Longer-term bonds are more sensitive to interest rate fluctuations, so this should also be considered.”
◇“High Yields, Low Exchange Rates Make Overseas Investments Attractive”
-Exchange rates are also a concern when buying overseas bonds.
“Another factor making the current situation unusual is that bond prices have become cheaper due to rising yields, while the exchange rate has also declined significantly. This deviates from typical patterns. Historically, rising bond yields coincided with dollar strength as funds flowed into dollar assets, making dollar investments expensive due to a weaker won. However, thanks to surging exports by Korean companies amid the AI boom, the exchange rate has fallen, making dollar-denominated investments relatively favorable.”
-Is a mid-1,300 Korean won exchange rate considered low?
“Judgment may vary. The market generally considers the exchange rate low if it falls below the average of the past three years. Based on this, the average dollar-won exchange rate over the past three years was approximately 1,404 Korean won, so the current rate can be considered low. However, exchange rates are influenced by numerous variables, making definitive statements difficult.”
-What should individuals consider before investing in overseas bonds?
“The biggest risk in bond investing is the issuer’s default. While the U.S. government’s default risk is extremely low, corporations are different. Highly rated issuers can suddenly default. A notable example is the 2023 collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in March, followed by Credit Suisse’s bankruptcy and merger with UBS the next month, due to rapidly rising interest rates in 2022. While high-yield bonds with higher risk and returns may seem attractive, investors must remember that defaults can result in losing both principal and interest.”

articles.title: The bond market may have already priced in the Fed's final hike of 2026 - KuCoin
articles.summary: The bond market may have already priced in the Fed's final hike of 2026  KuCoin
articles.full_text:
EX.IO Research Institute | October 14, 2026
The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield has been hovering above 5% for three weeks, neither rising further nor falling back. More and more market participants are whispering: Is this a sign that the Fed is about to stop?
Most people’s first reaction to this claim is skepticism—after all, the Fed only raised rates by 25 basis points on September 16, pushing the policy rate to 3.75%–4.00%, and Chair Powell’s remarks at Jackson Hole are still fresh in memory, while core PCE remains stubbornly stuck at 3.7%.
This Federal Reserve doesn’t look like it’s going to stop anytime soon.
But what we’re saying is that this seemingly naive market intuition may be closer to the truth than most serious analyses. The causality has simply been reversed: it’s not that “yields peaked so the Fed has to stop,” but rather that the bond market has already done the Fed’s tightening work for it—meaning the Fed may not need to raise rates again this year.
Regarding the potential price movements of major assets under the new scenario, let’s state the conclusion upfront: short-term U.S. Treasuries and cash-like assets will continue to enjoy a reliable yield of around 4%, while long-term bonds have a floor but no ceiling; U.S. equities are supported by AI-driven earnings, with valuations capped at around 5%, making index-level trends unlikely and stock-level divergence more pronounced; gold and bitcoin remain pressured by real interest rates in the short term, but the fundamental logic of “credit collateral” remains intact; and stablecoins backed by short-term U.S. Treasuries, along with tokenized U.S. Treasury products, are among the few structural winners in this high-interest-rate environment. Below, we break this down layer by layer.
To understand all of this, we need to go back to what happened in the bond market over the past two months.
Behind the surge in bond yields
On August 27, the day before Walsh took the stage at Jackson Hole, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield was at 4.67%. By September 15—just one night before the FOMC meeting—it had risen to 5.00%. In other words, by the time the Fed raised rates on September 16, long-term rates had already priced in the move entirely. That 12-0 unanimous rate hike was less a policy decision by the central bank and more a formal acknowledgment of market pricing.
This “market getting ahead of itself” script actually played out back in August. On August 19, the Treasury announced it would at least double the repurchase scale for 10- to 30-year Treasuries, aiming to ease pressure on long-term rates. Yields did soften for a few trading days, but then reversed course, regaining all lost ground and hitting new highs within eight trading sessions. At the time, J.P. Morgan sounded a note of caution: given that the fiscal deficit still equates to about 6% of GDP, such opportunistic debt management tactics address symptoms rather than root causes and may instead push up term premiums. Two months later, this proved prophetic—the New York Fed’s Kim-Wright model shows the 10-year term premium has risen to 1.08%, a level unseen at any percentile in the past five years.
Figure 1 | U.S. Treasury yields rise across the board (2025/7–2026/10) | Source: FRED, compiled by EX.IO Research Institute
By October 7, the 10-year yield touched 5.365% intraday, and the 30-year yield reached 5.73%, both hitting their highest levels since 2002. This was not just an American story: the UK’s 30-year bond yield rose above 6%, the France-Germany spread widened to its widest level since 2012, and the Bloomberg Global Aggregate Bond Index yield hit its highest level since 2000.
This is a systemic rise in global discount rates, and U.S. Treasuries are precisely the epicenter.
What does a sustainable 5% interest rate really mean?
To determine whether "stabilization at a high level" signals the end of rate hikes, you can't just look at the numbers—you need to break down the 10-year yield. The nominal yield consists roughly of three components: expectations for the future path of policy rates, inflation compensation, and the term premium—the extra return investors demand for holding long-duration assets.
FRED's data provides a very clean breakdown. From the beginning of the year to October 8, the 10-year nominal yield rose from 4.19% to 5.22%, an increase of 103 basis points; of this, the 10-year TIPS real yield increased from 1.94% to 2.87%, contributing 93 basis points; the term premium rose from 0.58% to 1.08%, adding another 50 basis points; while the breakeven inflation rate, which measures inflation expectations, moved only slightly from 2.25% to 2.35%, remaining anchored near the 2% target over the past decade.
Figure 2/Figure 3 | Yield Decomposition and Term Premium | Source: FRED, New York Fed Kim-Wright Model, EX.IO Research Institute
This structure highlights a crucial point: the market is not pricing in “runaway inflation,” but rather two other factors—the structural rise in the real interest rate floor, and the increased cost of holding U.S. long-term bonds. The former stems from economic resilience and the AI capital expenditure boom, which have raised returns on capital and financing demand; the latter comes from fiscal pressures—$1.9 trillion in annual deficits, a total national debt exceeding $40 trillion, and interest expenditures already reaching $1.17 trillion in the first ten months of this fiscal year.
This is precisely the foundation of the judgment that “further rate hikes may not be necessary.” Consider the Fed’s current position: financial conditions have already been tightened significantly by the bond market— a 5% risk-free rate and a real yield nearing 2.9% represent the most restrictive combination for the economy since 2008; meanwhile, inflation expectations remain unchanged, indicating the central bank’s credibility remains intact—and the central bank no longer needs to raise rates again to prove its resolve.
Thus, the market has already done what the central bank might have otherwise needed to do with policy tools—doing it again would only backfire.
Familiar 2023
The bond market has made decisions for the central bank before—not least three years ago.
In April 2023, the 10-year yield was still at a low of 3.25%; by October, it had surged past 5%. At the time, Logan, a prominent hawk and president of the Dallas Fed, made a statement that sounded surprising then: the rise in long-term yields “may imply a reduced necessity for further rate hikes.” Timiraos of “New Fed Wire” subsequently calculated that the tightening effect of that surge in long-term rates was equivalent to three 25-basis-point rate increases. What happened afterward is well known: the Fed did not raise rates again after July 2023, marking the peak of the cycle. The bond market truly delivered the final rate hike on behalf of the central bank.
Looking further back, in the 1994 "Bond Massacre," Greenspan's unexpected rate hike caused the 10-year yield to surge from 5% to 8% within a year, cementing the term "Bond Vigilantes" into mainstream vocabulary; in 2013, Bernanke's comment about "considering tapering" caused yields to jump by a full percentage point within weeks, forcing the Fed to delay Tapering by six months.
Throughout history, the pattern has been consistent: when long-term interest rates tighten at this pace and magnitude, the central bank’s optimal choice is often to pause and observe, rather than add further pressure on the market.
Today’s situation bears a striking mirror image of October 2023: the same 5% 10-year yield, the same upward movement driven by real rates and term premiums, and the same anchored inflation expectations. If there is any difference, it is that this time the “bond market has done the work” even more convincingly—the term premium stands at 1.08%, higher than in October 2023.
Employment data provided a way forward
Of course, mechanisms alone aren't enough—you also need a dignified way out. On October 2, that way out arrived.
In September, non-farm payroll job growth was only 29,000, less than one-third of the market expectation of 84,000 to 90,000, and the unemployment rate rose to 4.2%. After the data release, futures markets slashed the probability of an interest rate hike at the October 28 meeting from around 70% to below 20%. More intriguingly, institutions reacted in unison: Huatai, RBC, and TD all simultaneously pushed their prediction for a second rate hike from October to December—delayed, yet with noticeably softened language; Goldman Sachs was even more direct, stating that a rate hike in October is now highly unlikely, and that “the FOMC may ultimately conclude that no further hikes are necessary.”
The labor market’s “low hiring, low firing” state has given the Fed a convenient narrative: since employment is cooling and financial conditions have already been tightened to restrictive levels by the bond market, “wait and see” is no longer a sign of weakness, but of prudence. Wash’s comment at Jackson Hole in late August that financial conditions were “hardly restrictive” is outdated; today, the 10-year yield has risen over 50 basis points since his speech, and the market has already corrected that view.
That said, the statement must be completed in full. "No further rate hikes are likely" does not mean "no more rate hikes will happen." The current risk list is still quite long: Brent crude remains above $100; if the September CPI, to be released on October 14, exceeds expectations, the October 28 meeting will immediately become a genuine debate again; nine officials on the dot plot still expect at least one more hike this year, and market pricing for a December hike remains around 60%. Bank of America even forecasts three rate hikes in 2026.
In particular, if the inflation data differs significantly from market expectations, the conclusions in this article may need to be substantially revised.
Even so, the odds have shifted. The bond market has achieved the

articles.title: IMF warns of AI market correction, cyber threats to financial system - The Daily Star
articles.summary: IMF warns of AI market correction, cyber threats to financial system  The Daily Star
articles.full_text:
The IMF warned on Tuesday of "elevated" risks faced by the global financial system, with potential perils including an AI-related market correction and cyber threats that could have "severe" consequences.
The cautionary message was delivered by the International Monetary Fund's latest Global Financial Stability Report, published on the second day of its annual gatherings with the World Bank, held this year in Thailand's capital, Bangkok.
"These risks are plausible near-term catalysts for a sharp tightening of financial conditions and market turmoil," the report said.
The recent boom in artificial intelligence -- and the related rush to manufacture semiconductors and build data centres -- has provided a boost to global growth despite geopolitical pressures including the Middle East war.
However, "growing evidence suggests that AI capabilities can be delivered at lower investment levels... or that potential economic gains may not be as large as expected," the IMF warned.
"Weaker or less durable AI investments and profitability could be a shock that triggers a market correction."
And while AI is increasingly a source of economic vitality globally, it is also presenting unprecedented risks, said the Fund.
"Severe cyber incidents could undermine market confidence and disrupt critical financial market infrastructure and operations," it said.
The report adds to growing worries about AI and its wide-ranging impact on labour markets, education and inequality.
In one widely covered incident in July, AI agents developed by US firm OpenAI hacked Hugging Face, an AI model and application library, as the autonomous software escaped its confined testing environment.
As AI capabilities continue to improve, the risk of successful cyberattacks on "critical financial institutions or market infrastructure" is getting "worse", the IMF said.
The "impact could be severe as rapid digitization has increased the attack surface".
While frontier AI models could be used to stage such attacks, they also have a role to play in cyber defence, the IMF said.
Another growing risk to the global financial system is a spike in bond yields, which could trigger severe shocks due to the "foundational importance of sovereign bond markets", said the report.
"Bond markets are susceptible to further rises in energy prices reigniting inflation and forcing the tightening of monetary policy."

articles.title: Solidigm launches open bidding for $5b pre-IPO to boost valuation, eyes Nasdaq - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
articles.summary: Solidigm launches open bidding for $5b pre-IPO to boost valuation, eyes Nasdaq - CHOSUNBIZ  Chosunbiz
articles.full_text:
This article was displayed on the ChosunBiz MoneyMove (MM) site at 3:21 p.m. on Oct. 7, 2026.
Regarding the pre-IPO fundraising for Solidigm, the U.S. NAND flash subsidiary of SK hynix, Solidigm was confirmed to have told potential investor candidates that it would proceed through an open competitive bidding process. The strategy is to maximize the corporate value and financing terms through competition among investors. Solidigm has selected Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley as pre-IPO underwriters and is accelerating fundraising.
According to the investment banking (IB) industry on the 7th, Solidigm informed potential candidates that it would recruit pre-IPO investors through an open competitive bidding process. The fundraising size is being discussed at around $5 billion, but the specific bidding schedule and final investment size have not been decided. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are said to be gauging investment demand from institutional investors.
Initially, the industry expected Solidigm to secure investors mainly among overseas institutional investors such as global private equity funds (PEF) and sovereign wealth funds, as it is a U.S. corporation and the investment size is being mentioned in the trillions of won. However, with the decision to proceed through open bidding, domestic investors have also gained an opportunity to invest. Domestic securities firms, including Korea Investment & Securities Co., and large PEF managers are examining the possibility of investing. Many domestic financial institutions are actively considering participation.
Noh Jong-won, the former SK Americas president who led SK hynix's acquisition of Intel's NAND business in the past, will also participate in the Solidigm investment. Noh is known to be raising limited partners through the PEF manager TechBridge. As it is an open bidding format, TechBridge is also expected to compete with other investors on price and terms. Stonebridge Global is said to be participating in the investment alongside TechBridge.
An industry official said, "I understand that Solidigm's fundraising is proceeding through open bidding," and added, "Some PEF managers and large securities firms in Korea are reviewing participation."
Choosing open bidding is seen as a move to secure more favorable financing terms by comparing the prices and conditions offered by each investor. If multiple investors competitively submit prices, it allows Solidigm to confirm its market value while also creating room to raise the investment size and improve terms. The industry also sees an intention to establish a valuation basis for the future listing process by securing a high corporate value at the pre-IPO stage.
For pre-IPO investors, how concretely a subsequent Nasdaq listing materializes is crucial. Because pre-IPO investments typically target minority equity with an eye toward a follow-on IPO as the main exit route, uncertainty in the listing schedule and method can affect the prices or terms investors offer. The route for recouping funds becomes clear only if a Nasdaq listing takes shape.
The biggest variable in this process is the issue of dual listing. With SK hynix already listed on the domestic stock market, there are concerns that a separate Nasdaq listing by its grandchild company Solidigm could dilute the economic value of existing SK hynix shareholders. The minority shareholder platform ACT has also raised the possibility of shareholder value damage from a Solidigm listing and is asking SK hynix to reconsider the listing.
Under the rules and guidelines on dual listings implemented by the Financial Services Commission and the Korea Exchange (KRX) starting on Aug. 3, the parent company's board has a duty to protect shareholders even for overseas listings. Unlike listings of subsidiaries on domestic exchanges, overseas listings are excluded from the Korea Exchange's special review for dual listings, but the parent company must assess the impact on general shareholders through the board and prepare shareholder protection measures.
Since the possibility of a Solidigm listing emerged, SK hynix has repeatedly said that no specific listing plan has been finalized. On the 1st, SK hynix said, "We are reviewing various measures to strengthen Solidigm's competitiveness, but nothing has been decided," and added, "If we use external capital, we will thoroughly examine the impact on the economic value of existing shareholders compared with using our own funds, and if we proceed to review specific measures, the board will review the financial and business impact along with shareholder protection measures."

articles.title: British Pound Outlook: Lloyds Warns Against Following Fed Rate Rises - Exchange Rates UK
articles.summary: British Pound Outlook: Lloyds Warns Against Following Fed Rate Rises  Exchange Rates UK
articles.full_text:
Pound Sterling Forecast: Lloyds Warns Rate Rises May Offer Little Support
Higher UK interest rates could leave the Pound struggling for support, Lloyds warns, as following the Fed risks imposing greater costs on the economy.
Higher UK interest rates may no longer provide the lift to Sterling that investors once expected, according to Lloyds Bank, leaving policymakers facing a costly choice if the Pound weakens further.
Rates strategist Karim Henide writes: "Following the Fed may therefore impose the costs of tighter policy without currency relief."
Pound Sterling's performance on Monday was mixed, with GBP/USD near $1.3206, down around 0.2%, while GBP/EUR traded near €1.1835, close to its high for the year.
Lloyds still regards a November Bank of England increase as likely.
The British Pound has become less responsive to UK rates
Lloyds estimates that currency weakness still feeds inflation, while UK tightening has become less effective at supporting Sterling.
Henide writes: "Additionally conditioning the MPC's ability to retain optionality is sterling resilience. A 1% fall in GBPUSD adds c. 7bp to UK CPI over two years; further weakness could make inaction hard to sustain. However, the Bank Rate's influence on sterling has weakened sharply. 10bp of UK tightening lifted GBPUSD by c. 1.5% in 2017-19, but has had little effect since 2022."
A cheaper Pound raises the domestic cost of imports, including goods priced in Dollars.
The resulting inflation pressure could push the Monetary Policy Committee towards higher rates even if the currency response remains weak, leaving households and businesses facing more expensive borrowing without much relief from import costs.
MUFG sees a November rate rise supporting Sterling, while Lloyds' concern centres on the limited currency benefit of following the Fed beyond that meeting.
A November increase need not start a prolonged series
Henide argues that bond markets are treating the British and American policy outlooks too similarly despite the UK's less favourable trade-off between growth and inflation.
Henide writes: "The optimal 2027 average Bank Rate given consensus economic projections is c. 4.2% under a strict inflation target, and c. 3.5% for an MPC that looks through first-round energy effects (vs. 4.59% priced)."
Those are conditional model results for an annual average, rather than a year-end rate forecast.
To justify the pricing used in the report, Lloyds calculates that Brent would need to average about $125 throughout 2027, with policymakers fully responding to its direct inflation effects.
Henide writes: "A key reason behind the progressive suboptimality of hikes is the policy lag; the hikes would be expected to transmit after meaningful disinflation is expected to arrive, increasing the risk of undershooting target further out the curve. Under our scenario modelling, the priced path takes c. 0.3pp off CPI by 4Q28 (back-loaded), at the cost of a 0.38pp rise in unemployment."
The inflation reduction arrives largely later in the model, by which time earlier energy-price increases are expected to be dropping out of annual comparisons.
Lloyds also identifies a mismatch between markets' interest-rate and inflation expectations, with inflation contracts allowing for more persistent price pressures than its model produces even after the anticipated hikes.
Henide writes: "Pricing reflects an inflation path that looks as though the tightening is ineffective. We are sympathetic with this view, given the misalignment of the demand-focussed toolbox and the predominantly supply-focussed source of mandate pressures."
Persistent energy inflation could restrict the Bank's room to wait
The risk to that view is that expensive energy spreads into wages and other prices, making inflation harder to reverse.
Henide writes: "Therefore, how much optionality the MPC is reasonably able to retain depends on energy (second-round pass-through in particular). The UK has typically seen stronger second-round pass-through than the US, a natural argument against looking through first-round effects."
He nevertheless finds that energy's transmission into wider UK inflation has faded, potentially giving policymakers more scope to avoid responding mechanically to the initial price shock.
The BoE's September decision to hold Bank Rate at 3.75% reflected a similar tension.
Its statement said: "There has been little evidence so far of material second-round effects in price and wage-setting."
Policymakers nevertheless warned that the risk would grow if energy prices stayed elevated.
The next decision is due on 5 November.
Sterling's behaviour will help determine how much flexibility the MPC retains, Henide concludes: "Sterling is likely to be a key determinant of MPC responsiveness; a resilient currency affords the MPC room to resist imported Fed tightening; further weakness forces a more hawkish response, even if higher rates no longer support the currency as they did before 2022."
Near-Term GBP and Interest Rates FAQ
Does Lloyds expect a November BoE rate rise?
Yes, it considers an increase likely, but questions the case for following the Fed with prolonged tightening.
Why might higher interest rates fail to strengthen the Pound?
Lloyds finds that Sterling has become less responsive to UK tightening, leaving higher borrowing costs without the currency support seen in earlier years.
Is 3.5%-4.2% a firm Bank Rate forecast?
No. It describes conditional model estimates for the average rate during 2027, depending on how policymakers respond to energy-driven inflation.

articles.title: Is Inflation Speeding Up Again, or Is It Just Gas Prices? - Stock Titan
articles.summary: Is Inflation Speeding Up Again, or Is It Just Gas Prices?  Stock Titan
articles.full_text:
Gas got pricier in September, with the government’s weekly survey putting the average pump price at $4.36 a gallon, 7.3% more than in August. The prices underneath the headline (rent, services, most goods) held a 2.4% annual pace through August, and Wednesday’s Consumer Price Index from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, due at 8:30 AM ET on October 14, shows whether that changed. The same report fixes next year’s Social Security raise, which on our calculation from the official formula is already at least 3.4% unless prices drop by more than about 0.1% in September.
What happened to gas prices in September
Gas got a good deal more expensive in September. The U.S. Energy Information Administration’s survey of regular gasoline put the monthly average at $4.355 a gallon, up from $4.058 in August and $3.166 in September 2025, which is 7.3% more than a month earlier and 37.6% more than a year earlier. It was the highest monthly average since May, when the price hit $4.479. For a household that buys 50 gallons a month, a round number we picked for illustration, that is about $14.85 more in September than in August.
The climb came in the middle of the month. The weekly readings went from $4.157 on September 7 to $4.319 on September 14 and $4.478 on September 21, then held at $4.465 on September 28. By October 5 the price had eased to $4.354, which matters for October’s report, though September’s average is already set.
Show the data
| Category | Value | 
|---|---|
| Jan | $2.81 | 
| Feb | $2.91 | 
| Mar | $3.64 | 
| Apr | $4.10 | 
| May | $4.48 | 
| Jun | $4.05 | 
| Jul | $3.93 | 
| Aug | $4.06 | 
| Sep | $4.36 | 
A jump of that size is not common. In StockTitan’s copy of the weekly pump price series, a month over month rise in the average of 7.3% or more happened in 17 of the 141 months from January 2015 to September 2026, September included.
The pump price is a decent guide to the gasoline line in the CPI, although the two are measured separately, by different people and samples. In the six months from March to August 2026 the CPI gasoline index before seasonal adjustment moved in the same direction as the EIA monthly average every month, and the gap between the two changes was never wider than 1.7 percentage points (we compare them month by month in the chart below). Six months is a short record, but it makes the 7.3% rise at the pump a useful public clue to the CPI’s gasoline line before Wednesday.
Show the data
| Category | EIA pump price, monthly average | CPI gasoline, unadjusted | 
|---|---|---|
| Mar | 25.1% | 24.9% | 
| Apr | 12.8% | 11.1% | 
| May | 9.2% | 8.6% | 
| Jun | -9.6% | -9.7% | 
| Jul | -2.9% | -2.1% | 
| Aug | 3.2% | 2.5% | 
Gasoline made up about 3.85% of the CPI basket in August, by our update of the July weight in the BLS August release, Table 1, so if the CPI gasoline index rose by the same 7.3% before seasonal adjustment, gasoline alone would add about 0.28 percentage point to the month’s overall price change. That is a calculation and not a forecast, since the CPI keeps its own sample and its own timing within the month.
The seasonally adjusted number that makes the headline can come out bigger still. Seasonal adjustment strips out the price swings that recur every year. In September 2025, a 1.1% rise in the unadjusted gasoline index turned into a 3.6% rise in the seasonally adjusted one. Airline fares, which depend on jet fuel, were up 23.4% over the year to August, a story we looked at in why plane tickets cost so much more this holiday season.
What the report means for the 2027 Social Security raise
Wednesday’s report is the last piece of the formula for next year’s Social Security cost of living adjustment, and the July and August numbers already put that raise at 3.4% or more unless CPI-W, the index it uses, falls by more than about 0.12% in September. The rule is written out by the Social Security Administration: "A COLA effective for December of the current year is equal to the percentage increase (if any) in the CPI-W from the average for the third quarter of the current year to the average for the third quarter of the last year in which a COLA became effective." The result is rounded to the nearest tenth of a percent.
CPI-W is a version of the index built on the spending of households that live mainly on wages, and it runs close to the headline number (3.5% over the year to August, against 3.4% for the all items index). Its third quarter 2025 average was 317.265, from the monthly values of 316.349, 317.306 and 318.139 on the BLS CPI-W series. For 2026 the July value is 327.104 and the August value 328.481, so only September is missing. If September merely matched August, the quarter would average 328.022, which is 3.39% above the 2025 average and rounds to a 3.4% raise.
| September CPI-W change from August, before seasonal adjustment | Social Security raise this produces, rounded | 
|---|---|
| A fall of more than about 0.12% | 3.3% or lower | 
| From a 0.12% fall to a 0.17% rise | 3.4% | 
| From 0.17% to 0.46% | 3.5% | 
| From 0.46% to 0.75% | 3.6% | 
| From 0.75% to 1.04% | 3.7% | 
For a sense of scale, CPI-W rose 0.26% from August to September 2025 before seasonal adjustment, a pace that would land in the 3.5% row. The table is our arithmetic from the SSA rule and the published index values, so the number that counts is the one SSA computes from Wednesday’s CPI-W, and it applies to benefits starting with the December 2026 payment that arrives in January 2027. For comparison, the raise paid in 2026 was 2.8%, according to SSA. On a hypothetical benefit of $2,000 a month, each tenth of a point is worth $2 a month, so a 3.4% raise would add $68 before any deductions.
What rent and services say about lasting inflation
Gasoline moves the monthly number, and housing, the biggest single weight in the index, is a large part of how long higher inflation sticks around. In the July 2026 weights that BLS publishes in Table 1 of the August release, shelter (mainly rent and what BLS calls owners’ equivalent rent) made up 35.3% of the basket, and gasoline 3.8%, so shelter weighs about nine times as much as gas.
Show the data
| Part | Value | Share | 
|---|---|---|
| Shelter | 35.3% | 35.3% | 
| Gasoline | 3.8% | 3.8% | 
| Everything else | 60.9% | 60.9% | 
Shelter has been calm. It rose 0.3% in August after 0.1% in July and was up 3.0% over twelve months, with rent up 2.7% and owners’ equivalent rent, the BLS estimate of what homeowners would pay to rent their own home, up 3.1%. Both have moved in small steps lately, between 0.1% and 0.3% a month from June to August on a seasonally adjusted basis.
The index for all items less food and energy, which economists call core inflation, carries that steadiness. It rose 2.4% over the year to August, down from 2.5% in July, while energy was up 16.3%. Inside core, prices of goods other than food and energy were up only 0.7% over the year, and services other than energy were up 3.0%. A few lines pull hard in opposite directions: airline fares rose 23.4% over the year and motor vehicle insurance fell 5.1%, while used cars and trucks were 2.3% cheaper than a year earlier.
Food sits in between. The food index rose 2.7% over the year, with groceries up 2.2% and meals away from home up 3.4%. Eggs rose 2.9% in August alone while lettuce fell 6.2%, the kind of swing that makes a shopping trip feel different from the statistics.
The reason this split matters is persistence. A price rise that comes from gasoline tends to reverse when fuel gets cheaper, as it did in June 2026, when the gasoline index dropped 9.7% and the all items index fell 0.4% in a single month. A rise that comes from rent and services tends to build over many months. The Fed’s minutes point to a third path, energy costs that stay high long enough to spread into other prices, which is why core services matter as much as rent. That reading is ours, and Wednesday’s core number is the first test of it for September.
The August report in brief
Prices rose 0.4% in August after 0.1% in July on a seasonally adjusted basis, and 3.4% over twelve months, the same annual rate as in July, according to the BLS release of September 11. BLS said "the index for gasoline rose 3.9 percent in August, accounting for over one third of the monthly all items increase."
The year has had two halves. The annual rate was 2.4% in January and February 2026, jumped to 3.3% in March when the gasoline index rose 21.2% in one month on a seasonally adjusted basis, peaked at 4.2% in May and has been at 3.4% or 3.5% since June. Core inflation never followed it up: it has stayed between 2.4% and 2.9% all year, and energy, up 16.3% over the year to August, is the main thing the core leaves out.
Show the data
| Category | All items | Core, without food and energy | 
|---|---|---|
| Jan 2025 | 3.0% | 3.3% | 
| Feb 2025 | 2.8% | 3.1% | 
| Mar 2025 | 2.4% | 2.8% | 
| Apr 2025 | 2.3% | 2.8% | 
| May 2025 | 2.4% | 2.8% | 
| Jun 2025 | 2.7% | 2.9% | 
| Jul 2025 | 2.7% | 3.1% | 
| Aug 2025 | 2.9% | 3.1% | 
| Sep 2025 | 3.0% | 3.0% | 
| Nov 2025 | 2.7% | 2.6% | 
| Dec 2025 | 2.7% | 2.6% | 
| Jan 2026 | 2.4% | 2.5% | 
| Feb 2026 | 2.4% | 2.5% | 
| Mar 2026 | 3.3% | 2.6% | 
| Apr 2026 | 3.8% | 2.8% | 
| May 2026 | 4.2% | 2.9% | 
| Jun 2026 | 3.5% | 2.6% | 
| Jul 2026 | 3.4% | 2.5% | 
| Aug 2026 | 3.4% | 2.4% | 
A 0.4% month is not unusual on its own. In StockTitan’s copy of the seasonally adjusted CPI series, a monthly rise at least as large as August’s (0.396% before rounding) came in 84 of the 438 months from January 1990 to August 2026, about one month in five. What stands out in 2026 is the path, a surge from March to May, a 0.4% fall in June, then a slow rebuild. BLS published no index for October 2025, so the chart above skips that month.

articles.title: Why the European Central Bank Cannot Let France off the Hook. - The Unseen and The Unsaid
articles.summary: Why the European Central Bank Cannot Let France off the Hook.  The Unseen and The Unsaid
articles.full_text:
France’s rising debt and borrowing costs do not justify an unconditional European Central Bank (ECB) intervention. The ECB should let market pressure encourage fiscal consolidation, remain ready to contain a broader crisis and condition any French bond purchases on spending cuts and fiscal reform.
France’s ballooning public debt—now around €3.5 trillion, or roughly 118% of GDP—has pushed investors to demand sharply higher compensation for holding French government bonds. The 10-year French yield recently approached 5%, its highest level since 2002, while the difference over Germany’s benchmark 10–year Bund widened to approximately 1.4 percentage points; remarkably, French borrowing costs have now risen even above those of Italy and Greece. As the graph from the FT below shows, French yields, a little over 2 years ago, used to be a whole percentage point below Italian ones.
The fiscal outlook offers little relief: the European Commission expects France’s deficit to remain around 5.1% of GDP in 2026, with debt forecast to reach 121% of GDP in 2027 and, under its baseline scenario, approximately 130% by 2034.
Yet despite the movements in spreads, and the growing alarm about French spending and political budgetary gridlock, the ECB has so far stated that it sees no cause to intervene in the French bond market.
Why France does not qualify for ECB intervention
In September, ECB President Christine Lagarde declined to comment directly on widening French spreads, saying they reflected “how markets perceived the strength” of individual sovereign bonds. On October 1, Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel reinforced this position, saying that the ECB’s bond-buying tools were designed to safeguard price stability, “not to target specific sovereign bond spreads” (Reuters).
Two days later in an FT interview, Banque de France governor Emmanuel Moulin was even more explicit: “The conditions are not in place now for an intervention by the ECB,” whose role, he said, is “not to deal with countries’ budget problems.”
The ECB’s current primary tool for intervention, the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), is tasked with ensuring that the monetary policy stance is transmitted smoothly across all euro-zone members. It is meant to keep ECB interest-rate decisions from affecting euro-area countries in sharply different ways for reasons unrelated to their finances. When member states’ interest rates diverge for reasons the ECB considers unrelated to “fundamentals”, the TPI can be used to purchase marketable public sector debt within a maturity range of 1–10 years.
However, use of the TPI is conditional on meeting all four criteria, and France violates the first: compliance with the EU Fiscal Framework. The Council opened an Excessive Deficit Procedure (EDP), obliging a deficit correction to above agreed limits, against France on 26 July 2024. In January 2025, it required France to eliminate the excessive deficit by 2029 by restricting the growth of net nationally financed expenditure to 0.8% in 2025, 1.2% annually from 2026–28, and 1.1% in 2029. While the EDP is ongoing, use of the TPI is explicitly prohibited. It is important the ECB sticks to its guidelines; French borrowing costs are a corrective signal, not a malfunction in monetary-policy transmission.
Could bond markets force a course correction?
It is a step forward that the ECB is thus far allowing larger spreads that reflect the fiscal path of member states. Higher interest costs will force French politicians to face the cost of running sustained deficits since 1973 and finally make hard choices. It could try to raise tax revenue; however, according to the OECD, taxes already total 43.5% of GDP, second only to Denmark among OECD countries. Or it could cut public spending, which came in at 57% of GDP, second highest again among OECD states.
How long the ECB can stay out of French public finances comes down to interlocking questions: how long it can withstand French political pressure and how credible non-intervention is to French policymakers. If French policymakers truly believe the ECB won’t stabilize French interest rates through intervention, they might course correct before it comes to a full-blown crisis.
There are some early signs of higher rates disciplining French politics. The 2027 presidential front-runner, Marine Le Pen, recently released a plan for fiscal consolidation (spending cuts, transfer reductions, and/or tax hikes aimed at deficit reduction) at a National Rally (RN) press conference. Sparse on specific details for achieving its goals, it nevertheless outlines pragmatic and necessary spending and debt targets. According to Reuters, it aims to reduce the deficit to 3% by 2030, and 2.5% by 2032, the national debt from 121% to 112% by 2032, cut €140bn in spending net of a minimum of €30bn in tax cuts by 2032, and rein in public spending to below 50% of GDP. It also proposes an eventual golden rule capping debt at 60% of GDP, arriving by cutting net spending by 0.5% each year. Le Pen also promised significant cuts for the first time to healthcare systems, social housing, and civil servant headcounts, a major shift from previous stances.
It is not coincidental that the RN shifted course and promised fiscal reform at a moment in time when the markets see French bonds as risky. It is an early indication that bond market pain is starting to shape political discourse. While Le Pen’s plan lacks credibility, due in part to sparse details and tension with proposals such as reducing the young retirement age from 62 to 60, it does confirm the RN is on the right direction on fiscal matters.
France as a test of ECB discipline
Where does this leave the ECB? Arguably, in a position to address moral hazard in fiscal policy—the risk that governments, expecting central-bank support, will continue taking fiscal risks instead of putting their finances in order. If the ECB does not intervene until fiscal pain concentrates the minds of policymakers on a serious and detailed plan for fiscal consolidation, it will show other member states that there will be no bailouts. If a member with the stature and political weight of France won’t receive an ECB bailout, it will confirm to other states that their fiscal policy is their burden to bear and no one else’s.
The ECB should be ready to react to any bond crisis, and limit spillover and contagion to other eurozone markets, but any purchasing of French bonds should be conditional on spending cuts. Emergency measures should be judiciously applied and not subsidize current or future fiscal excess. The ECB Governing Council will have to walk a tightrope and convince both politicians and markets there will be no bailout, while readying all necessary tools in case of a crisis.
If its resolve fails, and it intervenes to subsidize French borrowing without imposing the needed discipline, it will put France and Germany on a collision course and threaten the existence of the Euro, perhaps the EU itself. Yet, if it can force a course correction, the Euro and ECB will be stronger than ever and send a clear message that it is not there to bail out member states. The crisis unfolding in France is both an existential threat and a golden opportunity. Though difficult and perhaps unlikely, if it can be mastered it could achieve what the ECB originally aspired to be: a truly independent central bank with a single mandate for price stability.
Lovely piece! Is the leadership structure of the ECB structured such that it might be more likely to bail out France on political grounds, or are there enough non-French admins of the bank to make this unlikely ?

Key Moments
- EUR/GBP trades just above 0.8450, hovering close to a 16- to 17-month low at 0.8447 after a 1.7% slide over the previous two weeks.
- Rising stress in French sovereign markets, reflected in a 137-basis-point OAT-Bund spread, is discouraging Euro demand.
- Investors are watching ECB President Christine Lagarde’s remarks and upcoming UK GDP and production data for policy guidance.
Euro Under Pressure Against Sterling
The Euro (EUR) continues to weaken against the British Pound (GBP) on Monday, extending a sharp decline that has seen the cross lose about 1.7% over the previous two weeks. The EUR/GBP pair is trading slightly above the 0.8450 area after failing to hold gains near 0.8490 on Friday, leaving the recent 16-month low at 0.8447 just a few pips below current levels.
Persistent worries over France’s public finances remain a central factor weighing on the single currency. Market participants are increasingly wary as they reassess exposure to Euro-denominated assets, with the political backdrop in France amplifying those concerns.
French Debt Concerns Hit the Euro
Investor sentiment toward the Euro has deteriorated as the yield spread between 10-year French OATs and equivalent German Bunds widens to 137 basis points, described as the highest level since the 2012 financial crisis. This growing differential is being interpreted as a sign of elevated credit and political risk in France.
A stalemate in French politics ahead of next year’s presidential elections, combined with mounting social unrest across the country, is creating what the article characterizes as a “toxic cocktail” for investors. These intertwined fiscal and political concerns have contributed to the Euro’s underperformance over recent weeks.
