articles.title: The British Pound drifts back to its floor as Crude Oil lifts the Dollar - FXStreet
articles.summary: The British Pound drifts back to its floor as Crude Oil lifts the Dollar  FXStreet
articles.full_text:
Every session since September 24 has bottomed within about 25 pips of 1.3200, and Monday was the 13th. GBP/USD closed near 1.3210 after a climb to just above 1.3250, made before London opened, was given back as Brent rose above $107 a barrel. The Dollar Index reached its highest since April 2025 on the same move, so Monday's slide had more to do with the Dollar than the Pound.
Four BoE hikes priced and the Pound near a three-month low
Bank of England (BoE) external member Mann said on Monday that UK inflation near 4% around the turn of the year could set off a wage-price drift. She added that services inflation will be hard to bring down without more hikes. Markets put the odds of a hike on November 5 near 90% and price the UK's Bank Rate at 4.75% within a year, four quarter-point moves above its current 3.75%. That's four hikes priced for an economy forecast to have shrunk in August.
Cleveland Fed President Hammack, who votes on Fed policy this year, said the same day that more tightening is needed, that she'd rather move in smaller steps taken quickly, and that Treasury yields are modest by historical standards. Futures already put a December Fed hike above 80%, so both sides of GBP/USD are priced for higher rates.
The UK imports more Crude Oil and fuel than it produces and pays for it in Dollars, and Brent is what moved the pair on Monday. GBP/USD made its high before London opened with Brent near $104.50, and its low came after Brent went through $107.
The bet against the Pound has worked against the Dollar and not the Euro
Speculators held a net 97.6K futures contracts betting on a weaker Pound in the week to October 6, about £6.1 billion, according to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), and they added 6.5K that week. Of the Fed, the European Central Bank (ECB), the Bank of Japan (BoJ) and the BoE, only the BoE hasn't raised rates this year. So far, £6.1 billion of bets on a weaker Pound has bought 13 sessions at the same floor.
The Pound was bought against the Euro ahead of Prime Minister Burnham's speech on relations with the European Union on Monday, and EUR/GBP fell to its lowest since June 2025. The Euro is 57.6% of the Dollar Index and the Pound 11.9%, so the index's 18-month high has come mostly from a weaker Euro, and GBP/USD has fallen less than EUR/USD on the way.
Bailey and Warsh speak 90 minutes apart in Bangkok on Friday
The US Consumer Price Index (CPI) for September is due on Wednesday at 12:30 GMT, forecast at 3.7% YoY from 3.4%, with core CPI at 2.5%. US retail sales follow on Thursday at 12:30 GMT, forecast up 0.3% after 1.2% in August. A strong pair of releases would add to Fed hike bets and push on the Dollar side of GBP/USD.
UK August Gross Domestic Product (GDP) comes out on Thursday at 06:00 GMT, forecast at -0.1% MoM after 0.4% in July, with industrial and manufacturing output also forecast at -0.1%. A contraction would leave the BoE's November case resting on inflation alone. The British Retail Consortium's September like-for-like sales figure comes first, at 23:01 GMT on Monday, forecast at 0.7% YoY after 0.5%.
External member Greene, who voted for a hike to 4% at the June, July and September meetings, speaks on Tuesday at 03:00 GMT. She said on October 8 that it's dangerous for the BoE to assume the bond market will do its work, which is the opposite of Governor Bailey's view that higher market borrowing costs have bought the BoE time.
Chief Economist Pill speaks on Wednesday and Thursday, and Deputy Governor Breeden on Thursday. Governor Bailey speaks at 02:00 GMT on Friday at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank meetings in Bangkok, and Fed Chair Warsh follows at 03:30 GMT, the day before the Fed's quiet period for its October 27-28 meeting begins. Chancellor Healey's Budget is on October 28 and the BoE decides on November 5.
Levels and bias
Resistance: 1.3250 stopped the bounces on October 8 and 9, and Monday's high just above it came before London opened and didn't hold. 1.3300 has capped every session since September 24 except a brief spike above it on September 30.
Support: 1.3200 has been the floor for 13 sessions, and only October 1 closed under it. 1.3180 is the low of that run and of late June, and GBP/USD last traded at 1.3150 in late June.
Bias: The lean turns short while 1.3250 caps on a closing basis, with 1.3180 the first objective and 1.3150 the second. The daily Stochastic Relative Strength Index (Stoch RSI) has climbed out of oversold to near 45 and is still rising, which is the main risk to the short. A daily close above 1.3250 ends it.
GBP/USD daily chart
Pound Sterling FAQs
The Pound Sterling (GBP) is the oldest currency in the world (886 AD) and the official currency of the United Kingdom. It is the fourth most traded unit for foreign exchange (FX) in the world, accounting for 12% of all transactions, averaging $630 billion a day, according to 2022 data. Its key trading pairs are GBP/USD, also known as ‘Cable’, which accounts for 11% of FX, GBP/JPY, or the ‘Dragon’ as it is known by traders (3%), and EUR/GBP (2%). The Pound Sterling is issued by the Bank of England (BoE).
The single most important factor influencing the value of the Pound Sterling is monetary policy decided by the Bank of England. The BoE bases its decisions on whether it has achieved its primary goal of “price stability” – a steady inflation rate of around 2%. Its primary tool for achieving this is the adjustment of interest rates. When inflation is too high, the BoE will try to rein it in by raising interest rates, making it more expensive for people and businesses to access credit. This is generally positive for GBP, as higher interest rates make the UK a more attractive place for global investors to park their money. When inflation falls too low it is a sign economic growth is slowing. In this scenario, the BoE will consider lowering interest rates to cheapen credit so businesses will borrow more to invest in growth-generating projects.
Data releases gauge the health of the economy and can impact the value of the Pound Sterling. Indicators such as GDP, Manufacturing and Services PMIs, and employment can all influence the direction of the GBP. A strong economy is good for Sterling. Not only does it attract more foreign investment but it may encourage the BoE to put up interest rates, which will directly strengthen GBP. Otherwise, if economic data is weak, the Pound Sterling is likely to fall.
Another significant data release for the Pound Sterling is the Trade Balance. This indicator measures the difference between what a country earns from its exports and what it spends on imports over a given period. If a country produces highly sought-after exports, its currency will benefit purely from the extra demand created from foreign buyers seeking to purchase these goods. Therefore, a positive net Trade Balance strengthens a currency and vice versa for a negative balance.
Author
Joshua joins the FXStreet team as an Economics and Finance double major from Vancouver Island University with twelve years' experience as an independent trader focusing on technical analysis.

articles.title: Trump Establishes Committee to Investigate Federal Reserve's Lisa Cook in Latest Effort to Fire Her - Industrial Distribution
articles.summary: Trump Establishes Committee to Investigate Federal Reserve's Lisa Cook in Latest Effort to Fire Her  Industrial Distribution
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump opened another chapter in his effort to fire Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook Friday by establishing a "committee of inquiry" to investigate allegations that she made false statements in mortgage applications.
The inquiry will include a hearing at the White House Nov. 5, Trump said in a written memo, that Cook "shall" attend to answer questions from the committee. The hearing wouldn't be public but a transcript would be published, the memo said.
Trump's extraordinary demand that Cook testify before the committee will likely renew concerns about threats to the Federal Reserve's independence. The president has repeatedly called for the central bank to cut its key interest rate, but just last month, the Fed raised it instead, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom Trump appointed earlier this year.
Trump's attempts to fire Cook from the Fed's seven-member board of governors represent the first time in the central bank's 113-year history that a president has sought to remove a Fed governor. Cook was appointed by former President Joe Biden and is the first Black woman on the Fed's board. Trump's attacks on her followed other efforts to oust or indict Black officials, such as New York Attorney General Letitia James and Gen. Charles Q. Brown, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
"As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law," Trump wrote in the memorandum.
Cook's attorneys, Abbe Lowell and Norman Eisen, said they were considering having Cook appear at the Nov. 5 hearing and respond to the charges.
"We have engaged with the White House to evaluate whether the process proposed has a possibility of being a genuine one and not simply a box checking exercise," Lowell and Eisen said in a statement. "Governor Cook welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her."
The "committee of inquiry" will be composed of Kevin Hassett, the president's top economic adviser, who has frequently echoed Trump's criticisms of the Fed; Keith Sonderling, the acting director of the Office of Government Ethics, whom the president has also appointed to lead the Labor Department, and Andrea Lucas, the chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, whom Trump appointed in November 2025.
Trump initially tried to fire Cook in August 2025 after alleging she had committed mortgage fraud by declaring two different properties to be her "primary" residence in mortgage applications in 2021. Mortgages on primary homes can often receive a lower interest rate or other beneficial terms.
Cook has denied any wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime. Lowell and Eisen have previously said Cook committed an "inadvertent error" and did refer to one of the properties as a vacation home in other documents.
"An inadvertent error is not fraud, as the President and a third of his cabinet should know because they reportedly did the same thing," Lowell and Eisen said in August.
The Federal Reserve declined to comment on Trump's announcement.
Trump and some of his economic advisers have blamed the Fed's broader rate-setting committee, which includes 12 voting members and 19 officials in total, for forcing last month's rate hike, even though it followed comments by Warsh in August that signaled higher rates were likely. As a member of the board of governors, Cook is also one of the 12 voting members of the committee. The vote to lift rates Sept. 16 was unanimous.
The move also follows a Supreme Court ruling in June that Cook could keep her job after Trump sought to fire her last year. That ruling included a footnote that said nothing prevented Trump from "trying again" as long as she was given proper notice and an opportunity to respond to the charges.
Trump said the committee of inquiry will seek to establish whether there is "cause" to fire Cook, as required under the law governing the Fed. The Supreme Court said in June that a for-cause firing required an alleged offense that was serious and related to an official's job.
Scott Alvarez, formerly the chief counsel for the Fed, said that President William Howard Taft set up a similar commission in 1912 to remove two officials from an independent agency. The commission created by Trump goes beyond the type of process the Supreme Court said was needed to fire Cook.
"It's an attempt to show that he's really giving Cook as much process as possible," Alvarez said.
Still, the allegations against Cook don't appear to meet the "for cause" standard set out by the Supreme Court, Alvarez said.
Other analysts said that Trump will likely use the process to ultimately fire Cook.
"We do not see why the White House would start this process if it were not trying to create a way to justify removing Cook from her job," Jaret Seiberg, managing director of TD Cowen's Washington Research Group, said in a note to clients.

articles.title: [不同来源] Central bank measures, intervention spark rupee's sharpest rally in six months - Kitco
articles.summary: Central bank measures, intervention spark rupee's sharpest rally in six months  Kitco
articles.full_text:
MUMBAI, Oct 12 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee rose about 1% on Monday after the central bank took steps to temper dollar demand in spot and derivatives markets, with likely intervention through dollar sales adding to the gains.
The rupee rose 1% to 95.77 per dollar from 96.73 on Friday, outperforming mostly rangebound Asian peers and posting its best single day gain since April, which had also been sparked a set of measures to shore up the unit.
India announced new steps on Saturday after the rupee neared its record low of 96.96 per dollar last week.
The changes involve redirecting oil companies' dollar purchases away from the spot market and tightening hedging rules as the currency hovers near record lows.
The oil window is expected to take out about $10-12 billion of monthly dollar demand from the spot market, per government data on oil imports.
The recent moves follow a series of other measures taken to shield the currency and bolster the country's balance of payments strained by a heavy import bill due to high oil prices and persistent capital outflows.
Banks turned cautious about offering forward dollar hedges to importers on Monday after the Reserve Bank of India's latest forex measures sharply raised costs and are expected to slow a hedging surge that had dragged the currency, bankers said.
Expectations of longer-term weakness pushed importers to step up purchases of forward dollars to record levels last month. That hedging demand, in turn, added strain on the currency, creating a cycle of depreciation expectations, increased hedging and further weakness in the rupee.
The RBI also likely intervened in the FX market on Monday to bolster the rupee's gains through dollar sales by state-run banks, traders said.
RALLY FACES A TEST
While the rupee has rallied sharply in the aftermath of the RBI's measures, the sustainability of the recovery will depend on whether underlying pressures subside, analysts say.
On Monday, the rally encountered one of its first hurdles when sharp rupee gains drew hedging-related flows into the non-deliverable forward market, a senior trader at a foreign bank said.
The flows were likely linked to hedging of foreign portfolio investments in India, the banker said. Persistent capital outflows - to the tune of over $30 billion from local stocks over 2026 so far - have been a persistent pain point for the rupee.
"Unless BoP pressures ease more broadly, gradual INR depreciation is likely to resume once their initial impact fades," analysts at ANZ said.
The firm has retained its medium-term INR depreciation view and said it will reassess levels after reviewing hedging and FX reserve data in the coming weeks.
India's FX reserves declined to $734 billion as of October 2 after hitting a record high of $785 billion in September.
Reporting by Nimesh Vora; Editing by Mrigank Dhaniwala, Sonia Cheema and Nivedita Bhattacharjee

articles.title: Starbucks says it is not buying Chipotle following deal speculation - Fox Business
articles.summary: Starbucks says it is not buying Chipotle following deal speculation  Fox BusinessStarbucks says it is not buying Chipotle after takeover speculation  CNBCStarbucks has explored takeover of Chipotle in restaurant megadeal  Financial TimesA Starbucks-Chipotle deal would be a high-stakes bet on Brian Niccol’s magic touch  Business InsiderStarbucks puts an end to acquisition reports  The Seattle Times
articles.full_text:
Starbucks is putting an end to speculation that it could acquire burrito chain Chipotle Mexican Grill.
A Starbucks spokesperson confirmed to FOX Business on Monday that the coffee giant is not buying Chipotle following a report that it had explored a potential deal.
"Our team is laser focused on executing our Back to Starbucks strategy. We have strong momentum and confidence in our long-term growth potential," the company reiterated. "We look forward to sharing our Q4 results, including FY27 guidance, later this month."
Talk of a possible deal began last week after the Financial Times reported that Starbucks had recently explored a potential bid for Chipotle with advisers.
The report cited people familiar with the matter.
"Starbucks has explored a takeover of Chipotle Mexican Grill, in an ambitious gambit to unite two of America’s best-known brands in a deal that would rank as the biggest-ever tie-up in the restaurant sector," the outlet reported.
Such a deal would have reunited Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol back at the center of the company he previously led.
Niccol spent six years as Chipotle's CEO before leaving in 2024 to take the top job at Starbucks.
During his tenure, Chipotle expanded its digital business and posted strong growth as it moved beyond earlier food-safety challenges, according to Reuters.
Chipotle shares jumped more than 7% following the initial report, while Starbucks shares fell about 3%, Reuters reported.
Those moves reversed Monday after Starbucks shut down the takeover speculation. Chipotle shares fell about 4% in afternoon trading, while Starbucks rose roughly 1.5%.
A combination of the two chains would have created a restaurant giant with roughly $50 billion in annual sales. Chipotle has a market capitalization of about $40 billion, according to Reuters.
Chipotle could not immediately be reached by FOX Business for comment.
Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Dollar Rises and Euro Falls in Cuba's Informal Market: Current Exchange Rates - CubaHeadlines
articles.summary: Dollar Rises and Euro Falls in Cuba's Informal Market: Current Exchange Rates  CubaHeadlines
articles.full_text:
At 10:00 a.m. local Cuban time, the informal currency market in Cuba kicked off the week showing mixed trends.
The U.S. dollar advanced by two pesos compared to the previous session, trading at 785 Cuban pesos, while the euro slightly dipped to 880 pesos, from 878 pesos the day before.
The MLC (a digital currency used for certain transactions) is approximately valued at 534 pesos, although this figure should be considered indicative due to the low volume of transactions backing it on Monday, October 12.
For a complete view of the exchange rate trends in Cuba's informal market, you can consult the detailed data.
The Dollar's Ascent
Currently, the U.S. dollar is priced at 785 Cuban pesos (CUP) in the informal market, with a buying rate of 780 CUP and a selling rate of 790 CUP.
This marks an increase of 2 pesos from the previous day, when the average was 783 CUP. Over the past week, the dollar has climbed from 773 pesos, reflecting a 12-peso rise or a 1.6% increase.
In the last month, the U.S. currency has surged from 693 pesos to its current 785 pesos, although part of this change might be due to methodological adjustments in the index.
The dollar is now at its highest point in the last 30 days, dominating the informal market amid a structural shortage of foreign currency.
Euro's Slight Decline
The euro is priced at 880 Cuban pesos (CUP) today, with a buying rate of 875 CUP and a selling rate of 885 CUP.
Compared to the previous day, when the average was 878 CUP, the euro has dropped by 2 pesos, yet it remains the most expensive currency in Cuba's parallel market.
On a weekly basis, the euro has risen by 5 pesos from the 875 it marked a week ago, a 0.6% increase. From 30 days ago, when it was at 787 pesos, the accumulated gain is 93 pesos, although this should be read cautiously due to potential index adjustments. It surpasses the dollar by 95 pesos, solidifying its dominant position in the informal market.
Indicative Value of MLC
The MLC is currently hovering around 534 Cuban pesos (CUP), with a buying rate of 499 CUP and a selling rate of 569 CUP.
Given the limited volume of transactions recorded during this time frame, this value should be seen as indicative.
Compared to the previous session, when the average was 497 CUP, there's an upward shift of 37 pesos, although the reliability of this figure is limited. A week ago, the MLC stood at 562 pesos, indicating a 5% decline over the week.
Exchange Rate Discrepancies
Over the past month, the dollar has fluctuated between a low of 693 CUP and a peak of 785 CUP, the latter being today's rate.
The euro has ranged from 787 CUP to 885 CUP, with the highest point recorded in recent days.
The MLC, displaying more volatility and fewer data points, has varied between 446 CUP and 603 CUP in the same period.
Gap with Official Rates
The official exchange rate set by the Central Bank of Cuba (Segment III) is 698 CUP for the dollar and 781 CUP for the euro, significantly lower than the rates governing the practical reality in the informal currency market.
Although Segment III was introduced as a more flexible currency mechanism, its official rate remains far from the informal market and fails to meet the real demand for foreign currency among the population.
Today, the gap between the markets surpasses 87 pesos for the dollar and 99 pesos for the euro.
In a scenario of persistent inflation, low state wages, and increasing partial dollarization of the economy, every fluctuation in the informal market directly impacts internal prices and the purchasing power of Cubans.
Methodology
The CiberCuba Exchange Rate Index is an analysis of the Cuban informal market based on automated scrutiny of thousands of currency exchange posts in Telegram and Facebook groups.
The calculation excludes atypical offers and spam, weights each transaction by its recency, and consolidates a representative value updated multiple times daily.
Conversion rates for U.S. Dollar (USD) to Cuban Peso (CUP) as of Monday, October 12, 2026:
- 1 USD = 785 CUP
- 5 USD = 3,925 CUP
- 10 USD = 7,850 CUP
- 20 USD = 15,700 CUP
- 50 USD = 39,250 CUP
- 100 USD = 78,500 CUP
Conversion rates for Euro (EUR) to Cuban Peso (CUP) as of Monday, October 12, 2026:
- 1 EUR = 880 CUP
- 5 EUR = 4,400 CUP
- 10 EUR = 8,800 CUP
- 20 EUR = 17,600 CUP
- 50 EUR = 44,000 CUP
- 100 EUR = 88,000 CUP
- 200 EUR = 176,000 CUP
Understanding Cuba's Informal Currency Market
Why is the U.S. dollar rising in Cuba's informal market?
The U.S. dollar is rising due to a structural shortage of foreign currency in Cuba, leading to increased demand in the informal market.
What is the significance of the gap between official and informal exchange rates?
The gap highlights the discrepancy between the official economic policies and the actual market conditions, impacting the real purchasing power of citizens.
How often are the informal market exchange rates updated?
The exchange rates are updated several times a day, based on the analysis of currency exchange posts in social media groups.

articles.title: WTI hits two-week high Middle East tensions overshadow Russian diesel supplies - FXStreet
articles.summary: WTI hits two-week high Middle East tensions overshadow Russian diesel supplies  FXStreet
articles.full_text:
West Texas Intermediate (WTI) Oil reverses course on Monday and climbs to a two-week high as doubts over a Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire and supply concerns in the Middle East keep a geopolitical premium in energy markets. At the time of writing, WTI trades around $93.50, up 2.75% on the day, recovering from an intraday low of $89.02.
Oil prices opened the week on a bearish note after US President Donald Trump announced on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate “energy ceasefire.” Trump also said on Friday that Russia would supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, equivalent to around 2.25 million barrels, to US and global markets, with additional shipments to follow.
However, these announcements provided only brief relief. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia struck six energy facilities in Ukraine on Monday, casting doubt on the ceasefire. Asked about Trump’s announcement, the Kremlin said, “Contacts are ongoing, we will inform you in due course.”
Middle East developments add further support to crude prices after Houthi strikes on Riyadh’s international airport over the weekend. The attacks come as Saudi-backed Yemeni forces fight to regain ground near Bab el-Mandeb, a key chokepoint for Red Sea shipping.
Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser said, “Globally, the squeeze on crude oil is serious,” adding, “Until Hormuz fully reopens and confidence returns, the pressure across the energy chain will only intensify.”
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said a third Oil supertanker struck a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz in the past two days. IRGC said the tanker was hit after disabling its navigation system, ignoring naval warnings and attempting to leave the waterway.
Meanwhile, OPEC Secretary General Haitham Al Ghais said on Monday that the group now expects global Oil demand to grow by 400,000 barrels per day in 2026, down from its forecast of 1.4 million at the start of the year.
WTI Oil FAQs
WTI Oil is a type of Crude Oil sold on international markets. The WTI stands for West Texas Intermediate, one of three major types including Brent and Dubai Crude. WTI is also referred to as “light” and “sweet” because of its relatively low gravity and sulfur content respectively. It is considered a high quality Oil that is easily refined. It is sourced in the United States and distributed via the Cushing hub, which is considered “The Pipeline Crossroads of the World”. It is a benchmark for the Oil market and WTI price is frequently quoted in the media.
Like all assets, supply and demand are the key drivers of WTI Oil price. As such, global growth can be a driver of increased demand and vice versa for weak global growth. Political instability, wars, and sanctions can disrupt supply and impact prices. The decisions of OPEC, a group of major Oil-producing countries, is another key driver of price. The value of the US Dollar influences the price of WTI Crude Oil, since Oil is predominantly traded in US Dollars, thus a weaker US Dollar can make Oil more affordable and vice versa.
The weekly Oil inventory reports published by the American Petroleum Institute (API) and the Energy Information Agency (EIA) impact the price of WTI Oil. Changes in inventories reflect fluctuating supply and demand. If the data shows a drop in inventories it can indicate increased demand, pushing up Oil price. Higher inventories can reflect increased supply, pushing down prices. API’s report is published every Tuesday and EIA’s the day after. Their results are usually similar, falling within 1% of each other 75% of the time. The EIA data is considered more reliable, since it is a government agency.
OPEC (Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries) is a group of 12 Oil-producing nations who collectively decide production quotas for member countries at twice-yearly meetings. Their decisions often impact WTI Oil prices. When OPEC decides to lower quotas, it can tighten supply, pushing up Oil prices. When OPEC increases production, it has the opposite effect. OPEC+ refers to an expanded group that includes ten extra non-OPEC members, the most notable of which is Russia.

articles.title: Dow Rises 200 Points, Nasdaq Wavers: China Chip Competition Hits Tech Stocks, Oil Climbs - TradingView
articles.summary: Dow Rises 200 Points, Nasdaq Wavers: China Chip Competition Hits Tech Stocks, Oil Climbs  TradingView
articles.full_text:
- U.S. stocks traded mixed on Monday, with the Dow rising more than 250 points while the Nasdaq Composite fell amid pressure on semiconductor stocks.
- Salesforce shares climbed after Bank of America upgraded the stock to ‘Buy’ from ‘Underperform’ and raised its price target to $285 from $160.
- Micron and SanDisk declined amid concerns about growing competition from China’s CXMT.
U.S. equities traded mixed on Monday, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average rising more than 200 points while the Nasdaq Composite slipped as Micron Technology (MU) and other chip stocks tumbled on concerns about competition from China’s CXMT.
Adding to market pressure, oil prices climbed amid renewed Russia-Ukraine tensions. Investors were also looking ahead to bank earnings, upcoming inflation data, and a Friday speech by Kevin Warsh this week.
The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) edged 0.04% lower at the time of writing, the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (DIA) gained 0.40%, and the Nasdaq-100 tracking Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) slipped as much as 0.60%. Retail sentiment around QQQ on Stocktwits dropped to ‘bullish’ from ‘extremely bullish’ over the past day.
CRM Gains Drive Dow Jones
The Dow received support from Salesforce (CRM), which rose after Bank of America (BofA) gave it a double upgrade to ‘Buy’ from ‘Underperform’ and raised its price target to $285 from $160.
The firm cited improving prospects for Salesforce’s artificial intelligence strategy and stated that large companies are unlikely to abandon established software platforms that house their business data and workflows.
The Nasdaq, on the other hand, faced pressure from semiconductor stocks. Concerns that CXMT could pose bigger competition in memory chips weighed on Micron (MU), SanDisk (SNDK) and other chip companies in the sector. SNDK stock tumbled 5.6% in midday trade, while MU stock fell by around 3%.
Wells Fargo’s double downgrade on Adobe (ADBE) also did not help. The firm downgraded the software maker to ‘Underweight’ from ‘Equal Weight’ and lowered its price target to $225 from $270. It cited concerns about slowing organic growth and the challenge of meeting Adobe’s full-year targets.
S&P 500 Holds Steady
The S&P 500, which covers a broader cross-section of large U.S. companies, held relatively steady as gains in some stocks offset losses elsewhere. eBay (EBAY) was among the top gainers, alongside names like Meta Platforms (META) and Biogen (BIIB).
EBAY stock was also among the top-trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing, gaining as much as 5.5% in the midday trade and marking an over-four-month high. The rally came after Morgan Stanley named the company its top pick in the internet sector. Retail sentiment around the shares on the platform trended in ‘bullish’ territory over the past day.
Cerebras Systems (CBRS) was among the top trending tickers on Stocktwits and one of the market’s biggest losers, falling 9.6% in midday trade, extending its decline after a report last week suggested OpenAI was using Nvidia (NVDA) chips rather than Cerebras’ hardware for a feature of its latest AI model. CBRS stock hit a record low of $147.77, leaving it at less than half of its $350 IPO price.
Oil Prices Rise Ahead Of Bank Earnings, Inflation Data
Oil prices added another source of uncertainty for investors. West Texas Intermediate crude futures expiring in November rose over 2% to around more than $93 a barrel in midday trade, while Brent crude futures expiring in December also gained around 2% to trade near $107 a barrel.
The most recent uptick comes after renewed attacks on energy infrastructure and questions over an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine announced by President Donald Trump over the weekend. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia had already violated the agreement, raising doubts about whether the arrangement would ease risks to energy supplies.
The United States Oil Fund (USO) rose around 2.3% in midday trade on Monday. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the ETF trended in ‘bearish’ territory over the past day.
Major U.S. banks are also due to report quarterly results this week, while the September consumer price index will offer a fresh reading on inflation and could influence expectations for the Federal Reserve’s next policy decision. Kevin Warsh is scheduled to speak later in the week at an International Monetary Fund and World Bank event in Bangkok.

articles.title: Gold Price Forecast — XAU/USD ($4,165) Slips 0.69% as Dollar Hits 102.4 and 10-Year Holds 5.24% — $4,050 Downside vs $4,289 Upside - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: Gold Price Forecast — XAU/USD ($4,165) Slips 0.69% as Dollar Hits 102.4 and 10-Year Holds 5.24% — $4,050 Downside vs $4,289 Upside  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Gold Fails at $4,218 as Fed Hike Odds Hit 85% for December — $4,109.90 Low Now in Focus
Gold trades 25.5% below its $5,589.38 record as oil-driven inflation fears keep real yields and the dollar elevated | That's TradingNEWS
Key Points
- Spot gold falls $28.91, or 0.69%, to $4,164.96 after failing at an overnight high of $4,218.10.
- The dollar index tops 102.4, its strongest level since April 2025, as Fed hike bets hold firm.
- Traders price an 85% chance of a Fed hike by December, versus under 20% for October 28.
Spot gold traded at $4,164.96 an ounce on Monday, October 12, 2026, down $28.91 or 0.69% from Friday’s $4,193.87 settlement. December gold futures on Comex were at $4,192.30 near midday in New York, down $24.00 or 0.57% from Friday’s $4,216.30 close. The metal opened the week with a push toward $4,218.10 in early Asian trade, then gave back $53 from that high as the dollar firmed and crude oil reversed higher.
The intraday path was a straight line down from the overnight peak. Spot was at $4,175.60 by 4:32 a.m. ET, already $18.00 lower on the day, then slipped to $4,164.85 by 9:00 a.m. ET, below Friday’s $4,174.78 reading at the same hour. The 8:55 a.m. ET print of $4,163 put gold $6 under its October 9 level at that time. Every attempt to rebuild a bid during the U.S. morning ran into a dollar index above 102.4 and a crude market that had flipped from a 1% loss to a 2% gain.
Friday’s session had looked like the start of a recovery. Gold climbed more than 1% to a one-week high on a softer dollar and lower oil, and December futures closed up $59.30, or 1.43%, at $4,216.30. That move came three sessions after spot gold closed at $4,109.90 on October 7, its lowest level since August 5, following a 1.28% one-day drop. Monday’s reversal leaves the Friday rally looking like a short-covering bounce inside a downtrend rather than a turn.
The bigger picture is a metal that has lost a quarter of its value in nine months. Spot gold set a record of $5,589.38 an ounce on January 28, 2026. At $4,164.96 it trades 25.5% below that peak, a drawdown of $1,424.42 per ounce. Over the past month gold is down 3.12%, and against $4,389 a month ago the decline is 5.15%. Over 12 months the metal is up only 1.31%, a near-flat year for an asset that was the best-performing major market of 2025.
That loss of momentum came while equities kept rising. The S&P 500 was at 7,814.66 near midday, up 13.90% year to date through Friday. Gold’s failure to participate in a year of war, inflation and record stock prices comes down to one variable: the price of money. With the 10-year Treasury yield at 5.24% and the Federal Reserve still debating another hike, holding a metal that pays nothing has become expensive, and Monday’s tape showed that cost again.
Why Friday’s Rally Faded: Oil Reverses and the Dollar Pushes Above 102.4
Gold’s two-day advance into Monday rested on falling oil. Gold traded near $4,200 an ounce early in the session after rising for two straight days, as crude prices eased on hopes that Russian diesel supplies would relieve global fuel shortages and dampen inflation concerns. On Friday, President Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, the equivalent of 2.25 million barrels, to U.S. and global markets, with another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons after that. On Sunday he added that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt attacks on each other’s energy infrastructure. WTI futures fell more than 1% to below $90 a barrel in Asian hours.
Both legs of that story broke within hours. Ukrainian officials said they had not been consulted on the ceasefire, and Russian strikes on Ukraine’s power plants continued. Over the weekend, Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia’s main airport killed 12 people, and Trump suggested the United States may join Saudi retaliation. By midday in New York, November WTI was at $93.70, up $1.85 or 2.01%, and Brent was trading near $106 after hovering just below $107 at the U.S. equity open.
The diesel numbers explain why the oil market looked through the announcement. The first tranche of 2.25 million barrels compares with global diesel consumption of close to 29 million barrels a day, less than 8% of a single day’s demand. Even the full 1.8 million tons covers well under two days of world consumption. Once traders did that math, the inflation relief priced into gold on Friday came out.
The dollar did the rest. The U.S. dollar index traded above 102.4 on Monday morning, up from Friday’s 102.23 close and holding at a level last reached in April 2025. A stronger dollar makes each ounce more expensive for buyers in euros, yen, rupees and yuan, and it has been the steadiest headwind for gold since September. The dollar advanced modestly in thin holiday trading, supported by bets that the Fed will hike rates at least once more before year-end.
The holiday itself mattered. U.S. bond markets are closed for Columbus Day, which removed the Treasury market as a live counterweight. With no new yield data, the dollar became the only real-time rate proxy, and it moved against gold all morning. That combination of oil, dollar and frozen yields at 24-year highs turned a $4,218 overnight high into a $4,165 midday print.
25.5% Below the $5,589.38 Record: Anatomy of the 2026 Drawdown
Gold’s slide from its January peak has unfolded in stages, and each stage traces back to the same chain: war, oil, inflation, rates.
The first leg started with the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran in late February. Conventional wisdom says war is bullish for gold, and the initial reaction followed that script. The longer-term effect was the opposite. Spot gold has fallen more than 20% since the conflict began, pressured by expectations that conflict-driven inflation would keep interest rates higher for longer. Crude oil, not safe-haven buying, became the dominant transmission channel, and oil above $90 pushed central banks away from easing.
The second leg came in September, when both the Federal Reserve and the Bank of Japan raised rates. A Fed hike in a year when markets had expected cuts was a direct hit to the case for owning a non-yielding asset, and the Bank of Japan’s move removed one of the last sources of cheap global funding. Gold’s slide accelerated after those decisions and has not been reversed.
The third leg ran from late September into October. Spot gold traded at $4,265.30 on September 24, down 0.48% that session, with silver near $63.47. Within days the metal hit a seven-week low as December futures dropped 3.1% to $4,186.70 in a single session and spot silver fell close to 5% to $61.17. By October 2, spot gold was at $4,140.06, down 3.4% for the week, its second straight weekly loss. On October 7, spot closed at $4,109.90, the lowest since early August.
The numbers across the year are stark. Late in September spot gold was down 4.2% for 2026. Monday’s $4,164.96 sits at a similar point. Gold that was worth $5,589.38 on January 28 now buys 25.5% less, and an investor who bought the record high needs a 34.2% rally just to get back to breakeven.
There is a buyer’s case inside that drawdown. Gold is still up from $4,078 a year ago, and the decline has taken out the speculative excess that drove the January spike. Mining stocks have corrected even harder, and sentiment has swung from euphoric to defensive in nine months. That is the setup that preceded several of gold’s strongest multi-year runs. What it lacks is a catalyst, and every potential catalyst on the calendar this week runs through the inflation data.
The 5.24% 10-Year and the Real-Rate Squeeze on Gold
Gold’s biggest problem is a number it cannot influence: the 10-year Treasury yield at 5.24%. That is a 24-year high, reached on October 7 when the yield printed 5.28%, its highest level since 2002, and it has held in a 5.24% to 5.28% band since. On Monday the yield is frozen because the bond market is closed for Columbus Day, but the level alone is enough to weigh on bullion.
The opportunity-cost math is direct. An investor holding one ounce of gold at $4,164.96 is giving up $218.24 a year in risk-free income at a 5.24% yield. Across a $100,000 position, the forgone income is $5,240 annually. When the 10-year sat in the low 4% range during gold’s 2025 run, that cost was close to $1,000 lower per $100,000. The extra hurdle falls hardest on the institutional allocators who move gold’s price at the margin, the same pensions, endowments and wealth managers that buy through GLD and IAU.
Real yields amplify the effect. Gold competes most directly with inflation-adjusted Treasury returns, and those rose sharply as nominal yields outpaced inflation expectations through September. A surge in real yields was flagged as the biggest test of gold’s resilience, alongside a firmer dollar and the metal’s break below $4,230 an ounce. That break happened in late September and has not been repaired.
The global bond picture removes any escape route. Yields are rising across developed markets, with French government debt among the weakest in Europe, and talk of 30-year U.S. mortgage rates reaching 8% has returned. In past cycles, gold often benefited when one major bond market sold off and capital looked for a neutral store of value. In 2026 every major bond market is selling off at once, which raises the opportunity cost everywhere instead of pushing money into bullion.
The long-dated Treasury ETF, TLT, gained more than 2% in the second half of last week before yields ticked higher again on Monday, and gold’s Friday rally lined up with that brief bond bounce. The relationship is tight enough to trade: a 10-year back below 5.20% would likely lift gold through $4,218, while a print above 5.28% on Tuesday’s reopening would put the October 7 low of $4,109.90 back in play.
The Fed Path: Under 20% for October 28, 85% by December
The Federal Reserve sets the ceiling on gold this month. After raising rates in September, the central bank meets again on Oct

articles.title: Indian Gas Exchange secures Sebi's nod to float IPO - The Economic Times
articles.summary: Indian Gas Exchange secures Sebi's nod to float IPO  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
The proposed public issue is entirely an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 1.67 crore equity shares by promoter Indian Energy Exchange Ltd (IEX), according to the draft red herring prospectus (DRHP).
As the issue is entirely an OFS, IGX will not receive any proceeds from the IPO. The entire proceeds will go to the selling shareholder, IEX.
The company had filed its preliminary IPO papers in July. After reviewing the draft prospectus, Sebi gave its final observation on October 12.
Sebi's observations mark an important step in the IPO process, allowing the company to proceed with the preparations for the public issue, subject to applicable regulatory requirements.
Indian Energy Exchange holds over 47 per cent stake in IGX, and as per regulations, it has to bring it down to 25 per cent.
IGX was incorporated in November 2019 as a wholly-owned subsidiary of IEX.
Its electronic gas trading platform was inaugurated in June 2020, and it received authorisation from the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB) to operate as a gas exchange in December 2020.
The company operates a technology-enabled electronic marketplace for trading natural gas through standardised physical delivery-based contracts across multiple delivery hubs connected to India's national gas pipeline network.
According to the draft papers, unlike several international gas exchanges where a significant share of contracts are financially settled, IGX operates a physical delivery-based market and also offers forward contracts with tenures of up to six months.
For the financial year ended March 2026, the company reported revenue from operations of Rs 61 crore, compared with Rs 48.8 crore in FY25 and Rs 34.8 crore in FY24.
In January, IGX's Managing Director and CEO Rajesh Kumar Mediratta had stated that the country's first online delivery-based natural gas trading platform was targeting an IPO by December 2026.
Axis Capital and Motilal Oswal Investment Advisors are the book-running lead managers to the issue, while KFin Technologies is the registrar.

articles.full_text:
Defence startup Tonbo Imaging fixes IPO price band at ₹665-700 a share
The offer for sale of up to 12.17 million shares opens on October 15. The Bengaluru-based company has deployed more than 28,000 systems across 24 countries.
Listen to This Article
Defence electronics startup Tonbo Imaging India Ltd will open its initial public offering on October 15, 2026, with the bidding window closing on October 19. The anchor investor bidding date is October 14, one working day before the offer opens.
The price band has been set at ₹665 to ₹700 per equity share with a face value of ₹2 each. Investors can bid for a minimum of 21 shares and in multiples of 21 shares thereafter.
The offer comprises entirely an offer for sale of up to 12,174,046 equity shares.
Bengaluru-based Tonbo develops and manufactures sensing, processing, communication and guidance systems for surveillance, reconnaissance, targeting and control. Its product portfolio includes thermal imaging cores, weapon sights, handheld thermal imaging binoculars, targeting systems, missile seekers and fire control systems, offered through its Tactical Systems and Platform Systems verticals. The company is also developing directed energy systems to counter drone swarms. As of June 30, 2026, Tonbo Imaging had deployed over 28,000 systems across 24 countries.
The company is led by its promoters, Arvind Kondangi Lakshmikumar, managing director and chief executive officer, Ankit Kumar and Cecilia D’Souza. Tonbo Imaging designs and develops its products in India, enabling its electro-optics and infrared portfolio to remain free from US International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) restrictions. Since FY24, the company has owned 100 per cent of the intellectual property used in its products. It follows an asset-light operating model, with design, prototyping and testing undertaken at its Bengaluru R&D centre, while large-scale manufacturing is outsourced to certified electronics manufacturing partners.
Also Read
The equity shares of the company are proposed to be listed on BSE Limited and the National Stock Exchange of India Limited.
JM Financial Limited and IIFL Capital Services Limited are the book-running lead managers to the offer.
Tonbo Imaging reported revenue from operations of ₹362.65 crore in FY26, down 22.69 per cent from ₹469.08 crore in FY25, while profit after tax declined to ₹50.88 crore from ₹72.76 crore. The decline was primarily attributed to delays in executing international orders due to the West Asia conflict and the deferment of certain anticipated orders to FY27.
In Q1FY27, revenue from operations stood at ₹36.01 crore, with a net loss of ₹17.74 crore, reflecting lower revenue recognition amid seasonal factors and slower order execution.

articles.title: UK Growth Figures, US Inflation and French Protests: Sterling Update - FrenchEntrée
articles.summary: UK Growth Figures, US Inflation and French Protests: Sterling Update  FrenchEntrée
articles.full_text:
Here’s the latest currency news from our partner Moneycorp, to help you find out what your money is worth.
Sterling faces a busy week, with UK monthly activity figures and a series of Bank of England speeches likely to shape expectations for interest rates. Meanwhile, the euro remains under pressure from political uncertainty and protests in France and Spain, while markets await the latest US inflation data for clues on the Federal Reserve’s next move.
The International Monetary Fund’s latest global economic forecasts will also be in focus, with concerns over weak growth, rising borrowing costs and geopolitical tensions weighing on the outlook. Across North America, comments from the Bank of Canada and continued pressure on the Mexican peso add to a packed week for currency markets.
UK monthly activity figures in focus, alongside Bank of England speeches
This week sees the release of UK monthly activity figures for August on Thursday, alongside a series of Bank of England speakers throughout the week.
The case for a further increase in official interest rates continues to centre on inflationary pressures, although there remain limited signs that these pressures are being driven by the domestic economy.
Sterling remains under pressure against the US dollar but continues to hold up well against the euro. This divergence appears to be driven more by developments in those economies than by domestic UK factors.
One additional area of interest is today’s parliamentary debate on rejoining the European Union. However, this is unlikely to alter the UK’s position on EU membership in the near term, in my view.
IMF forecasts to offer few crumbs of comfort
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) will release its full global economic report this week, following earlier warnings about rising debt servicing costs.
The report, due on Tuesday, is unlikely to offer much relief to financial markets, given weak global growth, geopolitical tensions and further increases in government borrowing costs.
There could be downward revisions to growth expectations across the UK, the euro area and North America.
US CPI figures for September in focus this week
This week is likely to see considerable attention focused on the US consumer price index (CPI) inflation figures for September, due on Wednesday.
Markets will be watching to see whether core inflationary pressures have picked up or whether inflation remains largely concentrated in more volatile headline components such as energy, fuel and food.
Producer price index (PPI) figures, industrial production data and Federal Reserve staff projections are also due this week. However, alongside the CPI figures, comments from Fed officials are likely to attract the greatest attention.
Will the Fed argue for a further immediate increase in interest rates, or are concerns about parts of the US economy sufficient to keep policymakers on hold at their meeting at the end of October?
In my view, US dollar strength may prove another factor arguing against an additional rate increase at this month’s meeting.
Energy markets could also remain in focus, as renewed tensions in the Middle East and recent comments from President Trump regarding a possible energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine add another layer of uncertainty to the inflation outlook.
ECB speeches and political uncertainty to determine euro direction
The European Central Bank (ECB) appears to be preparing markets for another interest rate increase, potentially as early as the Governing Council meeting at the end of October.
Speeches last week indicated that several ECB officials believe acting sooner could provide a credibility boost to their efforts to tackle inflation, although I would question that assessment.

articles.title: Indian Gas Exchange IPO gets SEBI nod for ₹1.67 crore share offer by promoter IEX - CNBC TV18
articles.summary: Indian Gas Exchange IPO gets SEBI nod for ₹1.67 crore share offer by promoter IEX  CNBC TV18
articles.full_text:
Indian Gas Exchange has received SEBI approval for its IPO, featuring an offer for sale of up to 1.67 crore shares by promoter IEX. The move helps IEX reduce its stake to 25% while giving IGX public market visibility.
Indian Gas Exchange (IGX), India’s first online delivery-based natural gas trading platform, has received approval from the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) to launch its initial public offering (IPO), according to an update on the regulator’s website on Monday, October 12.
The proposed IPO will comprise an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 1.67 crore equity shares by promoter Indian Energy Exchange (IEX), according to the draft red herring prospectus (DRHP). As the issue consists entirely of an OFS, IGX will not receive any proceeds from the offering, with the entire amount going to IEX.
IGX filed its preliminary IPO papers in July, and SEBI issued its final observation on October 12, allowing the company to proceed with the next steps in the listing process, subject to applicable regulatory requirements.
The IPO is aimed at securing the benefits of a stock market listing, including greater visibility, a stronger brand presence and a public market for the company’s shares, the draft papers stated.
IEX holds more than 47% of IGX, and the listing is part of the process of reducing its stake to 25%, in line with applicable regulatory requirements.
IGX’s business and financial performance
Incorporated in November 2019 as a wholly owned subsidiary of IEX, IGX operates an electronic marketplace for trading natural gas through standardised physical delivery-based contracts across multiple delivery hubs connected to India’s national gas pipeline network.
Its trading platform was inaugurated in June 2020, and the company received authorisation from the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB) to operate as a gas exchange in December 2020.
Also read: ICICI Prudential AMC declares record dividend as Q2 profit rises 6%
Unlike several international gas exchanges, where a significant proportion of contracts are financially settled, IGX operates a physical delivery-based market. It also offers forward contracts with tenures of up to six months, according to the DRHP.
For the financial year ended March 2026, IGX reported revenue from operations of ₹61 crore, compared with ₹48.8 crore in the previous financial year and ₹34.8 crore in FY24.
In January, IGX Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer Rajesh Kumar Mediratta said the company was targeting an IPO by December 2026.
Axis Capital and Motilal Oswal Investment Advisors are the book-running lead managers for the issue, while KFin Technologies is the registrar.
IPO market activity
IGX’s Sebi approval comes amid continued activity in India’s primary market. Companies have raised more than ₹1.1 lakh crore through 96 public issues so far in 2026, according to the figures provided. Several more IPOs are scheduled to launch this month.

articles.title: Renewable energy assets in emerging markets could help mitigate risk for Norway’s sovereign wealth fund - Zero Carbon Analytics
articles.summary: Renewable energy assets in emerging markets could help mitigate risk for Norway’s sovereign wealth fund  Zero Carbon Analytics
articles.full_text:
Key points
- Norway’s sovereign wealth fund – the world’s single largest asset owner – is looking for ways to reduce its exposure to rising geopolitical and concentration risk.
- The Fund has a 2% cap on investments in unlisted renewables, set by Norway’s finance ministry. However, this type of asset only accounts for 0.5% of the Fund’s current portfolio, with investments limited to Europe and North America.
- ZCA analysis finds that meeting the 2% cap would mobilise an additional USD 37.7 billion for the global energy transition, while also de-risking projects and attracting additional capital. Raising it to 5% would mobilise over USD 110 billion. Even at this level, the Fund would not be the biggest investor in renewable energy globally.
- A study by the International Finance Corporation and the European Investment Bank has shown that renewable energy projects in emerging markets have default and loan recovery rates comparable to those in advanced economies, suggesting that perceived risk is often overstated.
- Diversification into emerging markets can improve resilience. They exhibit lower correlation with developed markets at specific points in the macroeconomic cycle because their returns are driven by different technology adoption, trade and consumption patterns – particularly relevant for renewables.
- Opening the Fund’s 2% unlisted renewables mandate to emerging markets could enhance portfolio diversification and mobilise USD 37.7 billion in additional energy transition finance – even without raising the cap.
- In the longer term, raising the cap to 5% would contribute to broader asset diversification and could mobilise over USD 110 billion.
Norway’s Sovereign Wealth Fund is looking for ways to diversify risk
Norway’s sovereign wealth fund is the world’s single largest asset owner. Its assets were valued at NOK 22,683 billion (USD 2.4 billion) as of the first half of 2026, and it holds stakes in around 1.5% of the world’s publicly listed stocks.
In November 2025, Norway’s government appointed a public committee to review the ethical investment framework governing the fund. The committee is scheduled to deliver its report on 15 October 2026.
At the same time, Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), which manages the fund, is considering how it can broaden its asset allocation strategy to mitigate concentration and geopolitical risks, at a time when US tech companies are dominating equity markets and government bonds are becoming riskier.
The fund is taking steps to pursue unlisted renewable energy infrastructure, within a 2% investment ceiling.
Since 2019, Norway’s finance ministry has allowed the Fund to allocate up to 2% of its portfolio to unlisted renewable energy infrastructure.
In its 2018 assessment of a potential renewable energy mandate, NBIM noted that the fund’s size and limited liquidity needs give the Bank an advantage in projects with high upfront capital requirements, with solar and wind farms highlighted as the most relevant candidates.
NBIM’s 2025 Annual report explained that its approach to unlisted renewables so far has been to “gradually approach investment opportunities and develop expertise.”
Renewables projects benefit from long-term power contracts with fixed prices, shifting investor risk away from regulatory and political risk, and toward power price movements and end-user profiles, which the Fund is “better suited to bear, and that the Bank has experience of assessing,” according to the 2018 assessment.
Its 2020-2022 strategy expanded on the rationale, noting the fund “seek(s) to invest in unlisted renewable energy infrastructure to improve the overall risk-return characteristics of the fund,” while its 2030 climate action plan set ambitions to “increase our investments in renewable energy infrastructure…focus(ing) on renewable electricity generation and storage, electricity grids, and renewable energy infrastructure funds.”
Norges Bank has also proposed that renewable investments can be carried out under the fund’s existing environment-related investment mandate, which could mean increasing the upper limit of its environmental mandates.
Unlisted renewables account for just 0.5% of the current portfolio, despite the 2% cap
The Fund has been gradually increasing its allocations to unlisted renewable energy infrastructure since the 2% cap was announced, driven by “improved return expectations” and better in-house expertise.
However, unlisted renewables still account for just 0.5% of the total portfolio as of mid-2026. In June 2026, direct investments in wind, solar and related assets amounted to 104 billion kroner (USD 11.2 billion), while the total portfolio was valued at 22.7 trillion kroner (USD 2.4 trillion), making unlisted renewables by far the smallest allocation among the Fund’s four primary asset classes.1The four primary asset classes are equities, fixed income, unlisted real estate and unlisted renewable energy infrastructure.
The Fund has been unusually explicit about plans to expand its renewable investments since the conflict in Iran caused clean energy-related stocks to gain in value. On 5 May 2026, NBIM’s CEO stated the Fund is on track to reach 1% of assets in unlisted renewable energy infrastructure by 2030, with potential expansion to 2%, given market opportunities.
Meeting the 2% cap would mobilise an additional USD 37.7 billion for the energy transition – raising it to 5% would mobilise over USD 110 billion
If the Fund’s 2% allocation ceiling were met, its unlisted renewables portfolio would be worth USD 48.9 billion (NOK 453.7 billion) per the fund’s current market value, implying that it alone would mobilise an additional USD 37.7 billion for the global energy transition, either by recycling capital for developers or by funding new projects.2Calculated as 2% of the fund’s current market value (22,683 billion kroner as of end-June 2026), minus the fund’s existing investments in unlisted renewables.
This roughly equals the total private sector clean energy investment in Africa in 2024.
Expanding the cap to a 5% allocation to unlisted renewables would amount to USD 122.2 billion (NOK 1.1 trillion) based on the overall fund’s half-year valuation – an additional USD 111 billion for the energy transition.3Calculated as 5% of the fund’s current market value (22,683 billion kroner as of end-June 2026), minus the fund’s existing investments in unlisted renewables.
This would also imply substantial further capital mobilisation for the energy transition, as the fund’s investments would likely de-risk projects and crowd in secondary capital.
Comparable funds are investing more in unlisted renewables
Even at these higher levels, the Fund would still not be the largest renewable energy investor globally. Brookfield has USD 144 billion worth of clean energy assets under management, with a total generating capacity of 46 GW.
Japan’s Government Pension Investment Fund, the world’s second-largest asset owner after NBIM, is also looking to increase both alternative and infrastructure investments, nudging them closer to the fund’s 5% cap, and taking initiatives toward impact investing to diversify its portfolio and reduce investment risk.
Emerging markets offer an opportunity as investors look to diversify globally
The Fund’s investment mandate, set by the Norges Bank’s Executive Board, currently states that direct investment in unlisted renewable energy infrastructure “can only be undertaken in developed markets in Europe and North America.”
However, elevated macro-level volatility has sparked a trend among investors to look towards Europe and emerging markets. Investors globally are strongly concentrated in sectors such as technology and, in turn, are exposed to geographic and market concentration risk.
In a September 2026 letter to the Finance Ministry, Norway’s sovereign wealth fund noted the interplay between geopolitical and concentration risk and that they may reinforce each other. It also stated there may be “reason to consider” broader diversification across asset classes through “an increased allocation to unlisted assets over time”, including unlisted renewable infrastructure, which could “give the fund exposure to a broader set of sources of risk and reduce the significance of the concentration in the equity index for the fund’s overall risk profile.”
As the Fund looks to diversify its risk exposure, emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs) offer an opportunity. They tend to have lower correlation with developed markets during macroeconomic shifts, meaning they can provide resilience during economic downturns in developed markets. This is because their returns are driven by different technology adoption, trade and consumption patterns – particularly relevant for renewable energy investments.
The Fund is already indirectly exposed to markets beyond Europe and North America in its unlisted renewable energy investments. Its investment in Brookfield’s Global Transition Fund II currently has underlying exposure to South America and Asia-Pacific, as well as North America and Europe, through entities such as India’s renewable energy development platform Evren.
Studies indicate a gap between perceived risk and actual performance of renewable energy assets in emerging markets
Investors tend to be cautious when investing in emerging markets due to a perception of high risk. However, the Global Emerging Markets Risk Database (GEMs), created by the European Investment Bank and the International Finance Corporation, drew on over 30 years of historical EMDE data and found that the likelihood of default was lower than expected, and the likelihood of recovery was higher than expected.

articles.title: Nobel economics prize rewards the theory behind ECB rate decisions - Brussels Signal
articles.summary: Nobel economics prize rewards the theory behind ECB rate decisions  Brussels Signal
articles.full_text:
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford for “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”. The two Americans have spent their careers explaining how the decisions of households and firms add up to inflation, unemployment and the slumps that governments try to cushion.
Hall teaches at Stanford University and Woodford at Columbia University. They share a prize of 12 million Swedish crowns, about €1.1 million, announced in Stockholm on October 12.
The academy said the pair had built models that allowed governments and central banks to time fiscal and monetary measures more precisely. John Hassler, who chairs the prize committee, said economies were now “better equipped to deal with shocks” such as energy crises.
That is close to a description of the European Central Bank’s past year. On June 11 the bank raised its three key interest rates by 25 basis points, the first increase since September 2023, after the war in the Middle East drove energy costs up and pushed euro area inflation above 3 per cent.
The deposit rate now stands at 2.25 per cent. ECB President Christine Lagarde presented the move as a signal meant to stop the energy shock from spreading into wider prices.
Woodford’s 2003 book Interest and Prices became the standard text for inflation targeting and he has advised the Riksbank, the Swedish central bank that funds the award. Much of his later work concerns expectations, which is why central banks now treat their own communication as an instrument of policy.
Hall, a senior fellow at Stanford’s Hoover Institution, long chaired the committee at the National Bureau of Economic Research that decides when American recessions begin and end. His research on consumption undercut the assumption that household spending moves predictably with income.
The theory has not settled the European quarrel over who should do the stabilising and with whose money. The European Commission rejected Italian and Greek requests for more room under the EU fiscal rules on October 8, with the bloc’s deficit projected to reach 3.5 per cent of GDP this year and average 10-year borrowing costs at 4 per cent.
Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis argued that adding exemptions would damage the credibility of the rules themselves. Eurogroup President Kyriakos Pierrakakis said ministers agreed that support measures should stay temporary and targeted.
The economics prize is not part of Alfred Nobel’s bequest. It was created by the Riksbank in 1968 to mark the bank’s 300th anniversary and first awarded a year later to Ragnar Frisch of Norway and Jan Tinbergen of the Netherlands.

articles.title: Food, fuel and precious metals drive September retail inflation to 23-month high of 5.5% - The Hindu
articles.summary: Food, fuel and precious metals drive September retail inflation to 23-month high of 5.5%  The HinduRetail Inflation Shoots Up To 5.54% In September, Onion Prices Double  NDTVRetail inflation rises to 5.54% in September on costlier food items  Telegraph IndiaRetail prices of 41 of 42 essential commodities up in a year; onion rates shoot up almost 113%  The Times of IndiaInflation generalisation: Why price pressures are spreading, and what it means for inter...
articles.full_text:
Retail inflation rose to a nearly two-year high of 5.5% in September 2026, driven up by a continued acceleration in food and fuel inflation, official data released on Monday (October 12, 2026) showed.
Inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI) in September 2026 was the highest since October 2024. The rate in September also marked a substantial increase over the 4.8% rate seen in August 2026. The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) upper comfort limit for retail inflation is 6%.
According to economists, this acceleration of inflation shows the RBI’s Monetary Policy Committee was correct in hiking rates in its most recent policy review last week.
“With the CPI inflation jumping to a slightly higher than forecast 5.5% in September 2026 and appearing set to cross 6% in the ongoing month, the MPC’s recent rate hike appears prescient,” Aditi Nayar, chief economist at ICRA said.
“While the monsoon has turned out to be fairly dismal, with inadequate replenishment of reservoirs clouding the outlook for rabi sowing, another rate hike in December seems quite certain,” she added. “Crude oil prices currently remain elevated, and their trajectory will keenly influence the likelihood and extent of further rate tightening in 2027.”
Inflation in the food and beverages category jumped to 7.4% in September 2026 from 5.7% in the previous month. The new series of the CPI does not provide category-wise historical data before January 2026. The data shows September’s food inflation rate is the highest during the period for which there is data.
Inflation in the transport segment came in at 5% in September 2026, having risen for the last five consecutive months. Taken together, the food and transport prices pushed inflation in the ‘restaurant and accommodation services’ segment to 9.4%, capping off a seven-month streak of consecutive acceleration.
The third segment that saw elevated inflation was that of ‘personal care, social protection and miscellaneous goods & services’, which saw inflation come in at 13.75% in September 2026, although this was the lowest it has been in the period for which there is data.
“In the case of personal care, where inflation was 13.8%, it is mainly due to silver and gold where prices are determined externally,” Madan Sabnavis, chief economist at the Bank of Baroda, said. “Industries like durables, FMCG, automobile have announced an increase in prices and this should get reflected in the CPI over the next few months.”

articles.title: Bank of England targeted in inflation installation stunt - City AM
articles.summary: Bank of England targeted in inflation installation stunt  City AM
articles.full_text:
The Bank of England has been targeted in an inflation installation stunt in the centre of the City of London.
Over the weekend, a satirical art piece appeared across the road from the central bank’s office on Threadneedle Street.
A black Canon printer, sitting atop a decorative silver-beaded pedestal surrounded by a stream of banknotes, was locked inside a tall transparent display case. The case, held up by a bright red frame, reads: “In case of emergency inflation. Break Glass.”
A pair of black handcuffs was also resting on the base of the pedestal.
The installation appears to satirise a Bank of England strategy known as “quantitative easing,” that involves the creation of new money to purchase government bonds from private institutions.
The method aims to inject liquidity into the financial system in a bid to lower interest rates, encourage borrowing and stimulate spending.
The Bank first started the programme in March 2009 following the financial crisis. In 2022, it began to reverse the operation with quantitative tightening, where it allowed bonds to mature without replacing them. Last month, the Bank laid out plans to slow down its reduction pace to ease pressure on public debt markets and bond yields.
Mystery artist plays on inflation fears
Questions are swirling in the City over who was behind the installation, with the style matching previous works of political street artist Banksy. Earlier this year it emerged that the removal of three Banksy stunts in London had cost taxpayers nearly £150,000.
The largest of those bills related to a mural painted on the Royal Courts of Justice in London in September 2025, which came with a hefty removal price tag of £85,000. A spokesperson for Banksy confirmed they were not behind the Bank stunt.
The new stunt targeting the Bank comes as inflation fears in the UK rise following economic turmoil from the Iran war. Printing money via quantitative easing would generally be expected to stoke inflation even more.
The latest inflation index report from accounting and advisory firm BDO showed a reading of 103.65, up from 102.18 in August. It marked its highest reading since June 2023.
Elevated costs and weakening demand were cited as putting pressure on businesses ahead of the forthcoming Autumn Budget.
The surge in inflation is tipped to take a chunk out of Chancellor John Healey’s headroom at the forthcoming Budget. Influential think tank the Institute for Fiscal Studies has forecast that Healey might have to top up department budgets by as much as £35bn by the end of the decade following rampant inflation.
A spokesperson for the City of London Corporation said: “The origins of this piece are currently unknown. Temporary protective measures have been put in place to ensure public safety while enquiries continue.”
The Bank of England were approached for comment.

The Pound to New Zealand Dollar (GBP/NZD) exchange rate climbed to 2.3641 on Monday, approaching October highs as renewed energy-price concerns weighed on the Kiwi.
UK GDP and New Zealand manufacturing figures will provide the next tests.
WEEKLY RECAP:
GBP/NZD edged higher on Monday after spending much of last week trading close to 2.36.
The pair gained 2.9% during September, with the New Zealand Dollar struggling against persistent energy-market volatility and a stronger US Dollar.
Pound Sterling has also faced pressure, although expectations of another Bank of England interest-rate increase have provided some support.
MUFG expects the BoE to raise rates in November but warns that confidence in Britain's public finances remains crucial ahead of the 28 October Budget.
The Kiwi faces a different problem.
New Zealand's inflation outlook has deteriorated, with higher fuel costs pushing consumer prices higher despite an uneven domestic recovery.
Westpac Chief Economist Kelly Eckhold now expects inflation to reach 4.2% in December, compared with an earlier forecast of 3.7% for September.
He cautioned: "Growth forecasts are revised down and have downside risks."
The Reserve Bank of New Zealand raised interest rates to 2.75% in September, although Westpac expects policymakers to pause at their next meeting on 28 October before increasing rates to 3% in December.
That prospective tightening offers the Kiwi some support, but weak housing activity and concerns about household spending have limited its recovery.
Near-Term GBP/NZD Forecast: UK GDP and New Zealand Manufacturing in Focus
For Pound Sterling, Thursday's UK GDP release is the week's principal event.
Economists expect the economy to contract 0.1% in August following July's 0.4% expansion. Manufacturing, industrial production and trade figures are also scheduled.
Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey's remarks on Wednesday and Friday could influence expectations for November's policy decision.
For the New Zealand Dollar, Tuesday brings visitor arrivals, followed by Thursday's BusinessNZ Manufacturing Index and Food Price Index, released late in the UK evening.
China's inflation and trade figures will also influence sentiment towards the export-sensitive Kiwi.
Stronger UK data alongside disappointing New Zealand manufacturing figures could push GBP/NZD towards 2.3800.
However, weak UK growth and improving New Zealand activity could pull the pair back towards 2.3400.
In the near-term, Exchange Rates UK Research forecast that the Pound to New Zealand Dollar exchange rate will trade within the 2.3400-2.3800 range.
