articles.title: SEBI Plans To Bring Share Buybacks, Tender Offers And OFS Under Clearing Interoperability By Next Month - Free Press Journal
articles.summary: SEBI Plans To Bring Share Buybacks, Tender Offers And OFS Under Clearing Interoperability By Next Month  Free Press Journal
articles.full_text:
SEBI plans to extend clearing corporation interoperability to tender offers, share buybacks and offers for sale by November 2026. The proposed expansion aims to reduce brokers' compliance costs, eliminate duplicate clearing arrangements and improve capital efficiency. SEBI Chairperson Tuhin Kanta Pandey said settlement safety would remain a priority throughout implementation
The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) plans to expand clearing corporation interoperability to include tender offers, share buybacks and offers for sale (OFS) by the end of November 2026.
The proposed move is expected to simplify clearing operations, reduce compliance expenses and improve capital utilisation for stockbrokers.
According to a report by Moneycontrol, SEBI Chairperson Tuhin Kanta Pandey recently outlined the implementation timeline at an event organised by the BSE Brokers Forum (BBF).
He said the regulator was working to address gaps in the existing framework while maintaining settlement safety.
Aims to reduce brokers' clearing costs
Although most exchange-traded products already fall under clearing interoperability, certain transactions remain excluded.
Consequently, brokers handling these activities may need separate arrangements with BSE Clearing Corporation and NSE Clearing, depending on the exchange involved.
Maintaining multiple clearing relationships increases administrative expenses and regulatory obligations.
Brokers must also provide margins, deposits and prescribed net worth while paying annual clearing fees for individual segments.
These requirements can tie up capital that could otherwise support trading operations.
The Brokers' Industry Standards Forum (ISF) had raised the issue with SEBI, highlighting the financial and operational burden of parallel arrangements.
Extending interoperability to the remaining transaction categories could help brokers consolidate clearing obligations and use collateral more efficiently.
As per the report, market participants have welcomed the proposal, citing potential reductions in infrastructure costs and operational complexity.
Clearing interoperability expansion targeted for November
Introduced in June 2019, clearing corporation interoperability allows eligible trades executed across different stock exchanges to be cleared through an interconnected framework.
It enables cross-exchange netting of qualifying positions and reduces the need to maintain separate collateral pools.
However, the exclusion of tender offers, buybacks and OFS has limited these benefits for certain market activities.
SEBI now intends to close this gap by bringing these transactions within the existing system.
The regulator is targeting implementation by November-end, although specific operational arrangements will depend on the final framework.
If implemented as proposed, the expansion could create more uniform clearing procedures across exchanges while reducing unnecessary capital commitments.
SEBI has emphasised that improved efficiency must not compromise the safety of trade settlement.

articles.title: Getting Paid 5%+ to Wait: Treasury Yields at Multi-Year Highs Make Bonds Sexy Again - Moomoo
articles.summary: Getting Paid 5%+ to Wait: Treasury Yields at Multi-Year Highs Make Bonds Sexy Again  Moomoo
articles.full_text:
Oil Swings, Inflation Test Ahead: CPI Is Pivotal for Fed, as Well as the Market
3.5M Views · 74 Posts 
Markets have diverged this year. Equities have run: the $S&P 500 Index (.SPX.US)$ is up about 14% and the $NASDAQ 100 Index (.NDX.US)$ about 22% year-to-date (as of October 9). Long-term Treasuries have moved the other way — $iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT.US)$ is down roughly 10% in price, the $iShares 7-10 Year Treasury Bond ETF (IEF.US)$ about 7%. Rising yields cut bond prices, but they also reset the entry point: the $U.S. 10-Year Treasury Notes Yield (US10Y.BD)$ now pays 5.24% and the $U.S. 30-Year Treasury Bonds Yield (US30Y.BD)$ 5.60%, per the US Treasury's daily yield curve — multi-year highs.
Why Treasuries — and Why ETFs
Two ways to win: earn the income today, and capture capital gains if yields decline. The Fed under Chair Kevin Warsh raised rates 25bp in September — its first hike since 2023 — yet its own longer-run rate projection sits at roughly 3.25%, well below today's long-end yields. That gap is the opportunity.
The best part: you don't have to time the turn. Even if yields go nowhere, the coupon still pays roughly 5–5.6% a year — the floor case is a positive return. And with the economy steady and inflation above target, a yield collapse is unlikely near term anyway. First collect the income, then let the rate cycle pay the rest.
Direct bond buying is clunky: the secondary market runs in ~$1,000-per-bond lots with dealer markups buried in the price, and laddering takes manual work.
Treasury ETFs strip that out. One share from ~$22, intraday liquidity, monthly distributions, and fees of 0.03%–0.15% a year — no per-bond markups to dig for.
How Investors Are Already Positioning
The money has been moving. $iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT.US)$ — the long-end Treasury fund — took in roughly $6.5 billion in a single month this fall, and fund-flow trackers show weekly flows into Treasury funds hitting their biggest since April 2025, with money-market fund inflows the largest since April 2020 (BofA Global Research, EPFR data). Cash isn't just sitting out the bond market — it's rotating in.
Trading volume tells the same story: daily turnover in $iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT.US)$ peaked near 84 million shares around the October 1 yield peak, more than double its typical pace, and the past 20 sessions have averaged about 1.5× the prior three months.
The options book leans even harder. On TLT's latest session, nearly four call contracts traded for every put (put/call volume ratio of 0.26 on 1.13 million contracts), and open interest — the third-largest of any US underlying, behind only $SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY.US)$ and $NVIDIA (NVDA.US)$ — holds roughly two calls for every put.
Traders are paying up for the exposure: implied volatility sits near its 90th percentile. After the well-received October 8 bond auction, calls led the way — positioning for a bounce. Put open interest grew through the sell-off too, so it's not a one-sided bet, but the book stays call-heavy — and that size of positioning says long bonds are back on the menu.
Which Treasury ETF to Choose?
Duration — a fund's sensitivity to rate changes — is the main choice.
($Vanguard Short-Term Treasury ETF (VGSH.US)$, $Vanguard Intermediate-Term Treasury ETF (VGIT.US)$, $iShares U.S. Treasury Bond ETF (GOVT.US)$ and $Vanguard Long-Term Treasury ETF (VGLT.US)$ offer similar exposure at 0.03% fees.) Short-term funds like SGOV are cash alternatives with near-zero price risk. Intermediate funds such as IEF balance yield and stability. Long-duration funds like TLT are the rate-sensitive end: bigger income, bigger swings.
How Much Could You Make or Lose?
The rule of thumb: price change ≈ −duration × change in yield. If yields fall 50bp, a fund with a duration of 7 gains roughly 3.5%; one with duration 15 gains about 7.5%.
On a $10,000 investment (illustrative price effects, before income and costs — not forecasts):
Income reshapes that picture over a full year. The chart below, from Bianco Research, lays it out for a 10-year Treasury: a 100bp drop in yields hands you roughly 12.7% in total return over 12 months (coupon plus price gains); if yields go nowhere, you still collect about 5.3%; even a 100bp rise only puts you down around 1.5%, because the coupon absorbs most of the price hit.
The asymmetry is the point: rising yields mostly eat into the coupon, while falling yields stack price gains on top of it. That's the bond risk-reward profile — small downside, bigger upside — at the intermediate and long end of the curve alike.
Over shorter horizons, though, price moves dominate — duration cuts both ways. That creates a break-even cushion: $iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT.US)$ yield covers roughly a 38bp rise in yields per year (5.55 ÷ 15); $iShares 7-10 Year Treasury Bond ETF (IEF.US)$ covers about 73bp. $iShares 0-3 Month Treasury Bond ETF (SGOV.US)$ cushion is effectively its entire 3.72% yield. Short duration = income cushion; long duration = price torque. And long Treasuries have mild convexity — they gain slightly more than they lose for equal-sized yield moves.
Leveraged ETFs: Higher Risk
$Direxion Daily 20+ Year Treasury Bull 3X Shares ETF (TMF.US)$, $ProShares UltraShort 20+ Year Treasury (TBT.US)$ and $Direxion Daily 20+ Year Treasury Bear 3x Shares ETF (TMV.US)$ aim for 3×, −2× and −3× the daily moves of 20+ year Treasuries. Because they reset daily, returns over weeks can diverge sharply from 3× the index move — compounding erodes value in choppy, sideways markets. These are short-term tactical tools (expense ratios 0.90%–0.97%), not buy-and-hold positions.
Where Do Tresury Yields Go Next?   hat to Watch Next?Where Do Treasury Yields Go Next?
The calendar is dense: CPI on October 14, an FOMC meeting October 27–28, midterm elections November 3, the Treasury's quarterly refunding announcement November 4, and another FOMC December 8–9. Each can move yields — and with them, every fund above. 
With key economic data ahead, the bigger question is whether the 10-year Treasury yield has peaked or still has room to rise. Even a modest move could have a meaningful impact on long-duration Treasury ETFs.
Bottom Line
Match your rate view to your duration: expect yields to fall and want price gains — longer funds; just want the yield with minimal drama — stay short. Either way, today's coupons mean you're getting paid to wait — and paid well — while the rate cycle plays out.

articles.title: What do rising bond yields mean for income hunters? - AJ Bell
articles.summary: What do rising bond yields mean for income hunters?  AJ Bell
articles.full_text:
Income investors need to be aware of the significant opportunities and risks that can emerge across financial markets because of developments in the bond market.
UK and US government bond yields have been rising since the end of June. Investors have increasingly priced in the risk that higher energy prices could add to inflation pressures at a time when government borrowing remains elevated and central banks are reluctant to signal imminent rate cuts.
Bond yields move inversely to prices, meaning recent market moves have left many areas of the bond market offering more attractive income opportunities. This has important implications for investors deciding where to generate income, not only within bond markets but also across equities. It also has a direct influence on annuity rates.
Fundamentally, higher yields available today mean investors can earn income levels that were simply unavailable for much of the past decade.
What it means for Gilts and Treasuries
Gilts and Treasuries are terms to describe UK and US government bonds, respectively.
Yields on these bonds have moved higher as investors weigh the inflationary impact of higher energy prices, sizeable government borrowing requirements and the prospect that central banks may keep interest rates higher for longer. That in turn has pushed up expectations for central banks to hold interest rates or increase them.
In early September, Britain sold £4.25 billion worth of 30-year government bonds with the highest yield since comparable records began in 1998 at 5.82%.
At the time of writing in early October, the yield on 30-year gilts had topped 6%; the 10-year gilt traded at 5.51% which was the highest level since 2007; and the 10-year US Treasury yield traded at 5.34%, revisiting levels not seen since 2002.
To put those figures into perspective, on the same day the FTSE 100 index of UK shares offered a 3.3% prospective dividend yield based on forecast payouts for the next 12 months.
Income investors might therefore think that bonds are the obvious place to put their money given the superior yields. However, there are three key areas to consider.
If inflation continues to move higher, the price of existing bonds could fall and lead to new bonds being issued at even greater yields.
Higher borrowing needs or concerns about the public finances can push gilt or Treasury yields higher if investors demand additional compensation for lending to the government.
Investors buying long-dated bonds should remember that higher yields do not eliminate capital risk. If yields continue to rise, bond prices can fall sharply, particularly for bonds with decades left until maturity.
The other key factor to consider is the fact bonds offer a fixed coupon, whereas shares can offer a growing income stream as dividends are not fixed. Inflation can eat into the purchasing power of coupon payments, which in plain English means that the income you receive from the bond might buy you less in the future. Shares have an edge as dividends can often keep pace with, or even outpace, the rate of inflation.
It’s important to take a balanced view with dividends, nonetheless. While dividends have the potential to grow over time and help offset inflation, they are never guaranteed and can be reduced during economic downturns.
None of this means investors should avoid bonds altogether. High-quality bonds have historically helped to reduce portfolio volatility, although longer-dated bonds can still experience significant price fluctuations when yields move sharply. It’s simply about recognising that higher bond yields are not a free lunch for income investors.
What’s the key takeaway?
A decade ago, government bonds had a hard time grabbing retail investors’ attention. Now they are giving shares a run for their money thanks to more attractive yields and typically lower credit risk. A rapid decline in the oil price could quickly change interest rate expectations again and potentially lead to lower bond yields. There is little visibility on whether, or when, that might happen, which means investors should treat the current investment environment as a fluid situation.
Locking in high bond yields now gives you certainty of cash flows if you hold to maturity. Bond prices could rise if higher energy costs slow economic growth enough to encourage future interest-rate cuts. The flipside is that bond yields could rise further such as if investors demand higher yields if inflation proves persistent. In that scenario, bond (and bond fund) prices would fall. What really matters is the return after factoring in inflation.
Rising bond yields: winners and losers
Investors might be thinking about how the shift in the bond market affects what’s already in their portfolio and whether they should rejig holdings and consider new ones. There are some clear winners and losers from rising bond yields, as now discussed.
Potential winners:
New buyers of gilts and Treasuries: Investors buying gilts and Treasuries today can generally obtain higher yields than were available a few years ago, regardless of whether the bonds are newly issued or purchased in the secondary market. AJ Bell customers can subscribe to notifications to receive alerts about upcoming bond offers or view a range of bonds and gilts available for online dealing.
Cash savers: Central banks often keep interest rates unchanged, or raise them, to fight inflation. As of 2 October, the market, on balance, expects the Bank of England to raise interest rates to 4.25% by the end of 2026, implying more attractive returns on cash. AJ Bell’s Cash savings hub is an easy way to access competitive rates on cash.
Annuity buyers: Rising bond yields improve the rates on annuities, which provide a fixed income for life. Annuity providers typically invest heavily in long-term bonds and other income-producing assets to back their income promises, so higher yields feed into better returns for retirees buying these products now. Annuities provide clarity over how much cash you will get each month, but payouts stop at the point of death. In comparison, any money left in a pension at death is left in someone’s estate. Some people use part of their pension to buy an annuity and keep the rest invested – but note that you cannot sell an annuity once purchased.
Annuities can also come in different shapes and sizes, such as being inflation-linked and versions that pay out a proportion to your partner when you die. The amount you get depends on the size of your pension pot, your age, where you live, health, lifestyle, market conditions and the type of annuity to choose. It’s important to understand how each version works and to shop around for the best deal if you decide that annuities are right for you.
Investors reinvesting maturing bonds: With UK and US government bond yields at multi-year highs, it’s possible that investors with maturing bonds might be able to reinvest that money and get a higher yield than they’ve been receiving up to now.
Potential losers:
Existing bondholders: Higher yields make existing bonds less attractive, which typically pulls down their market price. Investors holding individual bonds to maturity would still receive par value at maturity, assuming the government or issuer remains solvent.
Long-duration bond funds: Many investors access bonds via bond funds rather than buying them individually. Bond funds come in different durations, with some investing in bonds that mature in the next one to five years (short duration). Others mature over longer periods (long duration) and are more sensitive to changes in interest rate expectations, making their prices more volatile.
Investors should distinguish between individual bonds and bond funds. A holder of an individual gilt who keeps it until maturity knows what income they will receive and will typically get the bond’s face value back at maturity.
Bond funds have no maturity date, and their value continues to fluctuate as managers buy and sell bonds, meaning rising yields can have a more persistent impact on capital values.
Bond proxy shares such as utilities, REITs (Real Estate Investment Trusts) and telecom providers: Bond proxies are companies whose earnings and dividends are relatively stable and predictable, like the coupon payments from a bond.
Rising bond yields can make their dividends less competitive and their valuations can come under pressure. Investors value shares based on the present value of future cash flows. Higher bond yields tend to push up discount rates used in valuation models. This reduces the present value of future dividends, leading to lower share prices.
Many companies classified as bond proxies have large debts and they can suffer from a higher cost of borrowing which often coincides with rising bond yields. Anyone owning an equity income fund should check the level of exposure to bond proxy-type companies in the portfolio.

French debt stress keeps the euro under pressure, though oversold conditions and positioning argue for a pause.
The Euro to Dollar exchange rate looks oversold heading into a week dominated by US inflation data and French debt stress.

CIBC watches 1.1111, the midpoint of the 2025 trading range, as the next downside level.
Below there, the 61.8% retracement of the 2025-2026 rally at 1.1090 offers the next support.
Above: EUR/USD with Fibonacci retracements of the January 2025 to January 2026 rally.
How Much of France Is in the Price?
All this 'chart chatter' will count for nought if the massive flows wrought by global bond markets are not brought to heel. In this regard, France is the main driver, and how much bad news is already in the price determines the outlook.
The spread between French and German ten-year borrowing costs, the favoured measure of French stress, has nearly doubled since January.
Lloyds argues the market has priced too much.
"If the pace of convergence implicitly assumed proves slower than markets currently anticipate, the balance of risks may become increasingly asymmetric, leaving French assets more vulnerable to positive surprises than additional bad news," says Lloyds.
Commonwealth Bank of Australia says the pair stays vulnerable to further spread widening should French government debt risks escalate.
Goldman Sachs is tactically wary of extrapolating the euro's selloff, forecasting EUR/USD at 1.14 in three months, though it says risks are skewed lower on sustained European fiscal contagion.
Barclays' risk premium model points to a level well below 1.05 over the medium term.
"Our risk premium model still points to a premium of about 3.5% in EURUSD," says Barclays.
Positioning Into US Inflation
France is the wildcard and the U.S. inflation print due Wednesday is the scheduled calendar risk for dollar-based exchange rates. The consensus expects U.S. headline CPI inflation to rise to 3.6% year-on-year in September when the figures land.
"Positioning is rarely a good factor on which to make investment decisions, but whenever we have ignored it in favour of macro dynamics, nearly always we have gotten the tactical price action very wrong," says Barclays, noting the market has swung from very short to quite long dollars during this rally.
That suggests risks are skewed to dollar weakness on an on-target or below-target print. Upside price action would likely require a meaningful beat.
If the market judges France is now understood, and U.S. inflation behaves, some short-term tactical upside is possible, and positioning does not favour dollar strength into the inflation print.
A recovery would target the 38.2% retracement at 1.1361, while a break below 1.1135 opens 1.1090.

articles.title: How Africa Can Leverage the US-China Thaw - Businessamlive
articles.summary: How Africa Can Leverage the US-China Thaw  Businessamlive
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON, DC—Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the US produced a two-month extension of the current bilateral trade truce—and little else. Nonetheless, both leaders signaled that they want a more stable relationship ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November and the G20 in Miami in December. This creates an opportunity for emerging and developing in Africa and elsewhere.
For African countries, conditions have rarely been tighter than they are today. In sovereign-debt markets, they pay a premium on foreign-currency borrowing that macroeconomic fundamentals and default risk cannot fully explain. Kenya’s $1.5 billion ten-year Eurobond issuance last year was priced at 9.5%. In late 2024, Nigeria faced rates of 9.6% on 6.5-year Eurobonds and over 10% on ten-year notes. Sub-Saharan Africa routinely faces borrowing rates above 15%, compared to 3–5% in advanced economies.
US Treasury yields have increased significantly since those bonds were priced. Since the US Federal Reserve’s interest-rate hike last month, the ten-year Treasury yield has climbed above 5.3%—the highest level since 2002. Every basis point added to Treasury yields increases the cost of an African Eurobond. With another Fed rate hike possible this month, the next wave of African debt issuance—including a planned $815 million Eurobond in Kenya—will almost certainly cost even more.
Crucially, however, China is moving in the opposite direction: its ten-year government-bond yield has fallen to roughly 1.67%, and the gap with the ten-year Treasury is near a record high. Chinese capital markets are starting to look a lot more appealing.
Africa’s financing needs are huge, not least to meet rising energy demand. Though the continent boasts some of the world’s richest solar resources, and solar panels and batteries have never been cheaper (thanks in part to Chinese investment), capital costs have hampered renewable deployment in Africa. The International Energy Agency estimates that cutting capital costs by just one percentage point would save $150 billion per year in clean-energy financing globally.
Dollar borrowing at ultra-high rates constrains investment in domestic infrastructure, making renewables look artificially expensive compared to fossil fuels. It also contributes to a structural currency mismatch. China produces roughly 80% of the world’s solar modules, and imports of Chinese solar panels by African countries (not including South Africa) tripled from mid-2023 to mid-2025. These purchases are priced in renminbi or dollars, and the projects they power are often financed with expensive dollar debt, even as they produce local-currency revenues.
How can the US-China thaw help? When the two powers were locked in open confrontation, cooperation with either could look to the other like defection, creating real political risks. But détente means that Africa could combine American gas partnerships—crucial to provide baseload power, feedstock for fertilizer, and export earnings—with access to Chinese solar supply chains. A US that hosts Xi at a state dinner cannot justify penalizing African governments for doing with China, and vice versa. Geopolitical maneuvering room would enable Africa to ensure that each partner does what it does best: the US supports natural-gas development, and China provides solar and storage hardware.
Crucially, Africa must finance each investment in the currency that matches it. This is where Asian capital markets come in. African sovereigns and corporates can tap China’s onshore and offshore bond markets through Panda bonds (renminbi bonds issued by foreign entities in mainland China) and Dim Sum bonds (renminbi bonds issued offshore, notably in Hong Kong). Both Indonesia and Portugal have issued Dim Sum bonds in the last 15 months. The interest-rate divergence has sharpened each of these bonds’ three advantages.
The first is cost. Panda issuers now have a pricing edge of nearly 300 basis points over comparable dollar Eurobonds. Every 100 basis points saved is worth roughly $10 million a year in debt service on a $1 billion issue. Renminbi-bond issuers may still achieve lower all-in financing costs than issuers of US dollar- or euro-denominated bonds, even after accounting for hedging costs. With the gap between US and Chinese ten-year benchmarks now around 350 basis points, this advantage will only grow.
Given that a large share of Africa’s clean-energy capital spending goes to Chinese products, the second advantage is that borrowing in renminbi aligns liabilities with procurement costs and reduces exposure to dollar swings. The same logic can extend to gas.
The third advantage is diversification. Chinese regulators have urged domestic institutions to reduce their exposure to US Treasuries, and Chinese institutional investors are searching for yield. Well-structured, guaranteed African paper can meet that demand while reducing the continent’s dependence on a single set of Western capital markets.
Recent precedents are encouraging. In 2023, Egypt’s debut three-year Panda bond raised CN¥3.5 billion ($478 million) at 3.5%—jointly guaranteed by the African Development Bank and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB)—to fund clean transport and water projects. Afreximbank followed with a CN¥2.2 billion Panda bond in March 2025.
Beyond China, Japan’s Samurai market offers yen funding. Already, Kenya’s 2026–27 borrowing plan includes $881 million in Japan-linked financing, anchored by a $500 million Samurai bond. The time has come for Africa to begin building a genuine Asian funding curve.
There are still plenty of challenges ahead. Renminbi or yen debt is still foreign-currency debt serviced from local-currency revenues. Panda issuance also carries upfront costs, as the bonds are subject to Chinese ratings, audits, regulatory approvals, and rules on the use of proceeds. No financing structure can substitute for credible fiscal policy, macroeconomic reform, and investor confidence. And, of course, US-China relations could change.
To increase the chances of success, multilateral development banks should standardize and scale up partial credit guarantees for Panda, Dim Sum, and Samurai issuances. African treasuries should secure regulatory approvals and investor mandates before the upcoming G20 meeting. Meanwhile, the US and China should provide joint guarantees for African energy through the US Development Corporation, the AIIB, and the New Development Bank, in addition to supporting the African Development Bank and the World Bank Group in their efforts to increase energy access.
With dollar borrowing costs soaring and Chinese rates near record lows, the cost of inertia is high. Developing and emerging economies should borrow where capital is cheapest, and lock in the savings before the window closes.

articles.title: Trimming the Sails: Communicating My Reaction Function - Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland
articles.summary: Trimming the Sails: Communicating My Reaction Function  Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland
articles.full_text:
Introduction
Thank you to the National Association of Business Economics for having me and for choosing Cleveland for this year’s annual meeting.1
Cleveland exists because of its water access. In 1796, surveyor Moses Cleaveland chose the spot where the Cuyahoga River meets Lake Erie as the ideal site for settlement because it offered immediate access to inland and Great Lakes shipping lanes. The lake and river serve as foundational anchors for industrial growth in Cleveland. The winding Cuyahoga River and lakefront enabled the rise of massive steel mills, lumber yards, oil refineries, and the growth of manufacturing industries that followed.
But today, as we look over Lake Erie, I’m reminded of a more recreational function of the water. As any Clevelander will tell you, summers here are glorious. In the warmer months, boating on the lake is a popular pastime. From my office here in downtown Cleveland, I can see sailboats navigating the wind and waves amid often fast-changing weather conditions. And it strikes me that the skills needed to manage these maritime changes are not unlike the skills we monetary policymakers must employ in our own work as we adjust to economic changes in real time.
To navigate these changes, we must have both a destination and a course. Our destination of maximum employment and price stability is clear, but the course needed to reach that destination is not set; it is conditional on how the economy evolves. Based on current conditions, forecasts, and risks to the inflation side of our mandate, I believe a restrictive policy stance will be needed for us to reach our destination in a timely fashion.
Before I dive in further, I should note that the views I express today are my own and not necessarily those of the Federal Reserve System or my colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC).
Setting the Sails and Setting Monetary Policy
While the destination may be clear when you set sail, even with the best forecast, you don’t know in advance exactly how strong the wind will blow, how hard the waves will break, or how many tacks it will take. Sailing requires continually reading conditions—and adjusting the sails and the tiller in response—in order to reach your destination in time for dinner.
There are many parallels for policymakers. For one, we are clear on the destination. In the US, Congress has charged the FOMC with effectively promoting the goals of maximum employment and stable prices. Our reaction function explains how we respond to the winds, waves, and weather to reach our destination.
The course that we have to set for this $32 trillion economy depends on the numerous decisions of households, businesses, and governments that can shift from day to day or year to year. We, as policymakers, must be as informed as possible about all elements of the economy to achieve our objectives. Because of this, I find myself wearing multiple hats in my role at the Cleveland Fed.
First, there’s leading a Reserve Bank of more than a thousand people who are doing the work needed to help keep the economy running, like providing payments services to commercial banks, acting as fiscal agent to the US government, and ensuring fit currency is always available for the public.
Second, there’s thinking hard with our team of PhD economists about research, data, financial conditions, the economic outlook, and monetary policy.
And finally, there’s getting outside the Bank’s walls and into the Fourth Federal Reserve District. This means spending time in the communities of Ohio, western Pennsylvania, eastern Kentucky, and the northern panhandle of West Virginia. I want to hear directly from the people living and working in the Fourth District so that I can better understand how they experience the economy in their everyday lives.
I do a lot of listening in these meetings, but I also want the people of the Fourth District to better understand the role of the Fed in their lives. In these conversations, I explain our commitment to price stability and maximum employment and how our actions might play a role in their decisions to borrow and save.
This brings me to today’s topic: communication, specifically, why I think policymakers need to explain the information and the thought process behind our interest rate decisions. Explaining my reaction function is not a prediction for policy. It’s describing how I expect policy to adjust as conditions change.
Like in sailing, I can explain where I’m going, what I’m seeing, and how I might respond to shifting winds or waves or weather. But what I ultimately do depends on lots of factors, many of which are outside my control.
Why Explaining My Reaction Function Matters
While the Federal Reserve Act defines the destination, the FOMC’s Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy provides the coordinates. Over the longer run, 2 percent PCE inflation is most consistent with price stability. Maximum employment is the highest level of employment that can be achieved while sustaining price stability. While these objectives are generally complementary, the consensus statement says we follow a balanced approach in promoting them when they are not.
A reaction function describes how monetary policy typically responds to economic fundamentals to reach the goals. For example, when inflation is too high, monetary policymakers tend to raise interest rates to bring inflation back down. When the labor market is weak, policymakers tend to reduce interest rates to stimulate economic activity.
Simple monetary policy rules capture these reactions in a stylized way. The original Taylor rule provides one reaction function that relates the federal funds rate to the equilibrium real rate, inflation, and the state of the real economy. There are many simple policy rules, and the Cleveland Fed’s website presents a variety of predictions from rules that past research has found useful.2
Such policy rules are a starting point, but they have inherent limitations because the real world is complex. So speeches, like this one, and other communications help to flesh out my reaction function and explain its conditionality on current circumstances, along with how policy may need to respond if the winds suddenly shift.
Explaining the reaction function is accountability through transparency. As a policymaker, I believe I have a responsibility to the public to explain why I make the decisions I make. Transparency has the benefit of allowing consumers, businesses, and financial markets to make better-informed decisions.
Information on the reaction function also helps the public and financial markets anticipate policy actions, albeit with conditionality. If a consumer or a business borrows or lends money under a mistaken belief about how policymakers will or won’t move interest rates, that mistake could prove costly at the individual level and potentially for the economy writ large. Understanding the reaction function helps to limit unproductive volatility in financial markets. When markets don’t understand the reaction function, asset prices can lurch sharply as investors are caught wrong-footed.
On the other hand, when financial markets know how policy is likely to react, they re-price in anticipation of these moves. Between FOMC meetings, financial markets respond to data both based on the outlook for the real economy, but mainly on what the FOMC will do, not what it should do.
Explaining my thinking about policy also helps align expectations about the future. Many theoretical models used in macroeconomics posit that expectations play a crucial role in determining outcomes. In particular, being clear on the destination and the FOMC’s plan regarding how and when to get there helps anchor longer-term inflation expectations in line with our 2 percent objective, something which, in turn, makes it easier to achieve that outcome. History shows that it is very costly to restore the inflation anchor once it has been lost.
I want to draw a sharp line here. A reaction function is not forward guidance. Treating the two as interchangeable can turn a well-meaning explanation of logic into the expectations of a promise.
Forward guidance is a specific tool: an explicit commitment about the future path of policy, typically deployed when the federal funds rate is at the effective lower bound, like it was following the financial crisis.
Economists have used a different sailing reference here to compare forward guidance to Odysseus tying himself to the mast of his ship to safely pass by the Sirens—Cleveland’s soon to be WNBA team. With Odyssean forward guidance, the commitment itself is the point. In this case, policy plans to deviate from the usual reaction function in an effort to provide more accommodation than is otherwise possible at the effective lower bound. A reaction function promises no such commitment. It instead indicates how policy is likely to proceed, conditional on a specific set of circumstances.
What Feeds My Reaction Function
With the dual mandate as the destination, I see my reaction function as trimming the sails and minding the tiller to respond to changing conditions so we safely reach our destination. When feasible, I generally think it’s preferable to make smaller adjustments, and to do so relatively quickly, rather than to wait and risk needing a larger course correction.
So let me walk you through my reaction function and the variables I incorporate in making my monetary policy decisions. Specifically, my function relies on economic data, financial conditions, forecasts, risks, and what I hear directly from people living in this economy.
The gold standard, hard economic data are indispensable. They can also take time to produce. I consult a wide variety of official data releases along with other indicators from the private sector to see where the economy is today.
Researchers at the Cleveland Fed have developed multiple data series and indicators that we update on a regular basis.

articles.title: This is how the informal market closes in Cuba: the dollar and the euro gain ground at the end of the day - CiberCuba
articles.summary: This is how the informal market closes in Cuba: the dollar and the euro gain ground at the end of the day  CiberCuba
articles.full_text:
At 8:00 PM, local Cuban time, closes this Sunday, October 11, 2026, with the dollar and the euro rising compared to the previous day. The Cuban peso shows no signs of recovery, and foreign currencies remain firm at high levels. The MLC, with limited data available, provides only a rough reference.
The U.S. dollar is quoted at 785 Cuban pesos (CUP) at the close of this Sunday. This represents an increase of 2.5 pesos compared to the previous day, when the average value was 783 CUP. In the weekly comparison, the dollar remains at the same levels as seven days ago, when it also stood at 785 CUP. Over the monthly horizon, the U.S. currency has accumulated a rise of 93.5 pesos compared to the 692 CUP recorded 30 days ago, a 13.5% increase, although it is worth noting that this comparison may partially reflect adjustments in the index methodology. The dollar continues to set the tone of the informal market in a context of structural currency shortages.
The euro closes the day at 878 Cuban pesos (CUP), which indicates an increase of 2 pesos compared to the previous day's close, when it was at 876 CUP. In the weekly comparison, the European currency decreases by just 1 peso from 879 CUP a week ago, a virtually negligible variation. Compared to 30 days ago, the euro has gained 93 pesos, equivalent to an increase of 11.9%, although this figure should be viewed with the same caution as the dollar regarding potential methodological adjustments. It is established as the most expensive currency in the Cuban parallel market, surpassing the dollar by 93 pesos.
The MLC is around 535 Cuban pesos (CUP), although this value should be considered merely as a reference since the data available during this time frame is limited. Compared to the previous day, it has increased by 38 pesos, and in the weekly comparison, it has risen by 3 pesos from the 532 CUP of seven days ago. Without physical existence, its use is limited to the state-run businesses that accept it, which restricts its circulation compared to cash currencies.
- Exchange rate of the dollar USD to CUP: 785 CUP.
- Exchange rate of the euro EUR to CUP: 878 CUP.
- Exchange rate of MLC to CUP: 535 CUP (reference value, limited data).
The official exchange rate of the Central Bank of Cuba (Segment III), at 698 CUP per dollar and 781 CUP per euro, remains well below the rates that apply in everyday transactions in the informal currency market. The gap between the official dollar rate and the informal one exceeds 87 pesos; in the case of the euro, the difference approaches 97 pesos.
Exchange Rate Evolution
Although Segment III was presented as a more flexible exchange mechanism, its official rate remains far from that of the informal market and fails to meet the real demand for foreign currency from the population. In the past month, the official dollar has risen from 651 to 698 CUP, and the official euro from 757 to 781 CUP, a surge that highlights the sustained pressure on the Cuban peso even within the institutional channel.
In an environment of sustained inflation, low state salaries, and increasing partial dollarization of the economy, every fluctuation in the informal market directly affects internal prices and the purchasing power of Cubans. This Sunday’s close confirms that foreign currencies remain strong against a peso that cannot find its footing.
The informal currency market in Cuba operates outside of the state's financial institutions, through networks of buying and selling between individuals. Although the Cuban regime does not officially acknowledge it, it is the market that practically determines the real purchasing power of Cubans.
The Exchange Rate of CiberCuba is an index of the informal Cuban market created from the automated analysis of thousands of currency trading posts in Telegram and Facebook groups. The calculation disregards atypical offers and spam messages, weighs each transaction based on its age, and consolidates a representative value that is updated several times a day.
